items.title: LitPivot: Developing research ideas through dynamic contextualization within the literature landscape
items.content:
📄 Paper

Encountering a new paper can change a research idea's trajectory. The researcher may discover that someone has already addressed their proposed contribution, or find an unresolved problem in the paper that inspires a new direction of inquiry.

We call this process a literature-initiated pivot: a change in research direction prompted by reading prior work. It connects two activities that researchers often have to manage separately: developing an idea and deciding which literature to measure it against.

With collaborators at the University of Pennsylvania, we developed LitPivot, a system that helps researchers navigate these pivots. Using papers retrieved through Asta Paper Finder, LitPivot organizes literature around the part of a proposal being edited, offers critiques supported by excerpts from selected studies, and suggests revisions that researchers can accept, edit, or reject. LitPivot is intended to be used for early-stage research ideation, but the idea could possibly extend to longer writing tasks (i.e., writing the introduction section of a paper).

In a study with 17 researchers, domain experts rated research ideas developed with LitPivot as better grounded in the literature than those developed with a text editor and an AI chat tool. Participants also perceived their revised research ideas as more novel and useful, and reported a stronger understanding of the surrounding literature.

LitPivot will be presented at UIST 2026 in Detroit. Read the paper here.

Why pivoting is hard

Research ideas evolve through engaging with the literature. In our analysis of meeting notes from four completed computer science research projects, we identified 21 literature-initiated pivots across all four projects. These fell into two types: differentiating an idea from existing work to establish an idea’s novelty, and aligning an idea with existing work to build on it. This project itself went through two pivots before we settled on its contributions.

These changes can be difficult to navigate. In a formative study, five researchers developed proposals using a text editor and standard search tools. They struggled to develop their ideas while critically evaluating them against the literature. When a paper challenged an idea’s novelty, they wanted concrete suggestions for how to revise it, supported by prior work. These findings shaped LitPivot’s assessments, which pair literature-supported critiques with specific suggestions for revising the selected part of an idea.

How LitPivot works

In LitPivot, a researcher starts by writing a short proposal in an editor and enabling what we call facet highlighting, which segments an articulated idea into different facets (i.e., a problem, contribution, and evaluation). To check a proposed facet, the researcher clicks that segment in the draft. An adjacent panel groups related papers based on the selected facet (e.g., grouping papers by the evaluation methods they use when the evaluation facet is selected) and highlights the most relevant groups. The researcher selects papers, requests an assessment, and reviews a suggested revision alongside excerpts supporting the critique. The literature is then reranked based on relevance to the revised facet.

In particular, LitPivot separates a research idea into its problem, proposed contribution, and evaluation plan. Each facet has its own set and relevance ranking of related literature. LitPivot groups retrieved papers around the facet being edited, letting the researcher choose which ones the system should use to assess the draft.

Alongside scientific-writing environments such as Prism and agentic assistants such as Claude Code, LitPivot explores a new workflow for developing an early research idea: choosing literature to assess it against, using that evidence to revise it, and reconsidering which papers matter as the idea changes. Its paper groups and linked critiques make those steps explicit for each part of the proposal, while researchers control both the draft and the evidence used to assess it.

For a problem statement, LitPivot looks for evidence that the problem exists and reasons it matters. To assess a proposed contribution, it compares what the selected papers have already addressed with the limitations and future work they describe, looking for remaining gaps. For an evaluation plan, it checks whether the proposed tests address the research question and how similar work has been evaluated. The system then suggests a rewrite with supporting quotes attached.

Changing one facet of an idea can leave another out of date. LitPivot flags passages that may need revision, such as an evaluation plan that no longer adequately evaluates a revised contribution. Researchers can accept, edit, or reject suggestions, and request new papers or refresh the literature ranking as their proposal develops.

Paraphrased example from one study participant.

Our findings

In our lab study, 17 researchers each developed one assigned idea with LitPivot and another with a baseline tool—a text editor and an AI tool for asking questions about selected papers. Both conditions used the same collection of papers. Two domain experts, unaware of which system had been used, rated the resulting proposals on a single criterion: how well they used relevant literature to support and justify the idea. Proposals developed with LitPivot received higher ratings.

Participants in the same study also reported a stronger understanding of the surrounding literature and greater self-reported improvements in their ideas’ novelty and usefulness with LitPivot than with the baseline. Domain experts also reviewed the participants’ ideas and rated the ideas revised using LitPivot to be significantly better grounded in relevant literature.

One participant in our lab study started with a proposal to generate consistent, factual synthetic medical notes. LitPivot identified consistency across multiple hospital visits as a potential gap in the selected literature. The participant reviewed abstracts and removed papers about single-visit notes. After another assessment, they narrowed the proposal to detecting contradictions across notes from multiple visits. The example shows how revising an idea and choosing the literature used to assess it can inform each other.

In a follow-up study, five researchers used LitPivot on their own ongoing projects during 30-minute sessions. Participants used LitPivot across multiple project phases, not just at the beginning. Two used it to vet new ideas against the literature, while three used it to refine the framing of more mature ideas. One researcher highlighted how seeing parallel concepts from different domains helped them reframe their contribution.

These studies suggest that LitPivot can support both early exploration and the refinement of an existing research direction.

Supporting scientific discovery

At Ai2, we’re developing AI to help researchers formulate testable ideas and examine the evidence behind them. Asta supports that effort through theory generation from published findings (Theorizer), synthesis, and hypothesis generation and testing on data (AutoDiscovery), while HARPA generates promising hypotheses informed by emerging research trends. Scideator lets researchers recombine elements of prior work into new ideas and assess their novelty, and IdeaSynth supports iterative refinement with feedback grounded in the literature.

Our recent study, Old Ideas, Novel Problems, examines the limits of automated novelty evaluation, showing how small prompt changes can alter an AI judge’s verdict on the same ideas. LitPivot extends this line of work by making the choice of relevant literature part of the revision process. Researchers can change which papers they use to assess a proposal as their idea develops, then use critiques and supporting excerpts to decide how to revise it. The system connects those decisions across the proposal’s problem, contribution, and evaluation plan.

We hope insights from LitPivot help scientists build on existing knowledge and turn early ideas into new contributions to their fields.

items.title: Does Your Model Run on AWS Trainium? Look It Up
items.content:
Update on GitHub

In a previous post, we introduced TorchNeuron, the native PyTorch backend for AWS Trainium (the torch-neuronx package). With it, Transformers runs its own modeling code on Trainium, as it does on any other device, so any Transformers model on the Hub may run. Which ones actually do?

The torch-neuronx model support Space answers that question for the most popular models on the Hub. It tells you whether a model runs unmodified on Trainium, and gives you the script to run it yourself.

Look up a model

The Space opens on the Selected view: our own selection of models picked among the top models on the Hub by downloads and by trending score. Each row gives the result, the number of Trainium cores the model is sharded over, the wall time of the run (compilation included) and the peak device memory.

To look up a given model, switch to the Trending or Downloads view and type part of its name. These views follow the Hub's own rankings, one task at a time, whether a model was tested or not. When a model was left out on purpose, the Space tells you why (most of the time it was not prioritized, sometimes it is truly incompatible). You can also pick the versions of the Neuron compiler (neuronx-cc) and of Transformers to look at.

At the time of writing, only Transformers models are tested, and our selection is limited to text-generation and image-text-to-text models. We plan to expand to diffusers, sentence transformers, and other transformers tasks.

Run it yourself

Select a model to see how to run it. The Space lists the Neuron stack the model was tested on, the packages to install on top of it, and the run.py script that ran. The script follows the recipe of the TorchNeuron announcement: it loads the model with from_pretrained, sharded when it needs to be, then generates with a static cache and torch.compile(backend="neuron").

On a Trainium2 (trn2) instance with that stack, for example in the AWS Neuron Deep Learning Container, install the packages, then run:

python3 run.py

No need for torchrun: the script launches its own torch.distributed ranks when the model is sharded.

A first run starts by compiling the model's graphs. To skip that step, copy the graphs the same compiler built during the test, from the public NEFF cache bucket. The Space gives you the command, with the right compiler version:

hf buckets sync hf://buckets/aws-neuron/torch-neuronx-neff-cache/neuronxcc-<version> /tmp/neff_cache

What "runs" means

Each test loads the model on a trn2 instance, sharded over the smallest number of Trainium cores that can hold its weights. Most models are sharded with tensor parallelism. Mixture-of-experts models without a tensor-parallel plan use expert parallelism only. The test then generates 32 tokens and checks them. On a single core, the tokens are compared with those of a CPU run of the same checkpoint. When the model is sharded, a small judge model checks that the text is fluent English.

At the time of writing, only models that fit on 4 Trainium2 devices are tested, which means 16 cores at most. A PASS says nothing about throughput, or about longer generations.

The results are a dataset

Everything the Space shows comes from the public aws-neuron/torch-neuronx-model-support dataset, with one Parquet file per pair of neuronx-cc and library versions.

Each row holds a model's result, the error when it failed, the versions of the whole stack and the run.py that ran. You can query it directly:

import pandas as pd

df = pd.read_parquet("hf://datasets/aws-neuron/torch-neuronx-model-support/data")
df[df.model_id == "Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B"][["neuronx_cc", "library", "library_version", "neuron_cores", "result"]]

The dataset card gives the exact meaning of each result.

Next time you wonder whether a model runs on Trainium, look it up.

items.title: Turning Database Grading into RL Rewards: Post-Training Agents with ThinkingBox
items.content:
This is the follow up to our first blog post, The Agent Said It Was Done. The Database Disagreed. ThinkingBox-Training is now available on GitHub.

We built ThinkingBox to evaluate an agent's work by comparing the final database state with the expected outcome. We then used the same kind of executable signal as a reward on training tasks outside ThinkingBox-Bench. For Qwen3.8-27B, average success rose from 51.70% to 60.78%, while tasks completed correctly on all twenty attempts rose from 38 to 107 with 50 GRPO steps.

Figure 1. ThinkingBox turns executable checks of terminal database state into rewards for post-training agents on tasks outside ThinkingBox-Bench.

This is a joint blog by Microsoft and Hugging Face, special thanks to Mirco Milletari and Xiang Jiang from Microsoft, Sergio Paniego from Hugging Face and our former intern Zhuochun Li (University of Pittsburgh) for co-authoring/reviewing efforts.

We built ThinkingBox to catch agents that say they are done when they are not.

Each of its 507 tasks in ThinkingBox-Bench (our benchmark dataset) hands an agent a real backend and a set of tools, lets it work, then checks what really changed in the database. In the first post, we caught a model closing a customer's ticket as resolved while the carrier exception behind it was still open. Nine competent-looking tool calls, one wrong database row.

Then we noticed what we had built. For most tasks, an executable check can return 1 or 0 directly from the final database state. That is not just a grader. This can be a reward function.+

So we constructed a training pool from ThinkingBox-format tasks outside the benchmark and used their executable outcomes as rewards. The catch was choosing which tasks are suitable for agent training: most tasks are either already solved or hopeless for the model in front of you, and both teach it nothing.

Difficulty is policy-relative: a task is hard for the current model only until that model learns it.

We call this offline policy-relative difficulty. We estimated each task's success probability once using the base policy before training and kept the selected training pool fixed throughout the run.

What happened after training

We used offline policy-relative difficulty to build the training pool, then fine-tuned Qwen3.8-27B with GRPO for 50 steps. To recap, we evaluate each of the 507 benchmark tasks 20 times. pass@1 measures average success across all 10,140 attempts. pass@20 measures the share of tasks solved at least once. Observed 20/20 measures the share of tasks that pass every recorded attempt.

Table 1. Qwen3.8-27B results before and after 50 steps of GRPO on the offline-selected training pool.

Metric Base RL fine-tuned Change
Observed 20/20 38 (7.50%) → 107 (21.10%) +69 tasks
pass@1 (successful attempts) 5,242 (51.70%) → 6,163 (60.78%) +9.08 pt
pass@20 (tasks solved at least once) 453 (89.35%) → 446 (87.97%) −7 tasks

Training sharply increased repeatable success, with a small decline in at-least-once coverage. The rest of the post explains how we selected practice tasks, built the reward loop, and measured that tradeoff.

What does that improvement look like on one task? A traveler requests a room downgrade, but company policy requires manager approval first. Before training, the agent changed the booking and issued refunds without approval in 15 of 20 attempts. After RL fine-tuning, it preserved the booking and payment state in all 20.

Figure 2. One corporate hotel-booking task, 20 attempts per model. The base Qwen3.8-27B model changed the booking without required manager approval in 15 attempts. The RL fine-tuned model preserved booking and payment state in all 20; all expected records matched in 19.

Contents

  1. What the benchmark found, in sixty seconds
  2. Results: the dependability column moved
  3. Where the gains landed
  4. What dependability costs
  5. The training loop
  6. Offline policy-relative difficulty
  7. What earns a reward
  8. Run the training stack
  9. Where this goes next

In a hurry? The headline result is above. The implementation is in Run the training stack.

What the benchmark found, in sixty seconds

ThinkingBox-Bench grades agents on the database records they leave behind. Each of its 507 tasks starts a real backend, hands the agent a set of MCP tools and a simulated LLM user with private context, and at the end runs executable checks against the terminal database state. Checks are against the backend record that needs to be correct, not the specific tool calls. This incentivizes the model to discover possibly new solution paths rather than “rediscover” the human-backed solution, that might be suboptimal albeit correct.

In our first post we ran eighteen models through that benchmark twenty times each and reported a gap that headline accuracy hides. Kimi-K3 solved 93.89% of tasks at least once but completed only 68 of 507 tasks (13.41%) on all twenty recorded attempts. Claude Opus 5 inverted it: narrower coverage, far more consistency.

And bigger or better model did not close it. Claude Opus 5.5 scored 0.66 percentage points higher than Claude Opus 5 on pass@1, yet passed exactly the same number of tasks, 241, on all twenty attempts. That gain in headline accuracy bought zero additional dependability.

If you are choosing a model for work that touches production database records, pass@1 should not be read alone. Observed 20/20 shows which tasks succeed on every attempt, which is closer to what production reliability requires.

The executable terminal-state verdict was also the training reward. Before unpacking the training loop, here is what changed on the sealed benchmark.

Results: the dependability column moved

After training Qwen3.8-27B, we evaluated the selected step-50 checkpoint on the 507-task benchmark it had never trained on. The 507 tasks represent an out-of-distribution test set: their domains, databases, and most MCP tools were not encountered during RL training.

Table 2. ThinkingBox-Bench pass@1 (%) by domain, for selected models from our first blog's Table 2 and our fine-tuned model for different domains and overall. Observed 20/20 numbers are over the entire benchmark with 507 tasks. Each model is evaluated on all 507 tasks for 20 repeated trials. Bold marks the column leader; underline marks the runner-up.

Model Retail Auto insurance Travel Neobank Consulting Overall Observed 20/20
Claude Opus 5.5 80.97 68.40 54.28 71.25 61.58 67.16 241 (47.53%)
Claude Opus 5 80.71 65.80 49.95 70.62 66.19 66.50 241 (47.53%)
GPT-5.4 76.33 62.65 68.12 65.34 54.60 65.36 128 (25.25%)
GPT-5.6 Sol 67.65 65.30 60.34 59.09 57.52 61.91 82 (16.17%)
Qwen3.8-27B RLFT 67.91 56.45 62.69 62.40 54.51 60.78 107 (21.10%)
Claude Sonnet 4.6 72.35 54.40 58.94 56.39 54.31 59.19 102 (20.12%)
GPT-6 Astra 71.73 46.55 55.87 60.87 56.83 58.31 231 (45.56%)
Kimi-K3 82.24 50.80 61.83 41.35 51.63 57.37 68 (13.41%)
Qwen3.8-27B 64.03 47.85 53.41 47.88 45.69 51.70 38 (7.50%)

The headline result is the observed-20/20 row in Table 1. A 27B model that initially completed 38 (7.5%) of ThinkingBox-Bench on every attempt now completes 107 (21.1%) on every attempt, almost thrice. For comparison, observed 20/20 for Kimi-K3 is 68, GPT-5.4 with 128, GPT-6 Astra has 231, and Claude Opus 5.5 leads with 241.

Average success and repeatability produce different orderings. In Table 2, we notice that GPT-5.6 Sol scored slightly higher on pass@1 than the RL fine-tuned Qwen3.8-27B (61.91% versus 60.78%) but passed fewer tasks on all 20 recorded attempts: 82 versus 107. Claude Sonnet 4.6 scored lower on pass@1, at 59.19%, yet passed nearly the same number of tasks every time, at 102. Neither metric alone captures the full picture.

The observed pattern is consistent with sharpening: repeatable success rose while at-least-once coverage fell slightly. This is in-line with prior work. One explanation is that probability distribution moved toward trajectories that work repeatedly while some low-probability paths disappeared.

Overall, the model did not become broader. It became more repeatable. The next question is where those gains landed.

Where the gains landed

Figure 3. Domain-level base scores, RLFT scores, and percentage-point changes. Green change cells show gains and red cells show declines; blue shading indicates the score level within each metric.

Pass@1 and observed 20/20 rose in all five domains. Pass@20 was mixed: it increased in neobank and consulting, but declined in retail, travel, and auto insurance. Auto insurance had the largest breadth loss (−7.0 points), while retail had the largest observed-20/20 gain (+24.5 points).

What dependability costs

The first post priced consistency using simple math: divide the estimated cost of the full 20-run campaign by the number of tasks the model passed every single time.

Cost per dependable task = estimated cost of the 507 × 20 campaign ÷ tasks passing 20/20

Applying the same cost math to the fine-tuned checkpoint's measured token usage:

Table 3. Estimated evaluation cost and dependability for base and RL fine-tuned Qwen3.8-27B. Cost per successful attempt divides total estimated campaign cost (507 x 20) by the number of passing attempts.

Measure Base RL fine-tuned Change
Campaign cost, 20 runs $925.80 → $855.58 −7.6%
Cost per successful attempt $0.177 → $0.139 −21.4%
Tasks passing 20/20 38 → 107 2.8× as many
Cost per dependable task $24.36 → $8.00 −67.2%

At $8.00 per dependable task, the fine-tuned model came close to GPT-5.4 ($6.80), GPT-6 Astra ($7.45), and Claude Opus 5.5 ($7.80) in the companion comparison.

The single-attempt view

Figure 4 prices cost per successful attempt against pass@1.

Figure 4. The golden arrow traces Qwen3.8-27B base pareto cost position to the RLFT (diamond): pass@1 rises from 51.70% to 60.78% while estimated cost per successful attempt falls from $0.177 to $0.139. Ringed circles mark the Pareto cost frontier.

The move places the fine-tuned checkpoint close to GPT-5.6 Sol, although GPT-5.6 Sol remains cheaper and slightly higher on pass@1. Four models priced in our paper fall outside the plotted range.

The dollar values are a comparative serving index, not invoice or cloud bills. Serving the fine-tuned checkpoint would be the same as the base model. The calculation includes model inference cost, and excludes training run and policy-probe cost for curating the training dataset.

These results tell us what moved. The next sections explain the training loop and why selecting the right tasks matters the most.

The training loop

Figure 5. The six stages, now in context: candidate tasks feed in, the first three run once offline, the last three repeat for every group in the training run. The trained checkpoint is evaluated against ThinkingBox-Bench.

Selection runs once, offline, against the base policy model, i.e in this case Qwen3.8 27B; training then uses that fixed pool that has been curated. The dashed amber arrow in Figure 5 marks the path we did not take: re-probing difficulty during the training run.

Every rollout is a complete episode, not a text completion. It gets a fresh backend, an isolated MCP session, and GPT-5 Chat as the simulated user. Most rewards come from deterministic terminal-state checks; a minority of narrow rubric requirements can invoke the configured judge (GPT-5 Chat).

Training and evaluation must interpret Qwen output identically. That includes reasoning extraction, tool calls, argument typing, rendering, and isolated task state. Otherwise the reward measures a different agent from the one evaluated. The shared interpretation code is in trainer/core/tb_interpret.py.

For the reference run, we ran full-parameter RL fine-tuned Qwen3.8-27B on 187 tasks using token-mean GRPO. Each update generated 18 groups of 8 rollouts, or 144 episodes, across 24 H100s. Training ran synchronously with parameter and optimizer offload; AdamW used a 1e-6 learning rate and zero weight decay. We ran the training for 50 steps.

Zero-variance groups were replaced DAPO-style during training. System errors were handled separately: a backend timeout is not an incorrect agent outcome, so affected groups were refilled rather than scored as failures.

That explains how retained tasks were trained. The remaining question is which tasks entered the training pool.

Offline policy-relative difficulty

Before diving deep into the selection of training tasks, a disclaimer:

No ThinkingBox-Bench task was included in the RL training pool. The benchmark was reserved for evaluation.

ThinkingBox-Bench is out-of-distribution relative to the RL training pool: its domains, databases, policies, and most tools were not encountered during RL training. The two sets still share the ThinkingBox framework, simulated-user machinery, executable terminal-state grading, a few common tools, and a similar task style. These shared elements limit the scope of the transfer claim.

Why selection matters comes down to one arithmetic fact about GRPO. If all eight rollouts fail, the reward vector is [0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0]. If all eight succeed, it is [1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1]. In either case, centering within the group produces no task-reward advantage because no trajectory did better than another.++

A mixed group such as [0, 0, 0, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1] supplies the contrast GRPO can learn from. That distinction is expensive for a stateful agent: every rollout provisions an isolated backend, runs a real tool session, and calls a separate model to play the user.

The question that shaped this work was therefore not only which model or optimizer? It was: which candidate tasks should enter the fixed training pool?

We used an offline pass-rate filter on the posterior to select the training pool. It estimates which tasks are likely to produce contrasting terminal rewards under the base policy.

So we probe. Each candidate task is run repeatedly against the base policy model. The plain-language rule is simple: tasks the model always fails are unlikely to teach it yet; tasks it always passes are already learned; tasks it solves sometimes are where outcomes can provide contrast.

Estimating difficulty from limited probes

Each candidate task is run n times, producing k successes. We model its latent success probability with Jeffreys posterior probability:

success probability | k successes in n probes ~ Beta(k + ½, n − k + ½)

Figure 6. Offline policy-relative difficulty is estimated from repeated base-policy probes and used to retain tasks likely to produce contrasting rewards.

We partition the unit interval into five buckets with boundaries at 0.08, 0.40, 0.60, and 0.90, chosen as hyperparameters for these runs. Each task is assigned to the bucket containing the greatest posterior mass:

  • Rarely solved [0, 0.08): drop
  • Difficult [0.08, 0.40): keep
  • Intermediate [0.40, 0.60): keep
  • Frequently solved [0.60, 0.90): keep for full-parameter RLFT
  • Nearly always solved [0.90, 1]: drop

Further details are in Appendix C.4 of our ThinkingBox paper.

One task, end to end

Figure 7. Zooming in, one task through all six stages: GPT-5.4 screening, base-model probes, difficulty classification, a rollout group, terminal-state grading, and a GRPO update.

Figure 7 follows one candidate task that can potentially enter the training pool. For the Qwen3.8 27B full-parameter pool, GPT-5.4 first served as a solvability screen. The base policy then succeeded on few of the probes e.g 3 of 8, producing a Beta(3.5, 5.5) posterior. Its largest mass, 54.0%, fell in the Difficult band.

When sampled for training, the task produced the mixed reward group [0, 0, 0, 0, 1, 1, 1, 1]. Successful trajectories therefore received above-mean task advantage and failed trajectories below-mean advantage, giving GRPO contrast to learn from. A different policy model could place the same task in a different difficulty band.

The final Qwen3.8-27B curated training pool contained 187 tasks.

What earns a reward

Nothing about the trajectory. The reward is the task's own executable verdict.

When an episode ends, the sandbox extracts what actually changed in the backend and runs the task's deterministic checks against the terminal state. Any trajectory that produces the correct end state passes. Wrong, missing, or extra side effects fail. The reward is 1 or 0.

In the benchmark, the database grader can be thought of as the “examiner”: it caught agents that reported success and left the wrong record. In training, the same kind of check can be seen as the “teacher” on a different, disjoint set of tasks.

Two reward paths, one binary verdict

  • Executable check (the large majority). When the required outcome is represented in terminal state or side effects, a deterministic test accepts or rejects it; no LLM judge call is needed.
  • Judge-assisted check (a minority). When a narrow requirement cannot be determined cleanly from database state, the configured LLM judge answers a binary rubric question used by the executable test.

Run the training stack

We release the data-selection, rollout, reward, and Verl integration used to train Qwen3.8-27B in microsoft/thinkingbox-training. The repository README is the entry point. The detailed guides are:

  • docs/data-preparation.md for task hydration, policy probes, benchmark exclusion, and train/validation splitting;
  • docs/reference-q38-run.md for the validated 24-H100 Qwen3.8 configuration;
  • docs/evaluation.md for merging a checkpoint and running ThinkingBox-Bench 507 x 20.

Before you start

Tested on Linux and WSL with Python 3.12 and uv. You need NVIDIA GPUs with a compatible CUDA/NCCL stack, a local Qwen3.8-27B checkpoint, and OpenAI-compatible endpoints for the simulated user and judge. The validated reference configuration uses 3 nodes x 8 H100 GPUs; smaller custom configurations depend on model size, context length, and rollout concurrency.

The public sample task list exercises the interface. It is not the private 187-task training pool used for the reported run. Supply an authorized training source that remains disjoint from the public benchmark.

Install

Keep the three repositories side by side:

mkdir -p ~/thinkingbox-workspace
cd ~/thinkingbox-workspace

git clone https://github.com/microsoft/thinkingbox.git
git clone https://github.com/microsoft/thinkingbox-data.git
git clone --branch main https://github.com/microsoft/thinkingbox-training

git -C thinkingbox checkout 892964e7226044e5463ad188da119df838f4bec1
git -C thinkingbox-data checkout thinkingbox-bench-v1.0

Create the validated environment

The released stack targets Linux, Python 3.12, Verl 0.9.0, and the pinned package lock:

cd ~/thinkingbox-workspace/thinkingbox-training

uv venv --python 3.12
source .venv/bin/activate

uv sync --frozen --extra fast --extra tracking --extra eval-proxy
uv pip install -e ../thinkingbox
uv pip install --config-settings editable-mode=compat \
  -e ../thinkingbox-data/servers/thinkingbox_tools
uv pip install --config-settings editable-mode=compat \
  -e ../thinkingbox-data/servers/tb_business_ops_servers_202606

python scripts/prepare_verl.py --dest .deps/verl --install
python scripts/verify_verl_install.py
uv pip check

The final two commands should report a verified patched Verl checkout and no broken requirements. Do not run another automatic package sync afterward: it can replace the patched source installation with the vanilla Verl wheel.

Prepare the training data

Start with the publicly provided samples, or add your own authorized dataset in ThinkingBox format. Then run the repository's preparation script:

cd ~/thinkingbox-workspace/thinkingbox-training
source .venv/bin/activate
python data/prepare_data.py --help

The script aggregates policy probes, applies offline policy-relative difficulty filters and benchmark exclusions, and writes the selected train.yaml and test.yaml files. docs/data-preparation.md documents the input fields, loader contract, and complete command.

Configure and inspect the launch

Follow docs/reference-q38-run.md to start Typesense and the MCP servers, configure the simulated user and judge, set the model, task-list, checkpoint, and topology variables, and prepare the Ray cluster. Keep credentials in runtime secret injection rather than committed files or shell history.

Before allocating a training job, use the guide's dry-run command:

DRY_RUN=true ./scripts/run_train.sh \
  trainer.total_training_steps=50 \
  trainer.save_freq=5

It must exit zero without starting Ray or allocating GPUs. Read the emitted python -m verl.trainer.main_ppo command and every resolved override before launching the run.

Train

The launcher configures training; it does not provision hosts. On the reference three-node topology, export the same environment on every node, mount CHECKPOINT_DIR at the same absolute path, then start Ray:

# head node
ROLE=head NODE_IP="$HEAD_IP" GPUS_PER_NODE=8 \
  ./scripts/start_ray.sh

# each worker node
ROLE=worker NODE_IP="$WORKER_IP" \
  HEAD_ADDRESS="$HEAD_IP:6379" GPUS_PER_NODE=8 \
  ./scripts/start_ray.sh

After ray status reports all 24 GPUs, launch once from the head node:

export RAY_ADDRESS=auto
export GPUS=0,1,2,3,4,5,6,7

./scripts/run_train.sh \
  trainer.project_name=thinkingbox-training \
  trainer.experiment_name=q38-full-rlft \
  trainer.total_training_steps=50 \
  trainer.save_freq=5

Evaluate the checkpoint through OpenEnv

The first ThinkingBox post covers Typesense, the MCP Session Proxy, and OpenEnv setup. Merge the trained checkpoint following docs/evaluation.md, then serve it with vLLM.

From the OpenEnv repository root, set MERGED_MODEL to the merged model directory and THINKINGBOX_DATA to the pinned benchmark checkout. The historical checkpoint evaluation used this eight-A100 serving configuration:

vllm serve "$MERGED_MODEL" \
  --served-model-name q38-rlft \
  --host 127.0.0.1 \
  --port 8001 \
  --tensor-parallel-size 8 \
  --dtype bfloat16 \
  --max-model-len 262144 \
  --gpu-memory-utilization 0.85 \
  --max-num-seqs 16 \
  --max-num-batched-tokens 8192 \
  --language-model-only \
  --enable-chunked-prefill \
  --enable-prefix-caching \
  --reasoning-parser qwen3 \
  --enable-auto-tool-choice \
  --tool-call-parser qwen3_xml

In a separate terminal, start the OpenEnv compatibility proxy for the Qwen chat template from the ThinkingBox Training checkout. It listens on port 8014 and forwards to vLLM on 8001:

cd ~/thinkingbox-workspace/thinkingbox-training
source .venv/bin/activate
bash scripts/launch_sysmerge.sh

Keep it running during evaluation. From another terminal, check readiness:

curl --fail http://127.0.0.1:8014/readyz

Update the agent entry in the existing thinkingbox.yaml; retain its MCP, simulated-user, and judge configuration:

orchestrator:
  agent_model:
    type: aoai
    endpoint_url: http://127.0.0.1:8014/v1/chat/completions
    deployment: q38-rlft
    credential:
      type: api-key
      api_key: <your_api_key>
    is_reasoning: true
    temperature: 1.0
    top_k: 20
    top_p: 0.95
    max_completion_tokens: 8192
    timeout: 1800

Start OpenEnv as in the first post, with OPENENV_TB_CONFIG pointing to this thinkingbox.yaml and OPENENV_TB_DATASET to $THINKINGBOX_DATA. Once /ready succeeds, run the full protocol of 507 tasks × 20 attempts:

uv run --project envs/thinkingbox_env --frozen \
  thinkingbox-eval \
  --config "$PWD/thinkingbox.yaml" \
  --base-url http://127.0.0.1:8000 \
  --dataset "$THINKINGBOX_DATA" \
  --output q38-rlft-full.jsonl \
  --errors-output q38-rlft-full-errors.jsonl \
  --repeat 20 \
  --coverage-profile full \
  --aggregate-output q38-rlft-full-aggregate.json \
  --message-timeout 1800

The full profile validates all 10,140 expected task/repetition keys before aggregation.

Where this goes next

The useful part of this work is not one Qwen3.8-27B checkpoint. It is the training loop and training data curation that turns executable outcomes into rewards.

If you are training or evaluating an agent that touches real database records:

  1. Probe before you train. Take your own agent task set, run the base policy against it n times, and look at the band histogram. In our experience teams often have not inspected this distribution, and it is usually more lopsided than expected.
  2. Check your parity. Replay the same recorded model output through the training and evaluation parsers, and verify that both extract identical tool names and arguments. Otherwise, training may reward behavior that evaluation interprets differently.
  3. Report both coverage and repeatability. State how many tasks pass at least once in k attempts and how many pass all k. A model that occasionally finds a solution is not necessarily one that repeats it consistently.

Further details can be found in the following links:

  • Environment: envs/thinkingbox_env
  • OpenEnv: ThinkingBox environment documentation
  • Framework: microsoft/thinkingbox · tutorial
  • Benchmark: microsoft/thinkingbox-data · v1.0 release
  • Dataset viewer: microsoft/ThinkingBox-Bench
  • Paper: arXiv:2608.19741 or HF
  • RL training: microsoft/thinkingbox-training
  • Blog: The Agent Said It Was Done. The Database Disagreed.

             Jiang, Xiang and Olafsson, Kjartan and Guy, Tommy},

Disclaimer: every task in the public benchmark is a synthetic reconstruction. The workflows and policies are modeled on real enterprise agent patterns; the customers are not real.

ThinkingBox, ThinkingBox-Bench and ThinkingBox-Training is built by the Microsoft Copilot Studio team in partnership with Toloka with collaborators from the University of Pittsburgh, Northwestern University, Columbia University and UC Irvine who interned at Microsoft. Questions are welcome in the comments section below or on github or by email at firstnamelastname@microsoft.com.

 This is the follow up to our first blog post, The Agent Said It Was Done. The Database Disagreed. ThinkingBox-Training is now available on GitHub.
We built ThinkingBox to evaluate an agent's work by comparing the final database state with the expected outcome. We then used the same kind of executable signal as a reward on training tasks outside ThinkingBox-Bench. For Qwen3.8-27B, average success rose from 51.70% to 60.78%, while tasks completed correctly on all twenty attempts rose from 38 to 107 with 50 GRPO steps.

Figure 1. ThinkingBox turns executable checks of terminal database state into rewards for post-training agents on tasks outside ThinkingBox-Bench.




This is a joint blog by Microsoft and Hugging Face, special thanks to Mirco Milletari and Xiang Jiang from Microsoft, Sergio Paniego from Hugging Face and our former intern Zhuochun Li (University of Pittsburgh) for co-authoring/reviewing efforts.


We built ThinkingBox to catch agents that say they are done when they are not.
Each of its 507 tasks in ThinkingBox-Bench (our benchmark dataset) hands an agent a real backend and a set of tools, lets it work, then checks what really changed in the database. In the first post, we caught a model closing a customer's ticket as resolved while the carrier exception behind it was still open. Nine competent-looking tool calls, one wrong database row.
Then we noticed what we had built. For most tasks, an executable check can return 1 or 0 directly from the final database state. That is not just a grader. This can be a reward function.+ 
So we constructed a training pool from ThinkingBox-format tasks outside the benchmark and used their executable outcomes as rewards. The catch was choosing which tasks are suitable for agent training: most tasks are either already solved or hopeless for the model in front of you, and both teach it nothing.
Difficulty is policy-relative: a task is hard for the current model only until that model learns it.
We call this offline policy-relative difficulty. We estimated each task's success probability once using the base policy before training and kept the selected training pool fixed throughout the run.




What happened after training


We used offline policy-relative difficulty to build the training pool, then fine-tuned Qwen3.8-27B with GRPO for 50 steps. To recap, we evaluate each of the 507 benchmark tasks 20 times. pass@1 measures average success across all 10,140 attempts. pass@20 measures the share of tasks solved at least once. Observed 20/20 measures the share of tasks that pass every recorded attempt.

What does that improvement look like on one task? A traveler requests a room downgrade, but company policy requires manager approval first. Before training, the agent changed the booking and issued refunds without approval in 15 of 20 attempts. After RL fine-tuning, it preserved the booking and payment state in all 20.

What the benchmark found, in sixty seconds


ThinkingBox-Bench grades agents on the database records they leave behind. Each of its 507 tasks starts a real backend, hands the agent a set of MCP tools and a simulated LLM user with private context, and at the end runs executable checks against the terminal database state. Checks are against the backend record that needs to be correct, not the specific tool calls. This incentivizes the model to discover possibly new solution paths rather than “rediscover” the human-backed solution, that might be suboptimal albeit correct.
In our first post we ran eighteen models through that benchmark twenty times each and reported a gap that headline accuracy hides. Kimi-K3 solved 93.89% of tasks at least once but completed only 68 of 507 tasks (13.41%) on all twenty recorded attempts. Claude Opus 5 inverted it: narrower coverage, far more consistency.
And bigger or better model did not close it. Claude Opus 5.5 scored 0.66 percentage points higher than Claude Opus 5 on pass@1, yet passed exactly the same number of tasks, 241, on all twenty attempts. That gain in headline accuracy bought zero additional dependability.
If you are choosing a model for work that touches production database records, pass@1 should not be read alone. Observed 20/20 shows which tasks succeed on every attempt, which is closer to what production reliability requires.
The executable terminal-state verdict was also the training reward. Before unpacking the training loop, here is what changed on the sealed benchmark.

Overall, the model did not become broader. It became more repeatable. The next question is where those gains landed.




Where the gains landed



Figure 3. Domain-level base scores, RLFT scores, and percentage-point changes. Green change cells show gains and red cells show declines; blue shading indicates the score level within each metric.
Pass@1 and observed 20/20 rose in all five domains. Pass@20 was mixed: it increased in neobank and consulting, but declined in retail, travel, and auto insurance. Auto insurance had the largest breadth loss (−7.0 points), while retail had the largest observed-20/20 gain (+24.5 points). 




What dependability costs


The first post priced consistency using simple math: divide the estimated cost of the full 20-run campaign by the number of tasks the model passed every single time.
Cost per dependable task = estimated cost of the 507 × 20 campaign ÷ tasks passing 20/20
Applying the same cost math to the fine-tuned checkpoint's measured token usage:
Table 3. Estimated evaluation cost and dependability for base and RL fine-tuned Qwen3.8-27B.  Cost per successful attempt divides total estimated campaign cost (507 x 20) by the number of passing attempts.
Measure
      Base
      
      RL fine-tuned
      Change
    
Campaign cost, 20 runs
      $925.80
      →
      $855.58
      −7.6%
    
Cost per successful attempt
      $0.177
      →
      $0.139
      −21.4%
    
Tasks passing 20/20
      38
      →
      107
      2.8× as many
    
Cost per dependable task
      $24.36
      →
      $8.00
      −67.2%
    
At $8.00 per dependable task, the fine-tuned model came close to GPT-5.4 ($6.80), GPT-6 Astra ($7.45), and Claude Opus 5.5 ($7.80) in the companion comparison.




The single-attempt view


Figure 4 prices cost per successful attempt against pass@1.

Figure 4. The golden arrow traces Qwen3.8-27B base pareto cost position to the RLFT (diamond): pass@1 rises from 51.70% to 60.78% while estimated cost per successful attempt falls from $0.177 to $0.139. Ringed circles mark the Pareto cost frontier.
The move places the fine-tuned checkpoint close to GPT-5.6 Sol, although GPT-5.6 Sol remains cheaper and slightly higher on pass@1. Four models priced in our paper fall outside the plotted range.
The dollar values are a comparative serving index, not invoice or cloud bills. Serving the fine-tuned checkpoint would be the same as the base model. The calculation includes model inference cost, and excludes training run and policy-probe cost for curating the training dataset.
These results tell us what moved. The next sections explain the training loop and why selecting the right tasks matters the most.




The training loop



Figure 5. The six stages, now in context: candidate tasks feed in, the first three run once offline, the last three repeat for every group in the training run. The trained checkpoint is evaluated against ThinkingBox-Bench.
Selection runs once, offline, against the base policy model, i.e in this case Qwen3.8 27B; training then uses that fixed pool that has been curated. The dashed amber arrow in Figure 5 marks the path we did not take: re-probing difficulty during the training run.
Every rollout is a complete episode, not a text completion. It gets a fresh backend, an isolated MCP session, and GPT-5 Chat as the simulated user. Most rewards come from deterministic terminal-state checks; a minority of narrow rubric requirements can invoke the configured judge (GPT-5 Chat).
Training and evaluation must interpret Qwen output identically. That includes reasoning extraction, tool calls, argument typing, rendering, and isolated task state. Otherwise the reward measures a different agent from the one evaluated. The shared interpretation code is in trainer/core/tb_interpret.py.
For the reference run, we ran full-parameter RL fine-tuned Qwen3.8-27B on 187 tasks using token-mean GRPO. Each update generated 18 groups of 8 rollouts, or 144 episodes, across 24 H100s. Training ran synchronously with parameter and optimizer offload; AdamW used a 1e-6 learning rate and zero weight decay. We ran the training for 50 steps.
Zero-variance groups were replaced DAPO-style during training. System errors were handled separately: a backend timeout is not an incorrect agent outcome, so affected groups were refilled rather than scored as failures.
That explains how retained tasks were trained. The remaining question is which tasks entered the training pool.




Offline policy-relative difficulty


Before diving deep into the selection of training tasks, a disclaimer:
No ThinkingBox-Bench task was included in the RL training pool. The benchmark was reserved for evaluation.
ThinkingBox-Bench is out-of-distribution relative to the RL training pool: its domains, databases, policies, and most tools were not encountered during RL training. The two sets still share the ThinkingBox framework, simulated-user machinery, executable terminal-state grading, a few common tools, and a similar task style. These shared elements limit the scope of the transfer claim.
Why selection matters comes down to one arithmetic fact about GRPO. If all eight rollouts fail, the reward vector is [0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0]. If all eight succeed, it is [1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1]. In either case, centering within the group produces no task-reward advantage because no trajectory did better than another.++
A mixed group such as [0, 0, 0, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1] supplies the contrast GRPO can learn from. That distinction is expensive for a stateful agent: every rollout provisions an isolated backend, runs a real tool session, and calls a separate model to play the user.
The question that shaped this work was therefore not only which model or optimizer? It was: which candidate tasks should enter the fixed training pool?
We used an offline pass-rate filter on the posterior to select the training pool. It estimates which tasks are likely to produce contrasting terminal rewards under the base policy.
So we probe. Each candidate task is run repeatedly against the base policy model. The plain-language rule is simple: tasks the model always fails are unlikely to teach it yet; tasks it always passes are already learned; tasks it solves sometimes are where outcomes can provide contrast.




Estimating difficulty from limited probes


Each candidate task is run n times, producing k successes. We model its latent success probability with Jeffreys posterior probability:
success probability | k successes in n probes  ~  Beta(k + ½, n − k + ½)

Figure 6. Offline policy-relative difficulty is estimated from repeated base-policy probes and used to retain tasks likely to produce contrasting rewards.
We partition the unit interval into five buckets with boundaries at 0.08, 0.40, 0.60, and 0.90, chosen as hyperparameters for these runs. Each task is assigned to the bucket containing the greatest posterior mass:
Rarely solved [0, 0.08): drop
Difficult [0.08, 0.40): keep
Intermediate [0.40, 0.60): keep
Frequently solved [0.60, 0.90): keep for full-parameter RLFT
Nearly always solved [0.90, 1]: drop
Further details are in Appendix C.4 of our ThinkingBox paper.




One task, end to end



Figure 7. Zooming in, one task through all six stages: GPT-5.4 screening, base-model probes, difficulty classification, a rollout group, terminal-state grading, and a GRPO update.
Figure 7 follows one candidate task that can potentially enter the training pool. For the Qwen3.8 27B full-parameter pool, GPT-5.4 first served as a solvability screen. The base policy then succeeded on few of the probes e.g 3 of 8, producing a Beta(3.5, 5.5) posterior. Its largest mass, 54.0%, fell in the Difficult band.
When sampled for training, the task produced the mixed reward group [0, 0, 0, 0, 1, 1, 1, 1]. Successful trajectories therefore received above-mean task advantage and failed trajectories below-mean advantage, giving GRPO contrast to learn from. A different policy model could place the same task in a different difficulty band.
The final Qwen3.8-27B curated training pool contained 187 tasks. 




What earns a reward


Nothing about the trajectory. The reward is the task's own executable verdict.
When an episode ends, the sandbox extracts what actually changed in the backend and runs the task's deterministic checks against the terminal state. Any trajectory that produces the correct end state passes. Wrong, missing, or extra side effects fail. The reward is 1 or 0.
In the benchmark, the database grader can be thought of as the “examiner”: it caught agents that reported success and left the wrong record. In training, the same kind of check can be seen as the “teacher” on a different, disjoint set of tasks.
Two reward paths, one binary verdict
Executable check (the large majority). When the required outcome is represented in terminal state or side effects, a deterministic test accepts or rejects it; no LLM judge call is needed.
Judge-assisted check (a minority). When a narrow requirement cannot be determined cleanly from database state, the configured LLM judge answers a binary rubric question used by the executable test.




Run the training stack


We release the data-selection, rollout, reward, and Verl integration used to train Qwen3.8-27B in microsoft/thinkingbox-training. The repository README is the entry point. The detailed guides are:
docs/data-preparation.md for task hydration, policy probes, benchmark exclusion, and train/validation splitting;
docs/reference-q38-run.md for the validated 24-H100 Qwen3.8 configuration;
docs/evaluation.md for merging a checkpoint and running ThinkingBox-Bench 507 x 20.




Before you start


Tested on Linux and WSL with Python 3.12 and uv. You need NVIDIA GPUs with a compatible CUDA/NCCL stack, a local Qwen3.8-27B checkpoint, and OpenAI-compatible endpoints for the simulated user and judge. The validated reference configuration uses 3 nodes x 8 H100 GPUs; smaller custom configurations depend on model size, context length, and rollout concurrency.
The public sample task list exercises the interface. It is not the private 187-task training pool used for the reported run. Supply an authorized training source that remains disjoint from the public benchmark.




Install


Keep the three repositories side by side:
mkdir -p ~/thinkingbox-workspace
cd ~/thinkingbox-workspace

git clone https://github.com/microsoft/thinkingbox.git
git clone https://github.com/microsoft/thinkingbox-data.git
git clone --branch main https://github.com/microsoft/thinkingbox-training

git -C thinkingbox checkout 892964e7226044e5463ad188da119df838f4bec1
git -C thinkingbox-data checkout thinkingbox-bench-v1.0





Create the validated environment


The released stack targets Linux, Python 3.12, Verl 0.9.0, and the pinned package lock:
cd ~/thinkingbox-workspace/thinkingbox-training

uv venv --python 3.12
source .venv/bin/activate

uv sync --frozen --extra fast --extra tracking --extra eval-proxy
uv pip install -e ../thinkingbox
uv pip install --config-settings editable-mode=compat \
  -e ../thinkingbox-data/servers/thinkingbox_tools
uv pip install --config-settings editable-mode=compat \
  -e ../thinkingbox-data/servers/tb_business_ops_servers_202606

python scripts/prepare_verl.py --dest .deps/verl --install
python scripts/verify_verl_install.py
uv pip check

The final two commands should report a verified patched Verl checkout and no broken requirements. Do not run another automatic package sync afterward: it can replace the patched source installation with the vanilla Verl wheel.




Prepare the training data


Start with the publicly provided samples, or add your own authorized dataset in ThinkingBox format. Then run the repository's preparation script:
cd ~/thinkingbox-workspace/thinkingbox-training
source .venv/bin/activate
python data/prepare_data.py --help

The script aggregates policy probes, applies offline policy-relative difficulty filters and benchmark exclusions, and writes the selected train.yaml and test.yaml files. docs/data-preparation.md documents the input fields, loader contract, and complete command.




Configure and inspect the launch


Follow docs/reference-q38-run.md to start Typesense and the MCP servers, configure the simulated user and judge, set the model, task-list, checkpoint, and topology variables, and prepare the Ray cluster. Keep credentials in runtime secret injection rather than committed files or shell history.
Before allocating a training job, use the guide's dry-run command:
DRY_RUN=true ./scripts/run_train.sh \
  trainer.total_training_steps=50 \
  trainer.save_freq=5

It must exit zero without starting Ray or allocating GPUs. Read the emitted python -m verl.trainer.main_ppo command and every resolved override before launching the run.




Train


The launcher configures training; it does not provision hosts. On the reference three-node topology, export the same environment on every node, mount CHECKPOINT_DIR at the same absolute path, then start Ray:
# head node
ROLE=head NODE_IP="$HEAD_IP" GPUS_PER_NODE=8 \
  ./scripts/start_ray.sh

# each worker node
ROLE=worker NODE_IP="$WORKER_IP" \
  HEAD_ADDRESS="$HEAD_IP:6379" GPUS_PER_NODE=8 \
  ./scripts/start_ray.sh

After ray status reports all 24 GPUs, launch once from the head node:
export RAY_ADDRESS=auto
export GPUS=0,1,2,3,4,5,6,7

./scripts/run_train.sh \
  trainer.project_name=thinkingbox-training \
  trainer.experiment_name=q38-full-rlft \
  trainer.total_training_steps=50 \
  trainer.save_freq=5





Evaluate the checkpoint through OpenEnv


The first ThinkingBox
post
covers Typesense, the MCP Session Proxy, and OpenEnv setup. Merge the trained
checkpoint following
docs/evaluation.md,
then serve it with vLLM.
From the OpenEnv repository root, set MERGED_MODEL to the merged model
directory and THINKINGBOX_DATA to the pinned benchmark checkout. The
historical checkpoint evaluation used this eight-A100 serving configuration:
vllm serve "$MERGED_MODEL" \
  --served-model-name q38-rlft \
  --host 127.0.0.1 \
  --port 8001 \
  --tensor-parallel-size 8 \
  --dtype bfloat16 \
  --max-model-len 262144 \
  --gpu-memory-utilization 0.85 \
  --max-num-seqs 16 \
  --max-num-batched-tokens 8192 \
  --language-model-only \
  --enable-chunked-prefill \
  --enable-prefix-caching \
  --reasoning-parser qwen3 \
  --enable-auto-tool-choice \
  --tool-call-parser qwen3_xml

In a separate terminal, start the OpenEnv compatibility proxy for the Qwen chat template from the ThinkingBox Training checkout. It listens on port 8014 and forwards to vLLM on 8001:
cd ~/thinkingbox-workspace/thinkingbox-training
source .venv/bin/activate
bash scripts/launch_sysmerge.sh

Keep it running during evaluation. From another terminal, check readiness:
curl --fail http://127.0.0.1:8014/readyz

Update the agent entry in the existing thinkingbox.yaml; retain its MCP, simulated-user, and judge configuration:
orchestrator:
  agent_model:
    type: aoai
    endpoint_url: http://127.0.0.1:8014/v1/chat/completions
    deployment: q38-rlft
    credential:
      type: api-key
      api_key: <your_api_key>
    is_reasoning: true
    temperature: 1.0
    top_k: 20
    top_p: 0.95
    max_completion_tokens: 8192
    timeout: 1800

Start OpenEnv as in the first post, with OPENENV_TB_CONFIG pointing to this
thinkingbox.yaml and OPENENV_TB_DATASET to $THINKINGBOX_DATA. Once
/ready succeeds, run the full protocol of 507 tasks × 20 attempts:
uv run --project envs/thinkingbox_env --frozen \
  thinkingbox-eval \
  --config "$PWD/thinkingbox.yaml" \
  --base-url http://127.0.0.1:8000 \
  --dataset "$THINKINGBOX_DATA" \
  --output q38-rlft-full.jsonl \
  --errors-output q38-rlft-full-errors.jsonl \
  --repeat 20 \
  --coverage-profile full \
  --aggregate-output q38-rlft-full-aggregate.json \
  --message-timeout 1800

The full profile validates all 10,140 expected task/repetition keys before
aggregation.




Where this goes next


The useful part of this work is not one Qwen3.8-27B checkpoint. It is the training loop and training data curation that turns executable outcomes into rewards.
If you are training or evaluating an agent that touches real database records:
Probe before you train. Take your own agent task set, run the base policy against it n times, and look at the band histogram. In our experience teams often have not inspected this distribution, and it is usually more lopsided than expected.
Check your parity. Replay the same recorded model output through the training and evaluation parsers, and verify that both extract identical tool names and arguments. Otherwise, training may reward behavior that evaluation interprets differently.
Report both coverage and repeatability. State how many tasks pass at least once in k attempts and how many pass all k. A model that occasionally finds a solution is not necessarily one that repeats it consistently.
Further details can be found in the following links:
Environment: envs/thinkingbox_env
OpenEnv: ThinkingBox environment documentation
Framework: microsoft/thinkingbox · tutorial
Benchmark: microsoft/thinkingbox-data · v1.0 release
Dataset viewer: microsoft/ThinkingBox-Bench
Paper: arXiv:2608.19741 or HF
RL training: microsoft/thinkingbox-training
Blog: The Agent Said It Was Done. The Database Disagreed.

             Tsai, Liang-Chun and Ferri, Nicola and Milletari, Mirco and Liu, Jiaxiang and

             Jiang, Xiang and Olafsson, Kjartan and Guy, Tommy},

  url     = {https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.19741}

Disclaimer: every task in the public benchmark is a synthetic reconstruction. The workflows and policies are modeled on real enterprise agent patterns; the customers are not real.
ThinkingBox, ThinkingBox-Bench and ThinkingBox-Training is built by the Microsoft Copilot Studio team in partnership with Toloka with collaborators from the University of Pittsburgh, Northwestern University, Columbia University and UC Irvine who interned at Microsoft. Questions are welcome in the comments section below or on github or by email at firstnamelastname@microsoft.com.
+ A minority of tasks also include narrow binary rubric requirements for outcomes that the database cannot capture cleanly; those checks can invoke the configured LLM judge.
++ That zero-gradient problem has a standard batch-time fix: oversample, discard the degenerate groups, refill. The full-parameter run did exactly that, similar to DAPO with replacement of zero-variance groups. But refilling still pays full price for every wasted rollout before throwing it away.

summaries.zh: 本文介绍了微软和Hugging Face开发的ThinkingBox工具，用于评估智能体的数据库操作效果。该工具通过对比智能体操作后的数据库状态与预期结果，将评估结果转化为训练奖励，提升智能体性能。在Qwen3.8-27B模型上，使用ThinkingBox训练后，平均成功率从51.70%提升至60.78%，全对任务完成数从38增至107。该方法通过选择合适的非基准任务作为训练数据，利用执行结果作为奖励，有效提升了智能体的可靠性和重复成功率。
summaries.en: ThinkingBox evaluates agents by comparing their final database states to expected outcomes, then uses executable checks as rewards for post-training tasks. This method improved Qwen3.8-27B's success rate from 51.70% to 60.78% and increased tasks completed correctly from 38 to 107 with 50 GRPO steps. The approach selects tasks based on offline policy-relative difficulty, using their executable outcomes as rewards. Training focused on improving repeatable success, though at least-once coverage slightly declined. For example, an agent learned to preserve booking details requiring manager approval before training.

items.title: Ensemble forecasting with IBM Granite time-series models
items.content:
Four open Granite models, one extensible forecasting interface, and less guesswork about which model to use.

Pre-trained time-series models can forecast without training on your dataset, but you still have to choose one. A model that handles smooth industrial signals well may struggle with noisy retail demand or a long seasonal horizon, and the best choice depends on the series and the task.

Granite Timeseries Ensemble reduces that choice to a sensible default. One recipe combines four complementary Granite architectures and returns median and quantile forecasts, with no retraining and no fitted ensemble weights. Start with the Probabilistic Ensemble (uniform probability pooling), compare the adaptive Inter Quartile Range (IQR) Ensemble, and extend the same interface with compatible forecasters. The ensemble recipe and its default Granite members are permissively licensed.

The idea will be familiar from weather forecasting. Ensemble forecasts explore a range of possible outcomes, and systems such as the North American Multi-Model Ensemble combine different models for seasonal prediction. Time-series forecasting benefits in a similar way: complementary models offer different views of what comes next, and an ensemble merges those views into one forecast.

Try Granite Timeseries Ensemble

Install Granite TSFM and load the recommended four-model recipe directly from Hugging Face:

pip install "granite-tsfm>=0.3.11"

import pandas as pd

from tsfm_public.models.ensemble.modeling_ensemble import QuantileEnsembleForecaster

df = pd.read_csv(
    "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/zhouhaoyi/ETDataset/main/ETT-small/ETTh1.csv",
    parse_dates=["date"],
)

ensemble = QuantileEnsembleForecaster.from_pretrained(
    "ibm-granite/granite-timeseries-ensemble-r1",
)

result = ensemble(
    df.tail(1024),
    timestamp_column="date",
    target_columns=["OT"],
    context_length=1024,
    prediction_length=24,
)

print(result.prediction_outputs) # point forecast
print(result.quantile_outputs)   # quantiles

The recipe stores the ensemble configuration rather than merged model weights. It downloads the four member checkpoints at runtime, so allow extra time for the first run. For the full configuration, member checkpoints, evaluation details, and limitations, see the model card.

result.prediction_outputs contains the point forecast, while result.quantile_outputs contains the quantile predictions which by default range from 0.1 to 0.9. Applications can use the point value as a central prediction and selected quantiles to express forecast ranges. For example, the 0.1 and 0.9 quantiles define a central forecast interval with nominal 80% coverage.

The ensemble members

The default recipe combines four pre-trained Granite models with different architectures:

Model Architecture
Granite PatchTST-FM-r1 Patched Transformer
Granite PatchTST-FM-r2 Patched Conformer
Granite FlowState-r1.1 State-space model
Granite TTM-r3 Tiny Time Mixers (MLP mixer)

For background, see the PatchTST-FM-r1 paper, PatchTST-FM-r2 architecture overview, FlowState paper, and Tiny Time Mixers paper.

These architectures capture trends, seasonality, and local variation in different ways, so their errors need not coincide. A 50-year review of forecast combinations describes how combining forecasts can reduce the risk of picking the wrong single model, while stressing that member quality and diversity still matter.

Two ways to combine the forecasts

Each member returns quantile forecasts. The two main recipes use different rules to turn those forecasts into one predictive distribution and its median.

Probabilistic Ensemble: the recommended default

The Probabilistic Ensemble (uniform probability pooling) gives each member equal influence, pools their quantile forecasts in probability space, and extracts the requested quantiles from the combined values. Because the weights are fixed, there is no fitting step and no weighting hyperparameters to tune for a new series.

The forecast combination puzzle offers useful motivation: in point forecasting, simple equal-weight combinations have often held up well against methods with estimated weights. This recipe applies the same equal-influence idea to probabilistic forecasts. It is the default loaded in the example above.

IQR Ensemble: an adaptive alternative

The IQR Ensemble weights members according to their forecast spread, giving narrower intervals greater influence. It approximates each member’s interquartile range from the closest available quantiles around the 25th and 75th percentiles. Weights vary by sample, target, and horizon step, and like the Probabilistic Ensemble, nothing is fitted from historical forecast errors. Isotonic regression keeps the combined quantiles from crossing.

A narrower interval does not necessarily mean a more accurate or better-calibrated forecast, and IQR weighting can favor an overconfident member. If you want to experiment, the recipe exposes a temperature setting (higher values move the weights toward uniform) and an optional cap on any single member's weight.

Load the evaluated IQR recipe by changing only the subfolder:

ensemble = QuantileEnsembleForecaster.from_pretrained(
    "ibm-granite/granite-timeseries-ensemble-r1",
    subfolder="recipes/granite-iqr",
)

Which method should I use?

Your goal Start with Why
A simple default Probabilistic Ensemble Equal influence, no fitted weights
Adaptive weighting based on forecast spread IQR Ensemble Influence varies with each member's predicted spread

Start with the Probabilistic Ensemble. If forecast spread looks informative for your application, compare the IQR Ensemble against it on representative data, since accuracy and calibration depend on the series and the horizon.

Does the ensemble improve on its members?

We evaluated both recipes on 97 GIFT-Eval dataset configurations. The models forecast without fine-tuning, and test targets were not used to select or fit the aggregation method. Here we compare the official ensemble submission results with the four constituent models, using published leaderboard scores and ranks captured on 20 October 2026.

GIFT-Eval reports MASE for point forecasts and CRPS/MWQL (the benchmark's mean_weighted_sum_quantile_loss metric) for probabilistic forecasts. Scores are normalized to Seasonal Naive and geometrically averaged across configurations. Lower is better.

Forecast MASE ↓ MASE Rank ↓ CRPS / MWQL ↓ CRPS Rank ↓
Granite Ensemble R1 — Prob 0.683★ 47.175★ 0.471 50.948
Granite Ensemble R1 — IQR 0.684 48.773 0.471 47.619★
Granite PatchTST-FM-r2 0.685 51.371 0.467★ 48.918
Granite FlowState-r1.1 0.701 66.474 0.490 69.485
Granite PatchTST-FM-r1 0.717 74.794 0.488 68.134
Granite TTM-r3 0.724 83.062 0.520 88.959

★ Best value among the forecasts shown. Lower is better.

Rank columns average per-configuration ranks against the full GIFT-Eval reference leaderboard, not just these six forecasts, so rank values can shift as entries are added to the leaderboard.

Both ensembles outperform all four individual members on aggregate MASE and average MASE Rank. The Probabilistic Ensemble achieves the lowest MASE among these six forecasts: 0.683 compared with 0.685 for PatchTST-FM-r2. Lower average MASE Rank indicates stronger relative point-forecast performance across GIFT-Eval’s diverse dataset configurations. Together, these results support the ensemble as a practical starting point, without requiring developers to select the strongest individual architecture in advance. The MASE margin over the best single member is small, so the main benefit is robustness: you get comparable or better aggregate accuracy without knowing in advance which architecture will suit your data.

PatchTST-FM-r2 retains the lowest aggregate CRPS/MWQL score. The IQR Ensemble achieves the lowest average CRPS Rank among these six forecasts, while the Probabilistic Ensemble ranks behind PatchTST-FM-r2 on that measure. Aggregate error and average rank therefore favor different choices.

In the 20 October 2026 comparison, the ensemble approach ranks 3rd among eligible systems on MASE Rank and CRPS Rank. The figure below shows both recipes alongside the ten best eligible reference systems per metric. Some systems, including entries excluded as fine-tuned or non-permissively licensed, score better than either recipe, so the value of the ensemble is not that it tops the leaderboard. It is that a single default delivers strong, consistent results across many series without requiring you to choose a member.

Figure: GIFT-Eval average-rank standings on 20 October 2026, showing both Granite ensembles alongside the ten best eligible reference systems per metric. Eligible systems have replication code and no declared test-data leakage; fine-tuned entries and systems with known non-permissive licenses or member dependencies are excluded. Rank values are taken directly from the published overall leaderboard snapshot; filtering changes which systems are displayed, not their rank values.

Extend the recipe to other forecasters

The default recipe uses four Granite models, but the common Forecaster interface also accepts compatible external models. You can change the member mix or the aggregation method and keep the same downstream forecast format, with no merging or retraining of member checkpoints. That makes it easier to fit the ensemble into an existing forecasting stack, and to add forecasters suited to your domain as your needs evolve.

The repository also includes expanded recipes that add IBM Research checkpoints. These carry separate license terms, including non-commercial and research-use restrictions, so review each member's model card before using them.

For any new combination, check forecast compatibility, accuracy, calibration, latency, and licensing.

Evaluate the recipe for your application

GIFT-Eval is a broad benchmark, but aggregate gains don’t mean every series benefits, and average ranks don’t establish calibration. The way to find out how the recipes behave for your application is to backtest them on representative data:

  • Match your use case. Use historical forecast windows that reflect the data available at each forecast origin, the horizon you need, and the series you expect to serve.
  • Compare like with like. Run the Probabilistic Ensemble, the IQR Ensemble, and a strong individual member (such as PatchTST-FM-r2) on the same windows.
  • Look beyond point error. Assess quantile loss alongside MASE, and check the empirical coverage of the 0.1 to 0.9 interval against its nominal 80%.
  • Measure the cost. Record runtime and memory use to judge whether the benefit of combining four models justifies it for your workload.

Keep two limitations in mind. The current recipe forecasts multivariate channels independently, without using cross-channel information, and it loads four member checkpoints, which increases inference time and memory relative to a single member. Member context limits, horizons, preprocessing, and missing-value handling also differ, and neither aggregation method guarantees calibration or robustness under distribution shift, so keep monitoring forecasts after deployment.

Four open Granite models, one extensible forecasting interface, and less
guesswork about which model to use.
Pre-trained time-series models can forecast without training on your dataset, but you still have to choose one. A model that handles smooth industrial signals well may struggle with noisy retail demand or a long seasonal horizon, and the best choice depends on the series and the task.
Granite Timeseries Ensemble reduces that choice to a sensible default. One recipe combines four complementary Granite architectures and returns median and quantile forecasts, with no retraining and no fitted ensemble weights. Start with the Probabilistic Ensemble (uniform probability pooling), compare the adaptive Inter Quartile Range (IQR) Ensemble, and extend the same interface with compatible forecasters. The ensemble recipe and its default Granite members are permissively licensed.
The idea will be familiar from weather forecasting. Ensemble forecasts explore a range of possible outcomes, and systems such as the North American Multi-Model Ensemble combine different models for seasonal prediction. Time-series forecasting benefits in a similar way: complementary models offer different views of what comes next, and an ensemble merges those views into one forecast.




Try Granite Timeseries Ensemble


Install Granite TSFM and load the recommended four-model recipe directly from
Hugging Face:
pip install "granite-tsfm>=0.3.11"

import pandas as pd

from tsfm_public.models.ensemble.modeling_ensemble import QuantileEnsembleForecaster

df = pd.read_csv(
    "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/zhouhaoyi/ETDataset/main/ETT-small/ETTh1.csv",
    parse_dates=["date"],
)

ensemble = QuantileEnsembleForecaster.from_pretrained(
    "ibm-granite/granite-timeseries-ensemble-r1",
)

result = ensemble(
    df.tail(1024),
    timestamp_column="date",
    target_columns=["OT"],
    context_length=1024,
    prediction_length=24,
)

print(result.prediction_outputs) # point forecast
print(result.quantile_outputs)   # quantiles

The recipe stores the ensemble configuration rather than merged model weights. It downloads the four member checkpoints at runtime, so allow extra time for the first run. For the full configuration, member checkpoints, evaluation details, and limitations, see the model card.
result.prediction_outputs contains the point forecast, while result.quantile_outputs contains the quantile predictions which by default range from  0.1 to 0.9. Applications can use the point value as a central prediction and selected quantiles to express forecast ranges. For example, the 0.1 and 0.9 quantiles define a central forecast interval with nominal 80% coverage.




The ensemble members


The default recipe combines four pre-trained Granite models with different architectures:

Model
Architecture



Granite PatchTST-FM-r1
Patched Transformer


Granite PatchTST-FM-r2
Patched Conformer


Granite FlowState-r1.1
State-space model


Granite TTM-r3
Tiny Time Mixers (MLP mixer)




For background, see the PatchTST-FM-r1 paper,
PatchTST-FM-r2 architecture overview,
FlowState paper, and
Tiny Time Mixers paper.
These architectures capture trends, seasonality, and local variation in different ways, so their errors need not coincide. A 50-year review of forecast
combinations describes how combining forecasts can reduce the risk of picking the wrong single model, while stressing that member quality and diversity still matter.





Two ways to combine the forecasts


Each member returns quantile forecasts. The two main recipes use different rules to turn those forecasts into one predictive distribution and its median.




Probabilistic Ensemble: the recommended default


The Probabilistic Ensemble (uniform probability pooling) gives each member equal influence, pools their quantile forecasts in probability space, and extracts the requested quantiles from the combined values. Because the weights are fixed, there is no fitting step and no weighting hyperparameters to tune for a new series.
The forecast combination puzzle
offers useful motivation: in point forecasting, simple equal-weight combinations
have often held up well against methods with estimated weights. This recipe applies the same equal-influence idea to probabilistic forecasts. It is the default loaded in the example above.




IQR Ensemble: an adaptive alternative


The IQR Ensemble weights members according to their forecast spread, giving narrower intervals greater influence. It approximates each member’s interquartile range from the closest available quantiles around the 25th and 75th percentiles. Weights vary by sample, target, and horizon step, and like the Probabilistic Ensemble, nothing is fitted from historical forecast errors. Isotonic regression keeps the combined quantiles from crossing.
A narrower interval does not necessarily mean a more accurate or better-calibrated forecast, and IQR weighting can favor an overconfident member. If you want to experiment, the recipe exposes a temperature setting (higher values move the weights toward uniform) and an optional cap on any single member's weight.
Load the evaluated IQR recipe by changing only the subfolder:
ensemble = QuantileEnsembleForecaster.from_pretrained(
    "ibm-granite/granite-timeseries-ensemble-r1",
    subfolder="recipes/granite-iqr",
)





Which method should I use?





Your goal
Start with
Why



A simple default
Probabilistic Ensemble
Equal influence, no fitted weights


Adaptive weighting based on forecast spread
IQR Ensemble
Influence varies with each member's predicted spread




Start with the Probabilistic Ensemble. If forecast spread looks informative for your application, compare the IQR Ensemble against it on representative data, since accuracy and calibration depend on the series and the horizon.




Does the ensemble improve on its members?


We evaluated both recipes on 97 GIFT-Eval dataset configurations. The models
forecast without fine-tuning, and test targets were not used to select or fit
the aggregation method. Here we compare the official ensemble submission results
with the four constituent models, using published leaderboard scores and ranks captured on 20 October 2026.
GIFT-Eval reports MASE for point forecasts and CRPS/MWQL (the benchmark's
