items.title: NVIDIA Kumo Relational Outperforms Supervised Machine Learning on Relational Data, No Training Required
items.content:
TL;DR

NVIDIA Kumo Relational is a pre-trained relational foundation model that makes predictions directly on enterprise databases. Given a predictive query, it gathers historical examples as context examples and predicts outcomes such as churn, demand, or fraud in a single forward pass. It needs no task-specific training, no feature engineering, and no flattening of tables. Kumo Relational is the first few-shot foundation model to outperform supervised machine learning on common relational benchmarks. Across 41 tasks on 15 databases, it beats supervised relational deep learning models and expert-engineered gradient-boosted tree pipelines, and on the SAP SALT enterprise benchmark it surpasses AutoGluon ensembles by 8% in mean reciprocal rank (MRR). It scales to databases with 500B+ rows and works for humans and agents alike, through NVIDIA's open-source, GPU-native structured-data-models and kumo-engine libraries, or as an NVIDIA NIM.

  • Paper: https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.12596
  • Model Code: https://github.com/NVIDIA/structured-data-models
  • Model Weights: https://huggingface.co/nvidia/Kumo-Relational
  • Client Code: https://github.com/NVIDIA/structured-data-models-client
  • NIM Documentation: https://docs.nvidia.com/sdgm/rfm/overview

The Shift to Structured Data Foundation Models

Foundation models have already rewritten the playbook for language and vision. Not long ago, production NLP meant a dedicated model per task, each fed by its own pipeline of tokenization, lemmatization, and n-grams. LLMs made that stack largely obsolete for three reasons: they were more accurate than the best task-specific models, far simpler to put into production, and flexible enough to open a new era of agentic applications.

The same shift is now underway for structured data. Relational databases power the world's most critical business decisions, yet predictive modeling on them still requires weeks of feature engineering, task-specific training, and tuned pipelines. Structured data foundation models change that for the same three reasons:

Better accuracy today: As drop-in replacements, these models already beat many production pipelines, especially XGBoost. On RelBench V1 classification tasks, Kumo Relational outperforms gradient-boosted trees on expert-engineered features by nearly 4 AUROC points on average. On SAP SALT, it beats XGBoost on engineered features by 7 MRR points out of the box and by 13 MRR points after fine-tuning. These results make a compelling case for replacing production XGBoost pipelines with Kumo Relational.

Simplicity and agility: One pre-trained model replaces separate pipelines for individual tasks. A new prediction becomes a query instead of a project, so ML teams can finally take on use cases that traditional ML made too laborious to build at every level of the organization.

Agents that can predict: LLMs let agents read, write, and reason. Structured data foundation models let them anticipate what happens next, such as which customer will churn, and act on it. Kumo Relational is already built to be called by agents, and its Predictive Query Language (PQL) gives them a simple interface for asking predictive questions.

Today, we are introducing Kumo Relational (Paper, GitHub, HuggingFace), a pre-trained foundation model that brings this paradigm to relational data. Connect a database, describe what to predict, and get predictions in a single forward pass. No training required.

How Kumo Relational Works

Most foundation models for structured data operate on a single flat table. Real-world data lives in relational databases instead: users connected to orders connected to products, all evolving over time. Flattening these relationships into one row through manual aggregation (e.g., "average order value in the last 30 days") loses fine-grained structural signals and takes significant human effort.

Kumo Relational is a Relational Foundation Model that operates directly on the database, respecting its tables, foreign keys, and timestamps. It is pre-trained once on synthetic relational data that reflects real-world datasets and adapts to each new task through in-context learning by reasoning over context examples at inference time. Each example pairs a local subgraph around an entity at a point in time with its ground-truth target (e.g., "this user churned" or "this item sold 142 units").

Figure 1. Overview of the Kumo Relational system. Connect a database, specify a predictive query, and Kumo Relational handles the rest, from context generation to model inference.

To make a prediction, Kumo Relational has to do three things: (1) understand the values within each table, (2) relate records across tables, and (3) relate context examples with known targets to the entity being predicted. Here is how it works:

Figure 2. Kumo Relational architecture: (a) context input, (b) reasoning within tables, (c) reasoning across tables.

Automatic Context Generation: Tasks are written in the Predictive Query Language (PQL), a declarative interface where you state what to predict rather than how. For temporal tasks, Kumo Relational replays historical database states: it samples entity-centric subgraphs up to an anchor timestamp and computes each target from events after that timestamp, while serving the model only the data from before it. This prevents data leakage.

Reasoning Within Tables: A lightweight network processes each table independently via column attention (relating values within a column) and row attention (relating features within a row). The model learns which columns and rows matter for the current prediction and filters out noise before it propagates.

Reasoning Across Tables: A larger network distributes the row embeddings across the relational structure via graph attention over primary-key/foreign-key relationships, followed by cross-sample attention across context examples. This is where relational reasoning happens, such as linking a user's profile to their transaction history. Because this stage works on row embeddings rather than on every cell in every table, the design avoids quadratic cost and scales to large contexts and deeper subgraphs.

How Kumo Relational Was Built

Kumo Relational is pre-trained on entirely synthetic relational data simulated to reflect real-world relational databases with diverse predictive queries. Pre-training proceeds in stages, from single tables to increasingly complex relational structures.

The diverse relational databases needed for pre-training are rarely public, so synthetic data fills the gap. Kumo Relational's generator builds on the approach of PluRel (Kothapalli et al., ICML 2026), which extends single-table data generators to full relational databases. PluRel generates each database in three stages: a schema, foreign-key links between rows that cluster as they do in real data, and column values from Structural Causal Models with temporal trends and cross-table dependencies. Generation is lightweight, so pre-training data is effectively unlimited. Pre-training loss follows a power law as synthetic databases are added, with gains that carry over to real databases.

Through this pre-training, the model learns to filter, correlate, and aggregate information across tables instead of relying on fixed aggregations.

Performance

In the paper, we evaluated Kumo Relational on 41 benchmarks across 15 relational databases from RelBench V1 and V2, SAP SALT, and 4DBInfer, spanning e-commerce, medical, enterprise, social, and academic domains. None of these datasets were seen in pre-training. Kumo Relational outperforms the strongest supervised models in both classification and regression, including relational deep learning models and expert-engineered tabular ensembles. It is the top-performing in-context learning model on the RelBench leaderboard. On RelArena-α, it sits on the accuracy-efficiency Pareto front:

Figure 3. RelArena-α leaderboard as of 2026-09-21: Elo across tasks versus total task runtime (log scale). Kumo Relational is about 430× faster than rtl-plurel at similar accuracy.

On the SAP SALT enterprise benchmark, Kumo Relational surpasses large AutoGluon ensembles by 8% in mean reciprocal rank (MRR), and fine-tuning extends its lead over AutoGluon to 16%. It also holds up under hard conditions: it performs well with as little as 0.2% of the training data as context, stays stable when up to 75% of foreign-key links are removed, and barely degrades when noisy columns are added.

Limitations

Kumo Relational performs best on data with meaningful relationships and temporal dynamics, such as user behavior over time. On tasks with very large training sets, task-specific supervised models may still edge out in-context predictions. Predictive signals must be reachable within a limited number of hops.

Demo

Kumo Relational runs in-context learning natively over databases: in memory, through database and warehouse connectors, or through kumo-engine that handles 500B+ rows via memory-mapped I/O at up to 5 GB/s. The model itself is available in NVIDIA's newly released, GPU-native structured-data-models library, the same open-source library that powers our sister model, Kumo Tabular. The library downloads the weights from the Hugging Face Hub on first use, so you can load the model in a GPU-backed notebook and predict directly from it. The interface is designed to naturally extend tabular foundation models to relational signal by passing additional related multi-table context and query information:

import sdm  # pip install structured-data-models

model = sdm.models.KumoRelational(device="cuda")

pred = model(
    # In-context training table (fkeys/timestamps/targets):
    x_context=sdm.TableTensor(...),
    y_context=sdm.TableTensor(...),
    # Prediction examples (fkeys/timestamps):
    x_query=sdm.TableTensor(...),
    # Multi-table information for context/prediction entities:
    related_context_tables=sdm.RelatedTables(tables={...}),
    related_query_tables=sdm.RelatedTables(tables={...}),
)

See the library's relational examples for RelBench and SAP SALT pipelines.

To run the model as a separate service instead, deploy it as an NVIDIA NIM and point the open-source structured-data-models-client at it from your notebook. You write the prediction in PQL, and the client gathers the context examples and related tables, then sends the request:

import sdm_client  # pip install 'structured-data-models-client[relational]'

client = sdm_client.SDMClient(url="http://localhost:8001")  # NIM URL
query = sdm_client.PredictiveQuery(
    # Prediction task in Predictive Query Language (PQL):
    "PREDICT COUNT(orders.*, 0, 30, days) FOR EACH users.user_id",
    # Multi-table data as pandas DataFrames (keys/links inferred):
    {"users": ..., "orders": ...},
)
pred = client.predict(
    # Context examples and related tables for the entities to predict:
    query.materialize(indices=[1, 2, 3]),
    model=sdm_client.KumoRelational(),
)

See the client's example notebooks for end-to-end runs against a local NIM and on Databricks.

Start Building with NVIDIA Kumo Relational

NVIDIA Kumo Relational is available today. Read the research paper, explore the quickstart notebook, or start making predictions on your own data. The code is released under the Apache 2.0 license and the model weights under the OpenMDW License Agreement, version 1.1. NVIDIA believes Trustworthy AI is a shared responsibility, and we have established policies and practices to enable development for a wide array of AI applications. When downloaded or used in accordance with our terms of service, developers should work with their supporting model team to ensure this model meets requirements for the relevant industry and use case and addresses unforeseen product misuse. Please report model quality, risk, security vulnerabilities, or NVIDIA AI concerns here.

  • Paper: https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.12596

  • Model Code: https://github.com/NVIDIA/structured-data-models

  • Model Weights: https://huggingface.co/nvidia/Kumo-Relational

  • Client Code: https://github.com/NVIDIA/structured-data-models-client

  • NIM Documentation: https://docs.nvidia.com/sdgm/rfm/overview

  • Quickstart notebook: https://github.com/NVIDIA/structured-data-models-client/blob/main/examples/local/relational.ipynb

  • Related Research: Predictive Query Language (PQL), PluRel, Kumo Tabular, TabICLv2

Acknowledgements

We thank the entire Kumo team for their invaluable support. Special thanks go to Adi Wadaskar, Hema Raghavan, Manush Murali, Zack Drach, Vanja Josifovski, Myungwhan Kim, Siyang Xie, Alan Krumholz, Effy Fang, Abdullah Al-chihabi, Disha Dubey, Devan Johnson, Joseph Oliveira, Angela Liu, Miha Pelko, Vedaant Jain, Sally Liu, Aleksandar S. Sokolovski, and Alex Porter.

It is pre-trained once on synthetic relational data that reflects real-world datasets and adapts to each new task through in-context learning by reasoning over context examples at inference time. Each example pairs a local subgraph around an entity at a point in time with its ground-truth target (e.g., "this user churned" or "this item sold 142 units").

Figure 1. Overview of the Kumo Relational system. Connect a database, specify a predictive query, and Kumo Relational handles the rest, from context generation to model inference.
To make a prediction, Kumo Relational has to do three things: (1) understand the values within each table, (2) relate records across tables, and (3) relate context examples with known targets to the entity being predicted. Here is how it works:

Figure 2. Kumo Relational architecture: (a) context input, (b) reasoning within tables, (c) reasoning across tables.
Automatic Context Generation: Tasks are written in the Predictive Query Language (PQL), a declarative interface where you state what to predict rather than how. For temporal tasks, Kumo Relational replays historical database states: it samples entity-centric subgraphs up to an anchor timestamp and computes each target from events after that timestamp, while serving the model only the data from before it. This prevents data leakage.
Reasoning Within Tables: A lightweight network processes each table independently via column attention (relating values within a column) and row attention (relating features within a row). The model learns which columns and rows matter for the current prediction and filters out noise before it propagates.
Reasoning Across Tables: A larger network distributes the row embeddings across the relational structure via graph attention over primary-key/foreign-key relationships, followed by cross-sample attention across context examples. This is where relational reasoning happens, such as linking a user's profile to their transaction history. Because this stage works on row embeddings rather than on every cell in every table, the design avoids quadratic cost and scales to large contexts and deeper subgraphs.




How Kumo Relational Was Built


Kumo Relational is pre-trained on entirely synthetic relational data simulated to reflect real-world relational databases with diverse predictive queries. Pre-training proceeds in stages, from single tables to increasingly complex relational structures.
The diverse relational databases needed for pre-training are rarely public, so synthetic data fills the gap. Kumo Relational's generator builds on the approach of PluRel (Kothapalli et al., ICML 2026), which extends single-table data generators to full relational databases. PluRel generates each database in three stages: a schema, foreign-key links between rows that cluster as they do in real data, and column values from Structural Causal Models with temporal trends and cross-table dependencies. Generation is lightweight, so pre-training data is effectively unlimited. Pre-training loss follows a power law as synthetic databases are added, with gains that carry over to real databases.
Through this pre-training, the model learns to filter, correlate, and aggregate information across tables instead of relying on fixed aggregations.




Performance


In the paper, we evaluated Kumo Relational on 41 benchmarks across 15 relational databases from RelBench V1 and V2, SAP SALT, and 4DBInfer, spanning e-commerce, medical, enterprise, social, and academic domains. None of these datasets were seen in pre-training. Kumo Relational outperforms the strongest supervised models in both classification and regression, including relational deep learning models and expert-engineered tabular ensembles. It is the top-performing in-context learning model on the RelBench leaderboard. On RelArena-α, it sits on the accuracy-efficiency Pareto front:

Figure 3. RelArena-α leaderboard as of 2026-09-21: Elo across tasks versus total task runtime (log scale). Kumo Relational is about 430× faster than rtl-plurel at similar accuracy.
On the SAP SALT enterprise benchmark, Kumo Relational surpasses large AutoGluon ensembles by 8% in mean reciprocal rank (MRR), and fine-tuning extends its lead over AutoGluon to 16%. It also holds up under hard conditions: it performs well with as little as 0.2% of the training data as context, stays stable when up to 75% of foreign-key links are removed, and barely degrades when noisy columns are added.




Limitations


Kumo Relational performs best on data with meaningful relationships and temporal dynamics, such as user behavior over time. On tasks with very large training sets, task-specific supervised models may still edge out in-context predictions. Predictive signals must be reachable within a limited number of hops.




Demo


Kumo Relational runs in-context learning natively over databases: in memory, through database and warehouse connectors, or through kumo-engine that handles 500B+ rows via memory-mapped I/O at up to 5 GB/s. The model itself is available in NVIDIA's newly released, GPU-native structured-data-models library, the same open-source library that powers our sister model, Kumo Tabular. The library downloads the weights from the Hugging Face Hub on first use, so you can load the model in a GPU-backed notebook and predict directly from it. The interface is designed to naturally extend tabular foundation models to relational signal by passing additional related multi-table context and query information:
import sdm  # pip install structured-data-models

model = sdm.models.KumoRelational(device="cuda")

pred = model(
    # In-context training table (fkeys/timestamps/targets):
    x_context=sdm.TableTensor(...),
    y_context=sdm.TableTensor(...),
    # Prediction examples (fkeys/timestamps):
    x_query=sdm.TableTensor(...),
    # Multi-table information for context/prediction entities:
    related_context_tables=sdm.RelatedTables(tables={...}),
    related_query_tables=sdm.RelatedTables(tables={...}),
)

See the library's relational examples for RelBench and SAP SALT pipelines.
To run the model as a separate service instead, deploy it as an NVIDIA NIM and point the open-source structured-data-models-client at it from your notebook. You write the prediction in PQL, and the client gathers the context examples and related tables, then sends the request:
import sdm_client  # pip install 'structured-data-models-client[relational]'

client = sdm_client.SDMClient(url="http://localhost:8001")  # NIM URL
query = sdm_client.PredictiveQuery(
    # Prediction task in Predictive Query Language (PQL):
    "PREDICT COUNT(orders.*, 0, 30, days) FOR EACH users.user_id",
    # Multi-table data as pandas DataFrames (keys/links inferred):
    {"users": ..., "orders": ...},
)
pred = client.predict(
    # Context examples and related tables for the entities to predict:
    query.materialize(indices=[1, 2, 3]),
    model=sdm_client.KumoRelational(),
)

See the client's example notebooks for end-to-end runs against a local NIM and on Databricks.




Start Building with NVIDIA Kumo Relational


NVIDIA Kumo Relational is available today. Read the research paper, explore the quickstart notebook, or start making predictions on your own data. The code is released under the Apache 2.0 license and the model weights under the OpenMDW License Agreement, version 1.1. NVIDIA believes Trustworthy AI is a shared responsibility, and we have established policies and practices to enable development for a wide array of AI applications. When downloaded or used in accordance with our terms of service, developers should work with their supporting model team to ensure this model meets requirements for the relevant industry and use case and addresses unforeseen product misuse. summaries.en: NVIDIA Kumo Relational is a pre-trained relational foundation model that outperforms supervised machine learning on relational data without training. It predicts outcomes like churn or fraud by analyzing up to 10,000 historical examples from enterprise databases in a single forward pass, eliminating the need for feature engineering or table flattening. Across 41 tasks on 15 databases, it surpasses supervised models and expert-engineered pipelines, including an 8% lead over AutoGluon on SAP SALT in mean reciprocal rank (MRR). Kumo Relational scales to large databases and integrates with agents via NVIDIA's open-source library, simplifying predictive modeling for structured data.

items.title: How Specializing the Vocabulary of SLMs Can Cut Inference Cost by 77% in Real Applications
items.content:
Models specialized for a domain or a task by fine-tuning general open-source models, such as Qwen and Gemma, inherit a vocabulary built for many domains and general applications.

In an essay grader we run in production, that vocabulary split the text the model writes most into many tokens. This article previews some results from the VocabX paper, which we will publish soon: how we specialized the vocabulary around the cost of each token rather than its frequency, and cut measured inference cost by 77% without changing the base model.

The tokenizer is usually treated as a fixed property of the base model, inherited and left alone. For a model specialized in a single domain, it can be one of the largest cost levers, and it is set before any training step.

One of the systems we run in production is an automated grader for Portuguese essays, built on Qwen3-4B. It receives the essay, the prompt and the supporting texts, and returns a JSON assessment with a grade and a comment for each competency.

The model was already small, at 4 billion parameters, and had already been trained for the task. Its tokenizer, however, was still the original Qwen3-4B one, built for many languages and many kinds of text. In the grader, it was used for a single language, Portuguese, and a single response format. That had two costs: the text the grader writes on every request took more tokens than it needed, and at every generated token the model scored a vocabulary of 151,669 entries, including many this task almost never uses.

We rebuilt that vocabulary with a method we call VocabX, keeping the same base model, the same data and the same training recipe. The numbers in this article come from the current version of the paper, still under review, and may change before publication.

A Vocabulary Built for Everyone

The leading language models read and write in tokens, and the tokenizer decides how text becomes tokens. The tokenizers of the leading general-purpose models are trained on large collections of text from many domains and languages, from source code to contracts to Chinese. For a general-purpose model, that choice makes sense.

For a model used in a single domain, it creates two kinds of waste at once.

The first is fragmentation. The tokenizer splits into many pieces exactly what the domain repeats most. In the grader, every response starts with the same JSON envelope, the same competency names, the same evaluation phrases. In contracts, it is the boilerplate clauses. In code, the identifiers. Each of these sequences costs several tokens where one would do, and the model pays for every one of them on every request.

The second is excess. The vocabulary carries tens of thousands of entries the domain never uses, and the model computes a score for all of them at every token it generates. A model tuned to grade American school biology exams will almost never write in Chinese, yet it computes the probability of every Chinese-language token at every step. The vocabulary splits into many pieces what the domain repeats most, and carries entries the domain never uses.

Reading Is Cheap, Writing Is Expensive

The natural reaction is to count tokens and try to reduce the count. But the count is not the bill.

To see why a generated token costs more, it helps to look at how inference works. It has two phases. In prefill, the model processes the whole input in a single pass through the network: each weight read from GPU memory is reused for every input token, and the limit is compute. In decode, the model generates the response one token at a time, and each token needs a full pass. Each weight read is used only a few times, and the GPU spends most of its time waiting for data to arrive from memory: the limit becomes memory bandwidth.

This effect is strongest exactly where we operate: small models served with moderate batches. Batching requests splits the weight reads across them and eases the problem, but does not solve it. At every decode step, the model also reads the KV cache, the attention memory that holds the context already processed and grows with it. In the case we measured, the grader, a generated token costs 7.4 times a token read, but the ratio varies with the hardware, the problem, the batch size, the context length and other factors, and it can be larger than that. In general, the direction holds: generating costs more than reading.

Think of a shipping company that charges per box, but charges seven times more for outgoing boxes than for incoming ones. Reducing the total number of boxes helps. Reducing the outgoing boxes helps seven times more. A method that compresses input and output equally misses most of the possible savings.

The third component of the bill is the vocabulary itself. The model's last layer, the LM head, turns the internal state into a score for every possible token. To do that, it holds one row of parameters per vocabulary entry. In a model the size of Qwen3-4B, that matrix accounts for almost 10% of the parameters. It is a share that large models absorb without noticing, but it weighs on a small model.

And the cost is not paid only once. The input layer looks up only the row of the token being read, but the LM head reads and multiplies the entire matrix for every generated token. Since decode is already memory-bound, every extra row is more data to move at every step. An entry the domain never uses costs exactly the same as a frequent one. That is why adding tokens can lower the count and raise the bill at the same time. VocabX does not include this term in its selection criterion, but it controls vocabulary size in two steps: the sub-word merge replaces the base vocabulary with a smaller, domain-specific one, and macros enter under a fixed budget. In the grader, the output layer went from about 152,000 to about 65,000 rows.

Why Existing Solutions Fell Short

Adapting a model's vocabulary is not a new idea. Reference methods in the literature, such as fast vocabulary transfer (FVT), multi-word tokenization (MWT) and Liquid AI's in-place tokenizer expansion (in-place BPE), which continues BPE training from the original vocabulary, already reduce fragmentation. When we tested them on our problem, we found two limitations.

They choose tokens by frequency, not by cost. An expression that appears often in the input is worth more to them than one that appears less often in the response, even if the second is the more expensive one to serve.

They work on a single layer. They either adjust how words are cut into pieces, or merge whole phrases into one token. None of these three does both under the same criterion. And the grader's biggest waste was precisely in long, repeated spans such as the JSON envelope, which a sub-word method only reaches after merging each part, one by one.

How We Solved It

VocabX addresses both limitations, plus a third problem that appears on the obvious path to solving the first.

First, we changed the question. Instead of asking how many tokens a candidate saves, we ask how much cost and time it saves. Each eliminated token is multiplied by the price of the field it appears in: system prompt, user message or model response. In the case we measured, the grader, a token saved in the response is worth 7.4 times one saved in the input, and the vocabulary is built accordingly.

Second, we work on both layers at once. Back to the shipping company: you can cut boxes by packing each item better, or by recognizing that the same twelve-item kit ships every week and sending the kit in a single box. VocabX does both. At the sub-word layer, it rebuilds how domain words are cut into pieces. At the multi-word layer, it looks for whole spans that repeat, from short expressions to full lines and JSON envelopes, and turns each into a single token, which we call a macro token. Both layers are chosen under the same cost criterion, each with its own budget.

To find these spans, we use five miners, automatic searches for spans that repeat across the corpus, each specialized in one kind of repetition: long words, whole lines, expressions, complete sentences, and structures with punctuation such as JSON and tags. Averaged over eight corpora, the last one contributed the most, and on code it alone accounted for 17.5 points. Without all five, token reduction on the grader would drop by 55.6 points.

Third, we estimate what the sample cannot see. Choosing tokens by cost requires knowing how much each candidate still saves after the ones already chosen. Measuring that exactly would require reprocessing the entire corpus after every choice, tens of thousands of times. A common way to do this at scale is to measure on a sample of documents, and then a candidate absent from the sample gets zero gain.

An expression that appears 37 times in 50,000 documents shows up in a 400-document sample only about 26% of the time. In a contracts corpus, only 16.6% of the candidates appear in a 400-document sample; the rest are never evaluated.

A candidate's gain has two parts. One is how much it saves over the entire corpus, and that can be counted exactly, without a sample. The other is how much of that saving is not yet covered by the tokens already chosen, and only that part needs to be estimated. For candidates the sample cannot see, we use a statistical estimate based on the behavior of the ones it can see, instead of zero. A candidate that is rare in the sample but frequent in the corpus is back in the running.

That change alone, with the same sample and the same budget, raised token reduction on a contracts corpus from 44.7% to 52.8%.

What Changed in the Grader

To measure the real effect, we trained seven versions of the grader with the same base model, the same data, the same recipe and the same seed. The only difference between them is the tokenizer. All of them ran the same 500 requests on the same test machine, with an RTX 5090 GPU and the vLLM inference server, and cost was calculated from measured runtime.

The model's response dropped from 350 to 101 tokens on average. Cost dropped 77.0%. Quality, measured by the bench score, which combines grading accuracy and the accuracy of screening off-topic or rule-breaking essays, rose from 0.703 to 0.810.

Getting there required a course correction. The first version of the vocabulary fused each competency's grade with the surrounding JSON into a single macro token. It was the most compact option, but quality dropped: its bench score was 0.689, below the production grader's 0.703. With the grade inside the macro, each combination of grade and structure became a different variant of the same token, and the model chose both in a single step. Giving the grade its own token cost 2 extra tokens per response, raised the bench score to 0.810 and, in the measurement, was even cheaper: a 77.0% reduction, against 73.3% for the fused version.

The lesson applies beyond the grader. Compression has a cost when the compressed span carries the very decision the model exists to make. The goal is not the cheapest possible vocabulary, but the cheapest one that preserves the tokens that matter.

Beyond the Grader

To find out whether the gain was specific to our case, we compared VocabX with the three reference methods on five public domains (contracts, medical papers, scientific papers, news and Python code) and three model families (Qwen3, Llama-3.1 and Gemma-3). All methods used the same mining and test documents, and the same vocabulary ceiling.

VocabX compressed more than the strongest reference method in all fifteen combinations, by 1.2 to 9.3 points. In estimated inference cost, the pruned version of VocabX also led in all fifteen, with average margins of 10.2 points on Qwen3, 7.5 on Llama-3.1 and 13.6 on Gemma-3. On contracts, the pruned version reached 62.6% token reduction with 113,426 vocabulary entries, against 61.8% for the best in-place BPE configuration, which uses 207,803.

Paying Only for the Tokens That Matter

VocabX does not make the model smarter. It makes the model stop paying for text it does not need to write piece by piece, and stop scoring a vocabulary it will never use. In our grader, that cut measured inference cost by 77%, with the same base model and the same training recipe.

Specialization usually starts with data and weights. It can also start one layer earlier, in the vocabulary.

The full method, the tables for every experiment and the discarded interventions will be in the VocabX paper, which we will publish soon.

Sources

  • Dharma-AI. "VocabX: Cost-Weighted Vocabulary Adaptation for Domain-Specific Language Models." In preparation (2026).
  • Gee, Leonidas, et al. "Fast vocabulary transfer for language model compression." EMNLP Industry Track (2022).
  • Gee, Leonidas, et al. "Multi-word tokenization for sequence compression." EMNLP Industry Track (2023).
  • Smith, Jimmy T.H., et al. "In-Place Tokenizer Expansion for Pre-trained LLMs." arXiv:2607.15232 (2026).

Further Reading

  • Same Cluster, 33 Points More Utilization: What Changed Was the Order
  • GPU Management: Why Idle GPUs Are the New Grounded Aircraft
  • Why Specialization Is Inevitable
  • Specialization Beats Scale: A Strategic Variable Most AI Procurement Decisions Overlook
  • Text Degeneration: A Production Failure Mode That Most Benchmarks Do Not Track

Explore Dharma AI on Hugging Face to try our demos, download our open models, and see how specialized AI systems outperform general-purpose models in real enterprise applications.

That change alone, with the same sample and the same budget, raised token reduction on a contracts corpus from 44.7% to 52.8%.





What Changed in the Grader


To measure the real effect, we trained seven versions of the grader with the same base model, the same data, the same recipe and the same seed. The only difference between them is the tokenizer. All of them ran the same 500 requests on the same test machine, with an RTX 5090 GPU and the vLLM inference server, and cost was calculated from measured runtime.

The model's response dropped from 350 to 101 tokens on average. Cost dropped 77.0%. Quality, measured by the bench score, which combines grading accuracy and the accuracy of screening off-topic or rule-breaking essays, rose from 0.703 to 0.810.
Getting there required a course correction. The first version of the vocabulary fused each competency's grade with the surrounding JSON into a single macro token. It was the most compact option, but quality dropped: its bench score was 0.689, below the production grader's 0.703. With the grade inside the macro, each combination of grade and structure became a different variant of the same token, and the model chose both in a single step. Giving the grade its own token cost 2 extra tokens per response, raised the bench score to 0.810 and, in the measurement, was even cheaper: a 77.0% reduction, against 73.3% for the fused version.
The lesson applies beyond the grader. Compression has a cost when the compressed span carries the very decision the model exists to make. The goal is not the cheapest possible vocabulary, but the cheapest one that preserves the tokens that matter.




Beyond the Grader


To find out whether the gain was specific to our case, we compared VocabX with the three reference methods on five public domains (contracts, medical papers, scientific papers, news and Python code) and three model families (Qwen3, Llama-3.1 and Gemma-3). All methods used the same mining and test documents, and the same vocabulary ceiling.
VocabX compressed more than the strongest reference method in all fifteen combinations, by 1.2 to 9.3 points. In estimated inference cost, the pruned version of VocabX also led in all fifteen, with average margins of 10.2 points on Qwen3, 7.5 on Llama-3.1 and 13.6 on Gemma-3. On contracts, the pruned version reached 62.6% token reduction with 113,426 vocabulary entries, against 61.8% for the best in-place BPE configuration, which uses 207,803.





Paying Only for the Tokens That Matter


VocabX does not make the model smarter. It makes the model stop paying for text it does not need to write piece by piece, and stop scoring a vocabulary it will never use. In our grader, that cut measured inference cost by 77%, with the same base model and the same training recipe.
Specialization usually starts with data and weights. It can also start one layer earlier, in the vocabulary.
The full method, the tables for every experiment and the discarded interventions will be in the VocabX paper, which we will publish soon.

Gee, Leonidas, et al. "Multi-word tokenization for sequence compression." EMNLP Industry Track (2023).
Smith, Jimmy T.H., et al. "In-Place Tokenizer Expansion for Pre-trained LLMs." arXiv:2607.15232 (2026).

summaries.en: Specializing the vocabulary of language models (LMs) can reduce inference costs by 77% in real applications. Models like Qwen and Gemma inherit general-purpose vocabularies, leading to inefficiencies in specialized tasks. For example, an essay grader for Portuguese used a Qwen3-4B tokenizer designed for multiple languages, causing high token usage and unnecessary computation for unused entries. The VocabX method optimized the vocabulary based on cost per token, not frequency, achieving significant savings without altering the base model. This approach reduces fragmentation and excess in the vocabulary, focusing on frequently used tokens and minimizing costly computations during generation.

items.title: Profiling TorchNeuron (Part 1): System-level profiling on AWS Trainium.
items.content:
Many ML practitioners have some intuition about how to make models run fast, but fewer know how to analyze why a model is slow. In Part 1 of this series, you will learn how to systematically analyze inference performance and identify where the time is spent.

This post starts from scratch and assumes no prior profiling experience. The walkthrough uses AWS Trainium, a purpose-built AI chip for deep learning training and inference workloads, and TorchNeuron, its open source native PyTorch backend. TorchNeuron supports standard PyTorch workflows on Trainium, including eager execution, torch.compile, and standard PyTorch APIs, with minimal code changes. Additionally, TorchNeuron integrates with Neuron Kernel Interface (NKI) to enable custom operators and performance optimization for Trainium hardware. By the end, you should know:

  • How to configure torch.profiler with the Neuron backend and capture a clean trace.
  • How to read the key_averages() table to identify which operations consume Neuron device time and compare their Self CPU time.
  • How to follow one operation through Neuron Explorer, from framework dispatch through runtime scheduling to hardware execution on a NeuronCore.
  • How these signals change across three implementations of the same operation.

Neuron as a PyTorch Backend

Before you profile a workload, it helps to understand how Neuron integrates with PyTorch.

The Neuron backend uses PyTorch's PrivateUse1 extension point. This mechanism lets an accelerator integrate with the framework without adding a dedicated dispatch key such as cuda. The torch_neuronx package works with upstream PyTorch to register Neuron as a native backend for PyTorch code. For details about this extension mechanism, see Facilitating New Backend Integration by PrivateUse1.

Set Up the Profiler

You use two objects to profile a Neuron workload:

  • NeuronConfig controls which Neuron data streams and NeuronCores to capture and where to write the output. You pass it to torch.profiler.profile as experimental_config.
  • NeuronProfiler takes a NeuronConfig and provides an export_trace callback. The callback writes the framework trace, trace.json, alongside the Neuron system traces.
nc = NeuronConfig(
    modes=[ProfileMode.DEVICE, ProfileMode.RUNTIME],
    profile_output_dir=OUTPUT_DIR,
    capture_enabled_for_nc='0',
    correlate_device_time=True,
)
exporter = NeuronProfiler(nc)

The modes parameter selects the data streams to capture, such as device instructions and runtime traces. The capture_enabled_for_nc parameter selects the NeuronCores to trace. Setting correlate_device_time=True propagates device time from the trace into the key_averages() table, where you can compare CPU and Neuron device time. For the complete parameter reference and available ProfileMode values, see the NeuronConfig Profile Modes documentation.

Tooling: Neuron Explorer

Neuron Explorer is a browser-based viewer for the system trace, device timeline, and per-engine breakdown. You can access it through an SSH tunnel or the Visual Studio Code extension. In this post, you use Explorer to confirm what key_averages() reports numerically and inspect what happens between dispatches.

After profiling, the output directory contains the system trace and, when you capture device data, matched .neff and .ntff files. The Neuron Executable File Format (NEFF) contains the compiled Neuron executable, while the matching NTFF contains its hardware instruction trace. The files share a numeric hash that identifies them as a pair. To open the profile in Neuron Explorer, upload the complete output directory for a system or combined profile. For a device-only profile, upload the matching .neff and .ntff files individually. See Step 5: Upload your profile for the UI and command-line instructions.

Profile RMSNorm

For this first analysis, you profile RMSNorm, a small operation with a clear sequence of arithmetic and reduction operations.

You profile three implementations of the same operation:

  1. Naive RMSNorm with individual PyTorch operations: multiply, mean, add, reciprocal square root, and multiply.
  2. torch.rms_norm(), the PyTorch built-in lowered to a single fused Neuron kernel.
  3. Naive RMSNorm with torch.compile, using the same operations as the first implementation.

The scripts use the same inputs, profiler configuration, and schedule so the results are directly comparable.

All scripts to reproduce this work are available in the torch-neuronx examples directory.

Profile 1: Naive PyTorch Operations

Start by writing RMSNorm with individual PyTorch operations. Each line maps to one or more ATen operations and can create intermediate tensors.

device = torch.device('neuron')

x = torch.randn(4, 512, dtype=torch.bfloat16, device=device)
weight = torch.ones(512, dtype=torch.bfloat16, device=device)

def rms_norm_fn(t):
    x_sq = t * t                                    # square
    mean_sq = x_sq.mean(dim=-1, keepdim=True)       # mean of squares
    rms = torch.rsqrt(mean_sq + 1e-6)               # 1 / sqrt(mean_sq + eps)
    return t * rms * weight                         # normalize + scale

Call the profiler with two arguments required for the Neuron backend:

  1. Include ProfilerActivity.PrivateUse1 to collect activity from the Neuron device.
  2. Pass NeuronConfig as experimental_config to enable the Neuron-specific Kineto features.

The schedule uses wait=2, warmup=1, and active=1 across four prof.step() calls. This records one warm iteration without including initial setup overhead.

Call torch.neuron.synchronize() inside the profiler loop. Without this synchronization, the profiler can export before the device finishes and leave the Neuron time column empty.

with torch.profiler.profile(
    activities=[ProfilerActivity.CPU, ProfilerActivity.PrivateUse1],
    experimental_config=nc,
    record_shapes=False,
    on_trace_ready=exporter.export_trace,
    schedule=torch.profiler.schedule(wait=2, warmup=1, active=1),
) as prof:
    for step in range(4):
        with torch.no_grad():
            _ = rms_norm_fn(x)
        torch.neuron.synchronize()
        prof.step()

After profiling finishes, inspect the key_averages() table. Sort by self_privateuse1_time_total to place the operations with the highest device cost first. The table shown here is filtered to the RMSNorm operations that report Neuron device time. The full key_averages() output also includes CPU-side events such as allocations and host-to-device transfers.

print(prof.key_averages().table(sort_by="self_privateuse1_time_total", row_limit=4))

The key averages table shows that three aten::mul calls account for the largest share of Neuron device time.

The table shows which ATen operations ran, how often they ran, and how much time they spent on the CPU and Neuron device. aten::mul has the highest total device time because the function performs three multiplications.

Name # Calls Self CPU Self NEURON % NEURON
aten::mul 3 60.9 μs 1,164.5 μs 49.5%
aten::add 1 26.6 μs 434.6 μs 18.5%
aten::rsqrt 1 15.6 μs 415.0 μs 17.6%
aten::mean 1 21.1 μs 340.8 μs 14.5%

Self NEURON total: 2.355 ms

Each row maps directly to the function. aten::mul runs for x * x, x * rms, and the final multiplication by weight. aten::mean reduces the last dimension. aten::add adds the epsilon value and triggers a host-to-device copy because the scalar starts on the CPU. aten::rsqrt computes the reciprocal square root.

Neuron Explorer follows an aten::mul operation from framework dispatch through runtime scheduling to execution on the Neuron hardware lanes.

Read the Trace in Explorer

In Explorer, time flows from left to right and the event lifecycle flows from top to bottom. Each ATen operation follows the same pattern: creation in the framework lane, scheduling in the runtime lane as nrta_execute_schedule, and device execution in the hardware lane as nc_exec_running.

The system trace view organizes events into lanes. In the Default grouping mode, labels follow the pattern instance/PID/subsystem/identifier:

Lane Label suffix What it shows
Framework dispatch framework/TID:<id> Operator dispatch events (PrivateUse1 runtime), grouped by thread ID.
Framework device framework/Stream:<n> Device interaction events (PrivateUse1 driver), grouped by stream number.
Neuron Runtime neuron_rt/NC:<n> Neuron Runtime API calls, grouped by logical NeuronCore.
Neuron Hardware neuron_hw/NC<n>:<id> Hardware execution events, grouped by physical NeuronCore.

In eager mode, each operation runs independently. Use the dependency chain viewer to follow aten::mul.Tensor from the framework layer through runtime scheduling to device execution.

The dependency chain viewer highlights the lifecycle of one operation across the framework, runtime, and hardware lanes.

Profile 2: torch.rms_norm

Replace the individual operations with PyTorch's built-in rms_norm function. Neuron lowers the operation to one fused kernel:

def rms_norm_fn(t):
    return torch.rms_norm(t, [512], weight)

The fused RMSNorm appears as one device operation in the key averages table.

Name # Calls Self CPU Self NEURON % NEURON
aten::_fused_rms_norm 1 47.6 μs 403.3 μs 100%

Self NEURON total: 403.3 μs

The fused RMSNorm follows one framework-to-hardware path instead of dispatching each arithmetic operation separately.

Compare the Lowering Path

In the naive implementation, each operation crosses the dispatch boundary independently and follows its own framework-to-runtime-to-hardware path. In the fused implementation, one Python call covers the complete computation. The trace contains one dispatch and one hardware event, with no gaps between component operations.

Profile 3: Naive PyTorch with torch.compile

For the final example, compile the original naive RMSNorm function with torch.compile.

With @torch.compile(backend="neuron"), TorchDynamo captures the Python bytecode as an FX graph and AOTAutograd lowers it to ATen operations. The Neuron backend receives the complete graph instead of dispatching each operation separately. It fuses the operations, optimizes memory access, and compiles the graph into a single NEFF artifact. The artifact runs as one hardware dispatch.

@torch.compile(backend='neuron', fullgraph=True)
def naive_compiled(t):
    x_sq = t * t
    mean_sq = x_sq.mean(dim=-1, keepdim=True)
    rms = torch.rsqrt(mean_sq + 1e-6)
    return t * rms * weight

The compiled function appears as one Torch-Compiled Region in the key averages table.

Name # Calls Self CPU Self NEURON % NEURON
Torch-Compiled Region: 0/0 1 98.4 μs 375.5 μs 100%

Self NEURON total: 375.5 μs

The compiled graph follows one path through runtime scheduling and hardware execution.

The table shows one device execution, as in Profile 2, but the code takes a different path. Instead of calling a purpose-built fused operation, the compiler discovers the fusion from the original Python function. In this run, the Neuron time is comparable to torch.rms_norm, at 375 μs compared with 403 μs.

Side-by-Side Summary

Variant NEURON time Self CPU time Operator calls
Naive ops 2,355 µs ~125 µs 6
torch.rms_norm 403 µs ~48 µs 1
Naive + torch.compile 376 µs ~98 µs 1

Both torch.rms_norm and torch.compile fuse RMSNorm into one kernel dispatch. In these runs, either approach takes about one-sixth of the naive implementation's device time. Fusion removes the gaps between hardware executions and avoids materializing intermediate values such as x_sq and mean_sq between separately dispatched operations.

Conclusion

key_averages() shows which operations consume device time, while its full output also reveals CPU-side setup and transfers. Explorer provides the corresponding visual trace. You can follow one operation from framework dispatch through runtime scheduling to hardware execution and see the gaps that fusion removes.

You can use the same workflow on larger models: find a hotspot in the table, verify it in the trace, and then determine whether a fused operation or torch.compile can reduce its cost.

In Part 2, we will move into the device-level profile. You open the NEFF, inspect the TensorEngine, VectorEngine, and direct memory access (DMA) breakdown, and place the kernel on the roofline to determine whether it is compute-bound or memory-bound.

Special thanks to Aritra Roy Gosthipaty for the inspiration to begin this series, and to my peers Pinak Panigrahi, Samir Araujo, Akhil Azhikodan, Esha Lakhotia and the rest for reviewing!

items.title: Granite Speech 5.0: Transcribe, Translate, and Attribute more Accurately and Faster
items.content:
We're excited to share three updates to IBM's Granite Speech collection: a new speech-language model, granite-speech-5.0-2b, and revised versions of two models the community already uses, granite-speech-5.0-470m-turboctc and granite-speech-4.1-2b-plus. Together they cover the full range of enterprise speech work: transcription and translation with high accuracy, extremely fast transcription at the edge, and recordings where who spoke, and when, matter as much as what was said.

Model Status What's new Best for
granite-speech-5.0-2b New More accurate, noise- and reverb-robust automatic speech recognition (ASR), language-ID prompting, 2,000-term keyword biasing, better long-form translation High-accuracy multilingual transcription and translation
granite-speech-5.0-470m-turboctc Updated Multilingual, native punctuation and capitalization, and more robust to noise and reverb High-throughput and on-device transcription
granite-speech-4.1-2b-plus Updated Improved speaker attribution, timestamps, keyword biasing, and long-speech performance Meetings, calls, and other multi-speaker recordings

Granite Speech 5.0 2B: more accurate, more robust, more control

granite-speech-5.0-2b is the successor to granite-speech-4.1-2b at the same parameter count. It transcribes English, French, German, Spanish, Portuguese, and Japanese, and translates to and from English in those languages, plus English to Italian and Mandarin. It was trained on 390,000 hours of public audio, plus synthetic data built for Japanese ASR, keyword biasing, and translation.

What's new compared with 4.1 2B Speech:

  • More accurate, more robust English ASR: Higher accuracy on English short-form benchmarks, and better handling of noise, reverberation, and distant-microphone speech.
  • Language ID prompting: Name the input language in the prompt to steer multilingual transcription.
  • Better long-form and conversational translation: Translation holds up for longer with more natural speech, not just short read sentences.
  • Keyword lists up to 2,000 terms: Bias transcription and translation toward product names, people, and acronyms, in every supported language.
  • Punctuation and capitalization on request: Ask for formatted output in the prompt; capitalization F1 ranges from 89.7 to 99.5 across our test sets.

The model ships under Apache 2.0 with support in Transformers, vLLM, llama.cpp, and mlx-audio for Apple Silicon.

Chart 1: granite-speech-5.0-2b ranks #2 among top open-weight ASR models on average English WER (5.06%). Lower is better. Results are official, as of 21 October 2026, and averaged over the Open ASR Leaderboard’s public English short-form test sets.

Granite Speech 5.0 Turbo CTC: now multilingual, more robust, and even faster

When we introduced Turbo CTC in August, it was an English-only, 470M-parameter encoder built for speed. This revision keeps that footprint and adds the three things users asked for most:

  • Multilingual transcription: English, Japanese, Spanish, German, French, Italian, and Portuguese.
  • Native punctuation and capitalization: Transcripts come out ready to read, with no separate punctuation or truecasing step.
  • More robust in difficult acoustics: Training that explicitly targets reverberant audio makes Turbo CTC more robust in echoey rooms and far-field recordings.

It's also faster. By compiling a single Conformer block and reusing its graph across the stack, we cut warmup time and pushed Turbo CTC to 19,870 RTFx on the Open ASR Leaderboard, up from roughly 12,600 RTFx at launch: about 1.6x faster, at the same accuracy level.

Chart 2: Average WER vs. RTFx on the Open ASR Leaderboard (English short-form, 9 public test sets, as of October 2026). Lower WER and higher RTFx are better; RTFx is on a log scale.

Granite Speech 4.1 2B Plus: better at who said what, and when

The updated granite-speech-4.1-2b-plus is tuned for the recordings enterprises actually have: meetings, support calls, and interviews with several speakers running long. It keeps the 4.1 name because the architecture, prompt format, and API are unchanged, so it's a drop-in replacement for the current model with improved weights. This revision improves four areas:

  • Speaker attribution: More accurate labeling of who is speaking. Word diarization error rate (WDER) drops 7%, and speaker-attributed WER (cpWER) drops 7% overall.
  • Timestamps: Average timestamp shift (AAS) is cut by more than half, yielding tighter timing in captions, search, and review.
  • Long-speech performance: WER on long-form test sets drops 24%.
  • Keyword biasing: Errors on biased keywords fall 45% with 20-term keyword lists.
Capability Metric Previous release Updated model
Timestamps, all speech AAS (average timestamp shift) 210.86 98.54
Timestamps, short speech AAS (average timestamp shift) 29.27 26.20
Keyword biasing Biased-word WER, 20-term lists 11.79 6.48
Long-form speech WER, long-form test sets 13.53 10.22
Speaker attribution WDER 4.40 4.10
Speaker-attributed transcripts cpWER 30.50 28.48

Table 1: All metrics are error rates, so lower is better. For more detailed results, see the model card.

Get started

Not sure which model to pick? Start here:

  • Need high transcription accuracy, translation, or keyword biasing? Use granite-speech-5.0-2b.
  • Need raw speed or on-device transcription? Use granite-speech-5.0-470m-turboctc, and try it in the browser with our WebGPU streaming demo.
  • Working with meetings or multi-speaker calls? Use granite-speech-4.1-2b-plus.

These models are all released under an Apache 2.0 license with native support in Transformers. Full evaluation results, architecture details, training data, and usage examples are on each model card. We recommend pairing them with Granite Guardian for production deployments that need additional risk detection.

Give them a try and let us know what you think!

items.title: Hugging Face ❤️ TorchTPU: TPUs, Natively
items.content:
Update on GitHub

If you ever tried to run PyTorch on a TPU, you probably ported your code to torch_xla, or you ended up having to learn JAX. With TorchTPU, a native PyTorch backend, TPU is now just another device. It opens up native support of TPU in the Hugging Face ecosystem. Transformers, Diffusers and Kernels run natively on TPU. Pick a model from the Hub, send it to "tpu", and you're done.

Wait, what's a TPU? 🤔

TPU stands for Tensor Processing Unit. TPUs are Google's own AI accelerators. They are chips built for one job: the matrix math that neural networks spend most of their time on. Google has been designing them for about ten years, and uses them to train and serve its own models, including Gemini.

TPUs are available on Google Cloud, from a single chip up to pods of thousands of chips. They shine when you need a lot of compute, for training or for serving at scale.

The catch has always been software. The TPU stack grew up around TensorFlow and JAX, and PyTorch users had to work harder to get in.

The old way

Until now, running PyTorch on TPUs meant going through PyTorch/XLA (torch_xla). It worked, but it had its quirks. Tensors were lazy (the tensors, not you), so your code didn't always run when you thought it did. Small changes could trigger graph recompilations, and debugging was hard to reason about.

To make life easier, we built Optimum TPU. It gave Hugging Face models inference and training support on TPUs. Now that TorchTPU brings native support, Optimum TPU is not required anymore to run Hugging Face models with Transformers and Diffusers.

Enter TorchTPU 🚀

TorchTPU adds TPU as a new backend to PyTorch. You write regular PyTorch code. It comes with Pallas kernels tuned for TPUs, support for distributed training, and a torch.compile integration for when you want more speed. Installing it on a TPU VM takes one command:

pip install torch-tpu --extra-index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cpu

The extra index gives you the CPU build of torch. Without it, pip pulls the much bigger CUDA build, which you don't need on a TPU.

Your favourite libraries, now on TPU

Transformers

Transformers v5 was built around one idea: be the source of truth for model definitions, so they can run anywhere. "Anywhere" now includes TPUs. To load a model on a TPU, pass device_map="tpu". That's it.

from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM, AutoTokenizer

model_id = "Qwen/Qwen3.5-9B"
model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(
    model_id,
    device_map="tpu", # will load model directly on the TPU
)
tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(model_id)
inputs = tokenizer("The future of AI is", return_tensors="pt").to("tpu")
out = model.generate(**inputs, max_new_tokens=64)
print(tokenizer.decode(out[0], skip_special_tokens=True))

The model runs in eager mode by default. You can also use torch.compile for better performance, or run it in a distributed setup.

Images? Videos? Diffusers paints them on TPUs 🎨

TPU is now a first-class device in Diffusers. For prototyping or debugging, eager mode only needs pipe.to("tpu"). For deployment, compiled mode adds one compile call. Your pipelines and code stay the same, and there's no TPU fork to maintain.

import torch
from diffusers import StableDiffusion3Pipeline

pipe = StableDiffusion3Pipeline.from_pretrained(
    "stabilityai/stable-diffusion-3.5-medium", dtype=torch.bfloat16
)
pipe.to("tpu")  # eager mode: that's the whole change
# optional: compiled mode
pipe.transformer.compile(backend="tpu", fullgraph=True, dynamic=False)

image = pipe("a corgi astronaut planting a flag on a pizza moon").images[0]

The first call compiles, and every call after that with the same image size reuses the graph.

Models too big for one chip? Pass a TensorParallelConfig to from_pretrained and the transformer is sharded across chips as it loads, so the full model never has to fit in one place. Many popular pipelines support it out of the box, and the ones that don't are just a tp_plan away. The Diffusers TPU guide has the full recipe.

Here are some examples run on a Cloud TPU v6e-4:

TP=4 (each model split across four chips) · bf16 · batch 1

MiniMax-H3 (video + audio) Qwen-Image-2.1
"The fluffy plush Hugging Face mascot from the picture, a round yellow smiling face with rosy cheeks and two little open hands, stands at the prow of an ancient Greek trireme […] Sound of crashing waves, creaking timber, wind in the rigging, distant seagulls, and a low epic orchestral swell." · 1344×768, 5.2 s, 49 steps · 188 s compiled, 262 s eager "A capybara wearing a wizard hat, reading a book by candlelight, oil painting" · 1024×1024, 40 steps · 3.5 s compiled, 8.0 s eager "A neon shop sign that reads 'QWEN IMAGE 2.1', rainy night, reflections on wet pavement" · 2048×2048, 40 steps

Kernels

The Kernels Hub has ready-to-use TPU kernels. Load one with the Kernels library and give your model a speed boost.

TPU kernels are written in Pallas, which gives you low-level control over the hardware. You can also bring in kernels from the Tokamax library. Here is a ragged-dot kernel from Tokamax plugged into a Mixture-of-Experts model:

from kernels import get_kernel
from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM
from transformers.integrations.moe import ALL_EXPERTS_FUNCTIONS

repo_id = "tengomucho/ragged-dot-tpu"
kernel = get_kernel(repo_id, version=1, trust_remote_code=[repo_id])
ALL_EXPERTS_FUNCTIONS.register("tokamax_ragged_dot", kernel.experts_forward)
model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(
    "Qwen/Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507",
    experts_implementation="tokamax_ragged_dot",
)

The bigger the batch, the bigger the win. At batch size 64, decoding is 21.5× faster on Qwen3-30B-A3B and 12.8× faster on Gemma 4 26B-A4B.

Decode throughput on a TPU v6e-8, Hub kernel vs. the default implementation.

We test it so you don't have to 🧪

We're continuously improving TPU support in transformers by running the library test suite. We are working to add a nightly CI on TPU and make the results available in the (transformers dashboard)[https://huggingface.co/spaces/transformers-community/transformers-ci-dashboard].

The Transformers CI dashboard, with TPU results next to other accelerators. Work in progress!

It's not all green yet, and we're fine with that. Of the tests that run on TPU, 96.5% pass. Every failure we find becomes a small repro script and an issue on the TorchTPU repo. So far we have reported 34 issues, and 19 are already fixed. Running on TPU also caught a few bugs in Transformers itself, like in StaticCache and the Qwen3 tensor-parallel plans. We fixed those upstream.

If something breaks on TPU, we want to find out before you do.

Get started

TPUs are no longer a side quest for PyTorch users. Install TorchTPU, grab a model from the Hub, and send it to "tpu".

  • TorchTPU on GitHub
  • TPU kernels on the Hub
  • Cloud TPU documentation

We can't wait to see what you build 🤗. If you hit a problem, open an issue and tell us about it.

    "A capybara wearing a wizard hat, reading a book by candlelight, oil painting" · 1024×1024, 40 steps · 3.5 s compiled, 8.0 s eager
    "A neon shop sign that reads 'QWEN IMAGE 2.1', rainy night, reflections on wet pavement" · 2048×2048, 40 steps
  








Kernels


The Kernels Hub has ready-to-use TPU kernels. Load one with the Kernels library and give your model a speed boost.
TPU kernels are written in Pallas, which gives you low-level control over the hardware. You can also bring in kernels from the Tokamax library. Here is a ragged-dot kernel from Tokamax plugged into a Mixture-of-Experts model:
from kernels import get_kernel
from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM
from transformers.integrations.moe import ALL_EXPERTS_FUNCTIONS

repo_id = "tengomucho/ragged-dot-tpu"
kernel = get_kernel(repo_id, version=1, trust_remote_code=[repo_id])
ALL_EXPERTS_FUNCTIONS.register("tokamax_ragged_dot", kernel.experts_forward)
model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(
    "Qwen/Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507",
    experts_implementation="tokamax_ragged_dot",
)

The bigger the batch, the bigger the win. At batch size 64, decoding is 21.5× faster on Qwen3-30B-A3B and 12.8× faster on Gemma 4 26B-A4B.

Decode throughput on a TPU v6e-8, Hub kernel vs. the default implementation.




We test it so you don't have to 🧪


We're continuously improving TPU support in transformers by running the library test suite. We are working to add a nightly CI on TPU and make the results available in the (transformers dashboard)[https://huggingface.co/spaces/transformers-community/transformers-ci-dashboard].

The Transformers CI dashboard, with TPU results next to other accelerators. Work in progress!
It's not all green yet, and we're fine with that. Of the tests that run on TPU, 96.5% pass. Every failure we find becomes a small repro script and an issue on the TorchTPU repo. So far we have reported 34 issues, and 19 are already fixed. Running on TPU also caught a few bugs in Transformers itself, like in StaticCache and the Qwen3 tensor-parallel plans. We fixed those upstream.
If something breaks on TPU, we want to find out before you do.




Get started


TPUs are no longer a side quest for PyTorch users. Install TorchTPU, grab a model from the Hub, and send it to "tpu".
TorchTPU on GitHub
TPU kernels on the Hub
Cloud TPU documentation
We can't wait to see what you build 🤗. If you hit a problem, open an issue and tell us about it.

TorchTPU enables native PyTorch support for Google TPUs, integrating TPUs as a first-class device in the Hugging Face ecosystem. items.title: AnyLanguageModel 1.0: One Year of Local Models on Apple Platforms
items.content:
Update on GitHub

Last November, we introduced AnyLanguageModel on this blog: a drop-in replacement for Apple's Foundation Models framework that lets you choose the model and provider your app uses. We heard from app developers who were curious about local models but weren't always sure how to get started. They also wanted to avoid the added complexity of supporting multiple inference providers. AnyLanguageModel grew out of that feedback.

Local and hosted inference each have their strengths, and both have a role in building this new generation of intelligent apps. A shared API makes it easier to choose the right model for each task.

A year and dozens of releases later, AnyLanguageModel 1.0 is out, along with swift-huggingface 1.0 and swift-xet 1.0.

Here's what changed, and what's next:

A drop-in compatible API

The core idea of AnyLanguageModel remains the same: use the Foundation Models API with the model that fits your app. To get started, change your import statement:

- import FoundationModels
+ import AnyLanguageModel

The same session code then works with the system model, with open-weight models through llama.cpp, MLX, and Core ML, and with the hosted providers below.

Over the past year, we've added several major features:

  • Tool calling works with every provider.
  • Guided generation works with every provider, too, including nested @Generable types and arrays of them.
  • Image support lets you attach images to prompts using Foundation Models 27's syntax, including when you use the system model on iOS, macOS, and visionOS 27.

On OS 27, AnyLanguageModel also works with any model that conforms to Foundation Models' LanguageModel protocol, including Core AI models.

Alongside AnyLanguageModel, we've built out swift-huggingface and swift-xet to bring accelerated model downloads from the Hub to Swift apps.

Hosted models, too

Support for hosted models expanded this year, too. AnyLanguageModel now supports:

  • OpenAI's Chat Completions and Responses APIs
  • Open Responses, for any provider with a compatible endpoint
  • Anthropic's Messages API, with adaptive thinking and effort options
  • Google's Gemini API
  • Ollama
  • Private Cloud Compute, on OS 27
  • Hugging Face Inference Providers, and other OpenAI-compatible endpoints such as OpenRouter, through a custom base URL

With Inference Providers, you can use open-weight models that are too big to run on the device with the same session code:

let model = OpenAILanguageModel(
    baseURL: URL(string: "https://router.huggingface.co/v1/")!,
    apiKey: ProcessInfo.processInfo.environment["HF_TOKEN"]!,
    model: "openai/gpt-oss-120b",
    apiVariant: .chatCompletions
)

Hosted providers get the same features as local models: guided generation, tool calling with streaming, and token usage on responses.

Reasoning is now part of the transcript too. When you switch providers, reasoning blocks are automatically omitted from requests if the new provider can't replay them.

API keys come from a closure instead of a string, so your app can fetch short-lived tokens from your own server. The README explains when to let people bring their own keys and when to route requests through a proxy.

AnyLanguageModel also runs on Linux, so the same code can work on a server.

Open-weight models got better

While we've made local models easier to use, the models themselves have become more capable, making the small ones a good place to start. Here are some of the most downloaded models on the Hub right now:

  • Gemma 4 E2B from Google, in GGUF, about 3.4 GB at Q4_0 with quantization-aware training.
  • LFM2.5 2.6B from Liquid AI, in GGUF, about 1.7 GB at Q4_K_M.
  • Qwen3.8 27B for MLX from Alibaba, about 16 GB at 4 bits.

The first two fit on an iPhone, and Qwen3.8 27B runs on a Mac with 32 GB of memory or more. Selecting the MLX model takes one line:

let model = MLXLanguageModel(modelId: "mlx-community/Qwen3.8-27B-4bit")

And if you have four maxed-out Mac Studios handy, GLM-5.3 from Z.ai takes about 1.5 TB in BF16. For the rest of us, it's available through Inference Providers.

Upgrading to 1.0 

dependencies: [
    .package(
        url: "https://github.com/huggingface/AnyLanguageModel",
        from: "1.0.0",
        traits: ["MLX"]
    )
]

If you're upgrading an existing app, see the migration guidance in the AnyLanguageModel, swift-huggingface, and swift-xet release notes for help updating your code.

Community feedback and contributions have shaped several of our major features. Thank you to everyone who contributed for helping make AnyLanguageModel more useful to app developers.

What's next

Language models have proven to be a powerful tool for building intelligence into products. They're also one of many kinds of models developers can put to work. We're excited to bring the same approach to more capabilities: familiar Swift APIs with a choice of models running on the device. Coming soon: models that decide, and models that listen.

Links

  • AnyLanguageModel on GitHub
  • swift-huggingface on GitHub
  • swift-xet on GitHub
  • Introducing AnyLanguageModel
  • Introducing swift-huggingface
