items.title: MPS in PyTorch 2.15
items.content:
Update on GitHub

If you run models on your Mac or use MPS as your primary acceleration tool for computing, there's plenty to look forward to in PyTorch 2.15! FP8 arrives on MPS, language-model decoding gets faster paths through linear layers and softmax and new Metal kernels tackle some surprisingly expensive parts of audio, video and training workloads.

A quick word about who we are: we're the PyTorch team at Hugging Face. We contribute across PyTorch, and one of our focus areas is the MPS backend, where the goal is to make your Mac a first-class place to run and train PyTorch models. At the start of 2026, running even small models on MPS often meant working around unsupported operations, performance cliffs and unexpected memory growth. So we run real models from the Hugging Face Hub across language, image and video, find where MPS falls short and fix it upstream in PyTorch, more and more often by replacing MPSGraph with dedicated Metal kernels. Much of this post is the result of that work, done together with the PyTorch maintainers and community contributors.

TL;DR

  • FP8 comes to the Mac: store float8_e4m3fn values in half the space of BF16 and use scaled matrix multiplication and all other ops which are supported on CUDA/CPU!
  • MoE models decode 5–6.5× faster than in 2.14: Qwen3.6-35B-A3B goes from 9.4 to 61.3 tokens/s on an M3 Ultra, thanks to a native grouped matmul with a dedicated decoding path, fewer GPU-CPU syncs and faster top-k routing.
  • Less time per token for every LLM: single-row linear layers use specialized matrix-vector kernels, and softmax over the vocabulary is about 8× faster.
  • More linear algebra on the GPU: complex LU and triangular solves, faster small-matrix inverses, and faster QR decomposition.
  • Audio, video, and training get attention too: faster paths for convolutions, padding, dropout, interpolation backward and reductions. Wan2.2's video VAE decode now peaks at 8 GiB of memory instead of 270 GiB.
  • More control from Python: public MPS streams and more reliable event timing.
  • Updated requirements: MPS now requires macOS 15 or later; PyTorch 2.15 requires Python 3.11 or later.
  • A peek at 2.16: attention fully on Metal, more MPSGraph-to-Metal migrations and faster LLM decoding.

What this means for you

If you run models on a Mac with transformers, diffusers or tools like ComfyUI, here's what 2.15 changes in practice:

  • Much faster local LLMs. Mixture-of-experts models decode 5–6.5× faster than in 2.14: on an M3 Ultra with torch.compile, Qwen3.6-35B-A3B goes from 9.4 to 61.3 tokens/s and LFM2.5-8B-A1B from 23.6 to 123.6 tokens/s. Dense models benefit too, from faster linear layers and an 8× faster softmax for sampling. (More)
  • Video generation that fits in memory. Decoding a video with Wan2.2's tiled VAE used to push driver memory to 270 GiB; it now peaks at about 8 GiB. (More)
  • Correct image editing with Qwen-Image-2.1. On 2.14, the Qwen-Image-2.1 VAE encoder silently corrupted images on MPS, breaking image-edit workflows (reported in ComfyUI). The same padding change fixes it: an encode-decode round trip now matches CPU at 29.95 dB PSNR, up from 10.06 dB.
  • FP8 weights on your Mac. FP8 tensors take half the memory of BF16, and F.scaled_mm multiplies them directly on the GPU. (More)

Contents

  • Getting started
  • FP8 comes to MPS
  • Faster language-model decoding
  • Linear algebra gets a boost
  • Convolutions, padding, and training
  • Softmax and reductions
  • A much smaller memory footprint for video decoding
  • More control with MPS streams
  • More operations work on MPS
  • A sneak peek at PyTorch 2.16
  • Wrapping up

Getting started

You'll need an Apple silicon Mac with macOS 15 or later and Python 3.11 or later (see the 2.15 compatibility matrix). If your OS is too old or no Metal GPU is available, the MPS availability check now tells you why.

To try the release candidate in a separate environment:

uv pip install torch==2.15.0 --index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/test/cpu

FP8 comes to MPS

FP8 gives you another way to save memory on your Mac. PyTorch 2.15 adds torch.float8_e4m3fn tensors on MPS: one byte per value, half the storage of FP16 or BF16.

You can multiply these tensors with F.scaled_mm, which supports both tensorwise and rowwise scaling. Here's a small example with one scale per tensor:

import torch
import torch.nn.functional as F

def quantize_fp8(x):
    limit = torch.finfo(torch.float8_e4m3fn).max
    scale = x.abs().amax().clamp_min(1e-12) / limit
    return (x / scale).to(torch.float8_e4m3fn), scale

x = torch.randn(1, 1024, device="mps", dtype=torch.float32)
weight = torch.randn(1024, 1024, device="mps", dtype=torch.float32)
x_fp8, x_scale = quantize_fp8(x)
w_fp8, w_scale = quantize_fp8(weight)

y = F.scaled_mm(
    x_fp8,
    w_fp8.t(),
    scale_a=x_scale,
    scale_recipe_a=F.ScalingType.TensorWise,
    scale_b=w_scale,
    scale_recipe_b=F.ScalingType.TensorWise,
    output_dtype=torch.bfloat16,
)
print(y.shape, y.dtype)

Faster language-model decoding

Every LLM has a prefill phase and a decode phase. During decode, each new token goes through the model as a single row, so the big matrix multiplications turn into matrix-vector products. PyTorch 2.15 speeds up both kinds of layers that dominate this step: dense linear layers and mixture-of-experts layers.

Linear layers

MPS has had GEMV kernels for torch.mm since 2.14, but F.linear still went through MPSGraph. PyTorch 2.15 connects them to F.linear, so the common [1, 1, hidden_size] decoding input uses them directly, with eligible bias additions fused in. Across 96 BF16 layer shapes from real models, that's a 1.23× geometric-mean speedup. The biggest wins land on small projections, such as the gates in MoE models, where the old path left most of the memory bandwidth unused. Large layers and LM heads were already close to bandwidth-bound, so they stay near 1×.

Mixture-of-experts layers

A mixture-of-experts layer sends different numbers of tokens to each expert. Grouped matmul handles those uneven groups in a single operation, and 2.15 gives MPS a native implementation.

In 2.14, grouped matmul copied the group offsets to the CPU and looped over the groups. The new Metal kernels read the offsets directly on the GPU, using Metal Performance Primitives where available and a separate Metal path elsewhere. Small groups, the common case during decoding, get their own kernel as well.

For example, 64 tokens can be split into groups of 16, 32, and 16:

import torch
import torch.nn.functional as F

tokens = torch.randn(64, 64, device="mps", dtype=torch.bfloat16)
weights = torch.randn(3, 128, 64, device="mps", dtype=torch.bfloat16)
ends = torch.tensor([16, 48, 64], device="mps", dtype=torch.int32)

out = F.grouped_mm(tokens, weights.transpose(-2, -1), offs=ends)
print(out.shape)  # torch.Size([64, 128])

The decoding kernel shows up directly in token throughput. On an M3 Ultra with torch.compile, MoE models generate about 1.3× more tokens per second:

Linear algebra gets a boost

Complex-valued computations

Working with complex tensors gets easier. complex64 LU factorization, LU solve and triangular solve now run on MPS, which also unlocks the operations and gradients built on them, such as complex determinants. Here's a small system solved directly on the GPU:

import torch

a = torch.randn(8, 8, device="mps", dtype=torch.complex64)
a = a + 8 * torch.eye(8, device="mps", dtype=torch.complex64)
b = torch.randn(8, 2, device="mps", dtype=torch.complex64)

lu, pivots = torch.linalg.lu_factor(a)
x = torch.linalg.lu_solve(lu, pivots, b)
print((a @ x - b).abs().max().item())

Small matrices and larger solves

Small matrices get fast kernels too. For camera geometry and image transformations, batches of FP32 matrices up to 4 × 4 are inverted in a single Metal kernel that combines factorization and solving. Larger problems get attention as well: QR uses blocked updates, and triangular solves turn much of their work into efficient matrix multiplication.

Gated DeltaNet workloads get a dedicated fast path for batches of 16 × 16, 32 × 32 and 64 × 64 FP32 triangular systems with at least eight right-hand sides.

SVD is also more robust at numerical extremes. It now correctly handles very small singular values, very large or very small input magnitudes and basis completion with full_matrices=True, which in turn makes pseudoinverse and least-squares results more reliable.

Convolutions, padding, and training

Audio models, video decoders and training loops have their own expensive operations. This release gives several of them new paths through Metal:

Operation What changes in 2.15
conv1d forward Specialized kernels replace MPSGraph, plus an im2col-plus-matmul path for short outputs. Useful for audio and streaming-model shapes.
Constant padding Moves to Metal kernels, fixing runaway driver-memory growth in tiled video VAE decoding (more below).
Reflection and replication padding New Metal implementations that are faster and fix backward correctness.
Out-of-place dropout nn.Dropout and F.dropout now use the existing fused kernel.
Upsampling backward A Metal gather kernel replaces the MPSGraph resize-gradient path.
Channels-last conv2d backward Stays on an efficient channels-last path instead of an NCHW graph with costly strided access.

Softmax and reductions

Token sampling gets faster in 2.15 as well. softmax and log_softmax now run on dedicated Metal kernels, and large vocabularies benefit the most: an FP32 softmax over a [1, 128256] row of logits drops from 57 µs to 7 µs, about 8× faster than the MPSGraph version. The speedup holds across other common vocabulary sizes:

A much smaller memory footprint for video decoding

One of the most striking results in this release comes from the constant-padding change. The VAE decode in Wan-AI/Wan2.2-TI2V-5B-Diffusers makes 8,764 padding calls over a full 28-tile decode. With padding on Metal, peak driver memory drops from about 270 GiB to 8 GiB:

Memory metric MPSGraph padding Metal padding
Current tensor-allocation peak 4.422 GiB 4.095 GiB
Allocator-reserved peak 8.070 GiB 8.070 GiB
Total driver-memory peak 270.135 GiB 8.108 GiB

More control with MPS streams

You can now pick which MPS stream runs your work, directly from Python. torch.mps.Stream and the torch.mps.stream context manager provide the interface, and Tensor.record_stream lets the allocator track a tensor's use on another stream.

Here's a small example that sends work to a separate stream and synchronizes before reading the result:

import torch

x = torch.randn(1024, device="mps")
torch.mps.synchronize()
worker = torch.mps.Stream()

with torch.mps.stream(worker):
    y = x.square()
    x.record_stream(worker)

del x
worker.synchronize()
print(y.cpu().shape)

More operations work on MPS

Several more operations now run on MPS: torch.frexp, torch.logspace, torch.take and Tensor.put_, torch.heaviside, torch.special.laguerre_polynomial_l and unsigned-integer comparisons. logspace doesn't yet support integer or boolean outputs with more than one element.

Attention gets a correctness fix too: the MPS math implementation of scaled dot-product attention now handles batch and head broadcasting correctly.

A sneak peek at PyTorch 2.16

Work on 2.16 is already well underway. Some of the changes below have landed on main and are available in the nightlies; others are still in review, so details may change before the release.

Faster LLM decoding

Once a model's decode path no longer contains any MPSGraph ops, the GPU only starts on a token after the CPU has finished encoding all of its kernels. PyTorch 2.16 commits the command buffer every 16 kernels, so the GPU gets to work while the CPU is still encoding the rest. For compiled BF16 decoding at a 2048-token context:

Model Before After Change
LFM2.5-8B-A1B 108.8 tokens/s 126.0 tokens/s +16%
Qwen3.6-35B-A3B 52.9 tokens/s 62.8 tokens/s +19%
Qwen3.8-27B 12.1 tokens/s 12.6 tokens/s +4%

Attention runs entirely on Metal

Scaled dot-product attention is dropping MPSGraph completely: every shape will run on Metal kernels, with dedicated vector kernels for decoding and Metal Performance Primitives for half-precision prefill on newer macOS versions. The shapes that used to fall back to MPSGraph benefit the most. On an M5 Pro, decoding with grouped-query attention (32 query heads, 8 KV heads, head dim 80, 4K context) drops from 465 µs to 65 µs, and a 4K × 4K prefill with head dim 40 goes from 42 ms to 6 ms.

More MPSGraph to Metal migrations

The move away from MPSGraph continues. Batch norm forward and backward are in progress, while MSE loss (up to 12× faster on small inputs), std_mean and var_mean (up to 4× faster) and bincount have already landed. bincount is the most dramatic: when most values fall into a single bin, counting 4 million integers used to take 6.8 seconds and now takes half a millisecond.

A smaller install

Bundled shaders will build for Metal 3.1 by default, with Metal 4 versions compiled only for the kernels that need them. That shrinks libtorch_cpu.dylib by about 25%, from 384 MiB to 287 MiB, and lays the groundwork for Metal 4.1 shaders with faster matmuls and native FP8 matrix multiplication.

Wrapping up

PyTorch 2.15 brings FP8 to the Mac, faster LLM decoding for dense and MoE models, more linear algebra on the GPU and a long list of operations moved from MPSGraph to dedicated Metal kernels. Give the release candidate a try!

What's next for us

  • More MPS: 2.16 will run attention entirely on Metal, and we'll keep moving operations off MPSGraph.
  • torch.compile: we're working on getting rid of graph breaks, so more models compile end to end.
  • Your ideas: what else should we work on in PyTorch? If something is slow, missing or broken, on MPS or anywhere else, open an issue on GitHub and let us know.

A big thank you to Nikita Shulga, Kurt Mohler and Aaron Gokaslan for reviewing much of this work, and to everyone who contributed to MPS in this release.

If you run models on your Mac or use MPS as your primary acceleration tool for computing, there's plenty to look forward to in PyTorch 2.15! FP8 arrives on MPS, language-model decoding gets faster paths through linear layers and softmax and new Metal kernels tackle some surprisingly expensive parts of audio, video and training workloads.
A quick word about who we are: we're the PyTorch team at Hugging Face. We contribute across PyTorch, and one of our focus areas is the MPS backend, where the goal is to make your Mac a first-class place to run and train PyTorch models. At the start of 2026, running even small models on MPS often meant working around unsupported operations, performance cliffs and unexpected memory growth. So we run real models from the Hugging Face Hub across language, image and video, find where MPS falls short and fix it upstream in PyTorch, more and more often by replacing MPSGraph with dedicated Metal kernels. Much of this post is the result of that work, done together with the PyTorch maintainers and community contributors.




TL;DR



FP8 comes to the Mac: store float8_e4m3fn values in half the space of BF16 and use scaled matrix multiplication and all other ops which are supported on CUDA/CPU!
MoE models decode 5–6.5× faster than in 2.14: Qwen3.6-35B-A3B goes from 9.4 to 61.3 tokens/s on an M3 Ultra, thanks to a native grouped matmul with a dedicated decoding path, fewer GPU-CPU syncs and faster top-k routing.
Less time per token for every LLM: single-row linear layers use specialized matrix-vector kernels, and softmax over the vocabulary is about 8× faster.
More linear algebra on the GPU: complex LU and triangular solves, faster small-matrix inverses, and faster QR decomposition.
Audio, video, and training get attention too: faster paths for convolutions, padding, dropout, interpolation backward and reductions. Wan2.2's video VAE decode now peaks at 8 GiB of memory instead of 270 GiB.
More control from Python: public MPS streams and more reliable event timing.
Updated requirements: MPS now requires macOS 15 or later; PyTorch 2.15 requires Python 3.11 or later.
A peek at 2.16: attention fully on Metal, more MPSGraph-to-Metal migrations and faster LLM decoding.




What this means for you


If you run models on a Mac with transformers, diffusers or tools like ComfyUI, here's what 2.15 changes in practice:
Much faster local LLMs. Mixture-of-experts models decode 5–6.5× faster than in 2.14: on an M3 Ultra with torch.compile, Qwen3.6-35B-A3B goes from 9.4 to 61.3 tokens/s and LFM2.5-8B-A1B from 23.6 to 123.6 tokens/s. Dense models benefit too, from faster linear layers and an 8× faster softmax for sampling. (More)
Video generation that fits in memory. Decoding a video with Wan2.2's tiled VAE used to push driver memory to 270 GiB; it now peaks at about 8 GiB. (More)
Correct image editing with Qwen-Image-2.1. On 2.14, the Qwen-Image-2.1 VAE encoder silently corrupted images on MPS, breaking image-edit workflows (reported in ComfyUI). The same padding change fixes it: an encode-decode round trip now matches CPU at 29.95 dB PSNR, up from 10.06 dB.
FP8 weights on your Mac. FP8 tensors take half the memory of BF16, and F.scaled_mm multiplies them directly on the GPU. (More)




Contents



Getting started
FP8 comes to MPS
Faster language-model decoding
Linear algebra gets a boost
Convolutions, padding, and training
Softmax and reductions
A much smaller memory footprint for video decoding
More control with MPS streams
More operations work on MPS
A sneak peek at PyTorch 2.16
Wrapping up




Getting started


You'll need an Apple silicon Mac with macOS 15 or later and Python 3.11 or later (see the 2.15 compatibility matrix). If your OS is too old or no Metal GPU is available, the MPS availability check now tells you why.
To try the release candidate in a separate environment:
uv pip install torch==2.15.0 --index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/test/cpu





FP8 comes to MPS


FP8 gives you another way to save memory on your Mac. PyTorch 2.15 adds torch.float8_e4m3fn tensors on MPS: one byte per value, half the storage of FP16 or BF16.
You can multiply these tensors with F.scaled_mm, which supports both tensorwise and rowwise scaling. Here's a small example with one scale per tensor:
import torch
import torch.nn.functional as F

def quantize_fp8(x):
    limit = torch.finfo(torch.float8_e4m3fn).max
    scale = x.abs().amax().clamp_min(1e-12) / limit
    return (x / scale).to(torch.float8_e4m3fn), scale

x = torch.randn(1, 1024, device="mps", dtype=torch.float32)
weight = torch.randn(1024, 1024, device="mps", dtype=torch.float32)
x_fp8, x_scale = quantize_fp8(x)
w_fp8, w_scale = quantize_fp8(weight)

y = F.scaled_mm(
    x_fp8,
    w_fp8.t(),
    scale_a=x_scale,
    scale_recipe_a=F.ScalingType.TensorWise,
    scale_b=w_scale,
    scale_recipe_b=F.ScalingType.TensorWise,
    output_dtype=torch.bfloat16,
)
print(y.shape, y.dtype)





Faster language-model decoding


Every LLM has a prefill phase and a decode phase. During decode, each new token goes through the model as a single row, so the big matrix multiplications turn into matrix-vector products. PyTorch 2.15 speeds up both kinds of layers that dominate this step: dense linear layers and mixture-of-experts layers.




Linear layers


MPS has had GEMV kernels for torch.mm since 2.14, but F.linear still went through MPSGraph. PyTorch 2.15 connects them to F.linear, so the common [1, 1, hidden_size] decoding input uses them directly, with eligible bias additions fused in. Across 96 BF16 layer shapes from real models, that's a 1.23× geometric-mean speedup. The biggest wins land on small projections, such as the gates in MoE models, where the old path left most of the memory bandwidth unused. Large layers and LM heads were already close to bandwidth-bound, so they stay near 1×.




Mixture-of-experts layers


A mixture-of-experts layer sends different numbers of tokens to each expert. Grouped matmul handles those uneven groups in a single operation, and 2.15 gives MPS a native implementation.
In 2.14, grouped matmul copied the group offsets to the CPU and looped over the groups. The new Metal kernels read the offsets directly on the GPU, using Metal Performance Primitives where available and a separate Metal path elsewhere. Small groups, the common case during decoding, get their own kernel as well.
For example, 64 tokens can be split into groups of 16, 32, and 16:
import torch
import torch.nn.functional as F

tokens = torch.randn(64, 64, device="mps", dtype=torch.bfloat16)
weights = torch.randn(3, 128, 64, device="mps", dtype=torch.bfloat16)
ends = torch.tensor([16, 48, 64], device="mps", dtype=torch.int32)

out = F.grouped_mm(tokens, weights.transpose(-2, -1), offs=ends)
print(out.shape)  # torch.Size([64, 128])

The decoding kernel shows up directly in token throughput. On an M3 Ultra with torch.compile, MoE models generate about 1.3× more tokens per second:





Linear algebra gets a boost








Complex-valued computations


Working with complex tensors gets easier. complex64 LU factorization, LU solve and triangular solve now run on MPS, which also unlocks the operations and gradients built on them, such as complex determinants. Here's a small system solved directly on the GPU:
import torch

a = torch.randn(8, 8, device="mps", dtype=torch.complex64)
a = a + 8 * torch.eye(8, device="mps", dtype=torch.complex64)
b = torch.randn(8, 2, device="mps", dtype=torch.complex64)

lu, pivots = torch.linalg.lu_factor(a)
x = torch.linalg.lu_solve(lu, pivots, b)
print((a @ x - b).abs().max().item())





Small matrices and larger solves


Small matrices get fast kernels too. For camera geometry and image transformations, batches of FP32 matrices up to 4 × 4 are inverted in a single Metal kernel that combines factorization and solving. Larger problems get attention as well: QR uses blocked updates, and triangular solves turn much of their work into efficient matrix multiplication.
Gated DeltaNet workloads get a dedicated fast path for batches of 16 × 16, 32 × 32 and 64 × 64 FP32 triangular systems with at least eight right-hand sides.
SVD is also more robust at numerical extremes. It now correctly handles very small singular values, very large or very small input magnitudes and basis completion with full_matrices=True, which in turn makes pseudoinverse and least-squares results more reliable.




Convolutions, padding, and training


Audio models, video decoders and training loops have their own expensive operations. This release gives several of them new paths through Metal:

Operation
What changes in 2.15



conv1d forward
Specialized kernels replace MPSGraph, plus an im2col-plus-matmul path for short outputs. Useful for audio and streaming-model shapes.


Constant padding
Moves to Metal kernels, fixing runaway driver-memory growth in tiled video VAE decoding (more below).


Reflection and replication padding
New Metal implementations that are faster and fix backward correctness.


Out-of-place dropout
nn.Dropout and F.dropout now use the existing fused kernel.


Upsampling backward
A Metal gather kernel replaces the MPSGraph resize-gradient path.


Channels-last conv2d backward
Stays on an efficient channels-last path instead of an NCHW graph with costly strided access.










Softmax and reductions


Token sampling gets faster in 2.15 as well. softmax and log_softmax now run on dedicated Metal kernels, and large vocabularies benefit the most: an FP32 softmax over a [1, 128256] row of logits drops from 57 µs to 7 µs, about 8× faster than the MPSGraph version. The speedup holds across other common vocabulary sizes:





A much smaller memory footprint for video decoding


One of the most striking results in this release comes from the constant-padding change. The VAE decode in Wan-AI/Wan2.2-TI2V-5B-Diffusers makes 8,764 padding calls over a full 28-tile decode. With padding on Metal, peak driver memory drops from about 270 GiB to 8 GiB:


Memory metric
MPSGraph padding
Metal padding



Current tensor-allocation peak
4.422 GiB
4.095 GiB


Allocator-reserved peak
8.070 GiB
8.070 GiB


Total driver-memory peak
270.135 GiB
8.108 GiB










More control with MPS streams


You can now pick which MPS stream runs your work, directly from Python. torch.mps.Stream and the torch.mps.stream context manager provide the interface, and Tensor.record_stream lets the allocator track a tensor's use on another stream.
Here's a small example that sends work to a separate stream and synchronizes before reading the result:
import torch

x = torch.randn(1024, device="mps")
torch.mps.synchronize()
worker = torch.mps.Stream()

with torch.mps.stream(worker):
    y = x.square()
    x.record_stream(worker)

del x
worker.synchronize()
print(y.cpu().shape)





More operations work on MPS


Several more operations now run on MPS: torch.frexp, torch.logspace, torch.take and Tensor.put_, torch.heaviside, torch.special.laguerre_polynomial_l and unsigned-integer comparisons. logspace doesn't yet support integer or boolean outputs with more than one element.
Attention gets a correctness fix too: the MPS math implementation of scaled dot-product attention now handles batch and head broadcasting correctly.




A sneak peek at PyTorch 2.16


Work on 2.16 is already well underway. Some of the changes below have landed on main and are available in the nightlies; others are still in review, so details may change before the release.




Faster LLM decoding


Once a model's decode path no longer contains any MPSGraph ops, the GPU only starts on a token after the CPU has finished encoding all of its kernels. PyTorch 2.16 commits the command buffer every 16 kernels, so the GPU gets to work while the CPU is still encoding the rest. For compiled BF16 decoding at a 2048-token context:

items.title: TorchNeuron: running HF models on AWS Trainium is easier than ever
items.content:
Update on GitHub

TorchNeuron provides a new native backend for PyTorch on AWS Trainium. Transformers, Diffusers and Kernels natively support it, making it easier than ever to run models on Trainium and to share them on the HF hub.

TorchNeuron

TorchNeuron is a PyTorch plugin that brings a new backend for Trainium enabling support for eager mode, torch.compile and native distributed APIs like FSDP and TP. Read the Pytorch blog to learn more about TorchNeuron.

Starting Oct. 20, 2026, TorchNeuron will be available as a public beta. Researchers and developers will be able to install it with pip install torch-neuronx.

New backend, native interface in HF libraries

To date, the Hugging Face experience on AWS Trainium and Inferentia — AI chips designed respectively for cost-effective training and inference at scale — has been delivered through optimum-neuron. This library relies on the torch-neuronx package, which is based on PyTorch XLA. It was the natural choice at the time, but it meant thinking like a compiler: lazy tensors instead of eager execution, static shapes only, a recompilation for every graph break. Optimum Neuron existed to hide that complexity, and maintained custom code (modeling classes, trainers, etc) to do so.

TorchNeuron changes this. It integrates directly into PyTorch and exposes neuron as a native device, with eager execution, PyTorch's own distributed primitives (DTensor, FSDP2) and torch.compile.

For the Hugging Face libraries, Trainium becomes a device like any other: Transformers, Diffusers, Accelerate, PEFT and TRL run on it directly, with the same classes and scripts you would use on any other accelerator. From now on, we recommend that Neuron users use these libraries directly instead of going through Optimum Neuron.

Transformers

Inference

Text generation is now natively supported in Transformers for a wide range of models. With TorchNeuron, 89% of the top 100 most-used text-generation model architectures are supported out of the box, compared to 46% with Optimum Neuron v0.4.5. You just need to pass the device_map=neuron argument in your code and your model will be moved to the Neuron devices.

The following is an example of text-generation with tensor parallelism, which will enable to fully benefit from your Neuron instance. Note that it uses a static cache for generation as this is strongly recommended with Neuron to prevent frequent recompilations.

import os

import torch
import torch.distributed as dist
import torch_neuronx  # noqa: F401
from torch.distributed import DeviceMesh
from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM, AutoTokenizer, GenerationConfig
from transformers.distributed import DistributedConfig
from transformers.generation.configuration_utils import CompileConfig

MODEL_ID = "Qwen/Qwen3.8-27B"
MAX_SEQ_LEN = 1024
PREFILL_CHUNK_SIZE = 512

dist.init_process_group(backend="neuron")
world_size = dist.get_world_size()

model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(
    MODEL_ID,
    dtype=torch.bfloat16,
    distributed_config=DistributedConfig(tp_size=world_size),
    device_mesh=DeviceMesh("neuron", list(range(world_size))),
).eval()

tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(MODEL_ID)
if tokenizer.pad_token is None:
    tokenizer.pad_token = tokenizer.eos_token
tokenizer.padding_side = "left"

inputs = tokenizer.apply_chat_template(
    [{"role": "user", "content": "The future of AI is"}],
    add_generation_prompt=True,
    padding=True,
    tokenizer_kwargs={"pad_to_multiple_of": PREFILL_CHUNK_SIZE},
    return_tensors="pt",
)

generation_config = GenerationConfig(
    max_new_tokens=128,
    do_sample=False,
    use_cache=True,
    pad_token_id=tokenizer.pad_token_id,
    eos_token_id=tokenizer.eos_token_id,
    cache_implementation="static",
    max_cache_len=MAX_SEQ_LEN,
    prefill_chunk_size=PREFILL_CHUNK_SIZE,
    compile_config=CompileConfig(backend="neuron", fullgraph=False, dynamic=False),
)

with torch.no_grad():
    output_ids = model.generate(
        inputs["input_ids"],
        attention_mask=inputs["attention_mask"],
        generation_config=generation_config,
    )

if dist.get_rank() == 0:
    prompt_len = inputs["input_ids"].shape[1]
    print(tokenizer.decode(output_ids[0, prompt_len:], skip_special_tokens=True))

Training

Now that Neuron is a native PyTorch device, training on Trainium uses the same Hugging Face libraries as any other accelerator: Transformers, Accelerate, PEFT and TRL. You no longer need a dedicated trainer or a Neuron-specific fork of the model code. A standard TRL fine-tuning script runs on a Trainium instance with only a few Neuron-specific settings.

Here is a supervised fine-tuning script built on TRL's SFTTrainer. If you have fine-tuned a model with TRL on GPUs before, it should look familiar.

import os

import torch
from datasets import load_dataset
from transformers.distributed import DistributedConfig

from trl import ModelConfig, ScriptArguments, SFTConfig, SFTTrainer, TrlParser


def main(script_args, training_args, model_args):
    # The Neuron backend can't compile Dynamo's automatic dynamic shapes yet (https://github.com/huggingface/trl/issues/7660)
    torch._dynamo.config.automatic_dynamic_shapes = False

    training_args.model_init_kwargs = {
        "revision": model_args.model_revision,
        "trust_remote_code": training_args.trust_remote_code,
        "attn_implementation": model_args.attn_implementation,
        "dtype": model_args.dtype,
        "device_map": None,
    }
    if int(os.environ.get("WORLD_SIZE", "1")) > 1:
        # The model is sharded on the TP x FSDP grid as its weights are loaded
        training_args.model_init_kwargs["distributed_config"] = DistributedConfig(
            tp_size=int(os.environ.get("TP_SIZE", "1")),
            fsdp_size=int(os.environ.get("FSDP_SIZE", "1")),
        )

    # Prepare dataset
    train_dataset = load_dataset(
        script_args.dataset_name,
        name=script_args.dataset_config,
        split=script_args.dataset_train_split,
    )
    # UltraChat also has a string `prompt` column, which makes TRL treat it as a prompt-completion dataset.
    train_dataset = train_dataset.select_columns(["messages"])

    # Training
    trainer = SFTTrainer(
        model=model_args.model_name_or_path,
        args=training_args,
        train_dataset=train_dataset,
    )

    trainer.train()
    trainer.save_model(training_args.output_dir)
    trainer.end()


if __name__ == "__main__":
    parser = TrlParser((ScriptArguments, SFTConfig, ModelConfig))
    script_args, training_args, model_args = parser.parse_args_and_config()
    main(script_args, training_args, model_args)

Parallelism is handled natively by Transformers. You put a DistributedConfig with the tensor-parallel (TP) and FSDP sizes in model_init_kwargs, SFTTrainer passes it to from_pretrained, and the model is sharded as its weights are loaded. The Trainer sees that the model is already distributed and does not wrap it again. You don't need an --fsdp flag or an Accelerate FSDP config.

Nothing in the script is tied to Trainium: the same code runs on any hardware. A few things are worth knowing when you run it on Trainium:

  • Static shapes. The script disables automatic dynamic shapes in torch.compile and uses wrapped packing to produce sequences of up to 2048 tokens. With TRL ≥ 1.16, batches on Neuron are padded to a multiple of 128 tokens, limiting the number of input shapes. Compiled graphs are reused for subsequent steps with the same shapes.
  • torch.compile on. Passing --torch_compile true is all it takes: on a Trainium instance, torch.compile detects the device and picks the Neuron backend automatically, with nothing else to configure.
  • Async weight loading off. The built-in asynchronous weight loading in Transformers is not supported on Neuron, so for now we disable it with HF_DEACTIVATE_ASYNC_LOAD=1.

The command below launches training with torchrun, which starts one process per NeuronCore. TP_SIZE and FSDP_SIZE set the parallelism layout, and their product is the number of processes: here 4 x 8 = 32, matching --nproc_per_node. The 32 processes form a 4 x 8 grid. Tensor parallelism splits each layer across the 4 cores of a TP group, and FSDP shards the parameters, gradients and optimizer state across the 8 TP groups.

TP_SIZE=4 FSDP_SIZE=8 HF_DEACTIVATE_ASYNC_LOAD=1 uv run torchrun --nproc_per_node=32 sft_neuron_example.py \
    --model_name_or_path Qwen/Qwen3-8B \
    --dataset_name HuggingFaceH4/ultrachat_200k \
    --dataset_train_split train_sft \
    --output_dir Qwen3-8B-sft-tp4-fsdp8 \
    --dtype bfloat16 \
    --max_length 2048 \
    --packing true \
    --packing_strategy wrapped \
    --learning_rate 2e-5 \
    --warmup_steps 0.03 \
    --num_train_epochs 1 \
    --logging_steps 2 \
    --per_device_train_batch_size 4 \
    --gradient_accumulation_steps 4 \
    --save_only_model true \
    --torch_compile true

We ran it on 8 Trainium2 chips (32 NeuronCores), which is half a trn2.48xlarge instance.

Training runs to completion, and trainer.save_model writes a standard Transformers checkpoint. Nothing in it is tied to Neuron: you can push it to the Hugging Face Hub as is and load it on any other hardware.

Diffusers

Inference

Many pipelines from the Diffusers library are compatible with TorchNeuron in eager and compiled mode. FLUX.1-dev, FLUX.2, Qwen-Image, Qwen-Image-2.1 and H3 are also compatible with tensor parallelism to make the most of your Neuron devices. The following is an example showing how you can use TP:

import torch, torch.distributed as dist, torch_neuronx # TP
from torch.distributed.device_mesh import DeviceMesh # TP
from diffusers import QwenImage21Pipeline, QwenImage21Transformer2DModel, TensorParallelConfig

# Distributed devices initialization
dist.init_process_group(backend="neuron") # TP
dev = torch.neuron.current_device()
mesh = DeviceMesh("neuron", list(range(8))) # TP=8

# Pipeline initialization
model = "Qwen/Qwen-Image-2.1"
transformer = QwenImage21Transformer2DModel.from_pretrained(
    model,
    subfolder="transformer",
    torch_dtype=torch.bfloat16,
    parallel_config=TensorParallelConfig(mesh=mesh), # TP
)
pipe = QwenImage21Pipeline.from_pretrained(
    model,
    transformer=transformer,
    torch_dtype=torch.bfloat16,
)
pipe.vae.to(dev)
pipe.transformer.compile_repeated_blocks(backend="neuron", fullgraph=True, dynamic=False)

# Image generation
emb, mask, _ = pipe.encode_prompt(prompt="A capybara wearing a wizard hat, oil painting", device="cpu")  # text encoder stays on CPU
image = pipe(
    prompt_embeds=emb.to(dev),
    prompt_embeds_mask=mask.to(dev) if mask is not None else None,
    height=1024,
    width=1024,
    num_inference_steps=40,
    generator=torch.Generator("cpu").manual_seed(0), # same noise on every rank
).images[0]
if dist.get_rank() == 0:
    image.save("out.png")

You can run this piece of code with: NEURON_LOGICAL_NC_CONFIG=2 torchrun --nproc_per_node=8 run.py.

More and more pipleines will be compatible with TP. If a pipeline you like is not, you can also add support for it following this guide.

Kernels

Make sure to check out the kernels from the Neuron team as more and more Neuron kernels will become available on the Hub to speed up your models. Neuron kernels can be written using the Neuron Kernel Interface (NKI), which gives lower control to optimize operations. This way, users can run their own custom operations and share them on the hub.

You can use for example this kernel to speed up your vision transformers with up to a x2.4 speedup on Trainium!

Acknowledgments

Special thanks to the AWS team for their work on TorchNeuron and for their reactivity to our feedback to make the HF integration as good as possible.

TorchNeuron provides a new native backend for PyTorch on AWS Trainium. Transformers, Diffusers and Kernels natively support it, making it easier than ever to run models on Trainium and to share them on the HF hub.




TorchNeuron


TorchNeuron is a PyTorch plugin that brings a new backend for Trainium enabling support for eager mode, torch.compile and native distributed APIs like FSDP and TP.
Read the Pytorch blog to learn more about TorchNeuron.
Starting Oct. 20, 2026, TorchNeuron will be available as a public beta. Researchers and developers will be able to install it with pip install torch-neuronx.




New backend, native interface in HF libraries


To date, the Hugging Face experience on AWS Trainium and Inferentia — AI chips designed respectively for cost-effective training and inference at scale — has been delivered through optimum-neuron. This library relies on the torch-neuronx package, which is based on PyTorch XLA. It was the natural choice at the time, but it meant thinking like a compiler: lazy tensors instead of eager execution, static shapes only, a recompilation for every graph break. Optimum Neuron existed to hide that complexity, and maintained custom code (modeling classes, trainers, etc) to do so.
TorchNeuron changes this. It integrates directly into PyTorch and exposes neuron as a native device, with eager execution, PyTorch's own distributed primitives (DTensor, FSDP2) and torch.compile.
For the Hugging Face libraries, Trainium becomes a device like any other: Transformers, Diffusers, Accelerate, PEFT and TRL run on it directly, with the same classes and scripts you would use on any other accelerator. From now on, we recommend that Neuron users use these libraries directly instead of going through Optimum Neuron.




Transformers








Inference


Text generation is now natively supported in Transformers for a wide range of models. With TorchNeuron, 89% of the top 100 most-used text-generation model architectures are supported out of the box, compared to 46% with Optimum Neuron v0.4.5. You just need to pass the device_map=neuron argument in your code and your model will be moved to the Neuron devices.
The following is an example of text-generation with tensor parallelism, which will enable to fully benefit from your Neuron instance. Note that it uses a static cache for generation as this is strongly recommended with Neuron to prevent frequent recompilations.
import os

import torch
import torch.distributed as dist
import torch_neuronx  # noqa: F401
from torch.distributed import DeviceMesh
from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM, AutoTokenizer, GenerationConfig
from transformers.distributed import DistributedConfig
from transformers.generation.configuration_utils import CompileConfig

MODEL_ID = "Qwen/Qwen3.8-27B"
MAX_SEQ_LEN = 1024
PREFILL_CHUNK_SIZE = 512

dist.init_process_group(backend="neuron")
world_size = dist.get_world_size()

model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(
    MODEL_ID,
    dtype=torch.bfloat16,
    distributed_config=DistributedConfig(tp_size=world_size),
    device_mesh=DeviceMesh("neuron", list(range(world_size))),
).eval()

tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(MODEL_ID)
if tokenizer.pad_token is None:
    tokenizer.pad_token = tokenizer.eos_token
tokenizer.padding_side = "left"

inputs = tokenizer.apply_chat_template(
    [{"role": "user", "content": "The future of AI is"}],
    add_generation_prompt=True,
    padding=True,
    tokenizer_kwargs={"pad_to_multiple_of": PREFILL_CHUNK_SIZE},
    return_tensors="pt",
)

generation_config = GenerationConfig(
    max_new_tokens=128,
    do_sample=False,
    use_cache=True,
    pad_token_id=tokenizer.pad_token_id,
    eos_token_id=tokenizer.eos_token_id,
    cache_implementation="static",
    max_cache_len=MAX_SEQ_LEN,
    prefill_chunk_size=PREFILL_CHUNK_SIZE,
    compile_config=CompileConfig(backend="neuron", fullgraph=False, dynamic=False),
)

with torch.no_grad():
    output_ids = model.generate(
        inputs["input_ids"],
        attention_mask=inputs["attention_mask"],
        generation_config=generation_config,
    )

if dist.get_rank() == 0:
    prompt_len = inputs["input_ids"].shape[1]
    print(tokenizer.decode(output_ids[0, prompt_len:], skip_special_tokens=True))





Training


Now that Neuron is a native PyTorch device, training on Trainium uses the same Hugging Face libraries as any other accelerator: Transformers, Accelerate, PEFT and TRL. You no longer need a dedicated trainer or a Neuron-specific fork of the model code. A standard TRL fine-tuning script runs on a Trainium instance with only a few Neuron-specific settings.
Here is a supervised fine-tuning script built on TRL's SFTTrainer. If you have fine-tuned a model with TRL on GPUs before, it should look familiar.
import os

import torch
from datasets import load_dataset
from transformers.distributed import DistributedConfig

from trl import ModelConfig, ScriptArguments, SFTConfig, SFTTrainer, TrlParser


def main(script_args, training_args, model_args):
    # The Neuron backend can't compile Dynamo's automatic dynamic shapes yet (https://github.com/huggingface/trl/issues/7660)
    torch._dynamo.config.automatic_dynamic_shapes = False

    training_args.model_init_kwargs = {
        "revision": model_args.model_revision,
        "trust_remote_code": training_args.trust_remote_code,
        "attn_implementation": model_args.attn_implementation,
        "dtype": model_args.dtype,
        "device_map": None,
    }
    if int(os.environ.get("WORLD_SIZE", "1")) > 1:
        # The model is sharded on the TP x FSDP grid as its weights are loaded
        training_args.model_init_kwargs["distributed_config"] = DistributedConfig(
            tp_size=int(os.environ.get("TP_SIZE", "1")),
            fsdp_size=int(os.environ.get("FSDP_SIZE", "1")),
        )

    # Prepare dataset
    train_dataset = load_dataset(
        script_args.dataset_name,
        name=script_args.dataset_config,
        split=script_args.dataset_train_split,
    )
    # UltraChat also has a string `prompt` column, which makes TRL treat it as a prompt-completion dataset.
    train_dataset = train_dataset.select_columns(["messages"])

    # Training
    trainer = SFTTrainer(
        model=model_args.model_name_or_path,
        args=training_args,
        train_dataset=train_dataset,
    )

    trainer.train()
    trainer.save_model(training_args.output_dir)
    trainer.end()


if __name__ == "__main__":
    parser = TrlParser((ScriptArguments, SFTConfig, ModelConfig))
    script_args, training_args, model_args = parser.parse_args_and_config()
    main(script_args, training_args, model_args)

Parallelism is handled natively by Transformers. You put a DistributedConfig with the tensor-parallel (TP) and FSDP sizes in model_init_kwargs, SFTTrainer passes it to from_pretrained, and the model is sharded as its weights are loaded. The Trainer sees that the model is already distributed and does not wrap it again. You don't need an --fsdp flag or an Accelerate FSDP config.
Nothing in the script is tied to Trainium: the same code runs on any hardware. A few things are worth knowing when you run it on Trainium:
Static shapes. The script disables automatic dynamic shapes in torch.compile and uses wrapped packing to produce sequences of up to 2048 tokens. With TRL ≥ 1.16, batches on Neuron are padded to a multiple of 128 tokens, limiting the number of input shapes. Compiled graphs are reused for subsequent steps with the same shapes.
torch.compile on. Passing --torch_compile true is all it takes: on a Trainium instance, torch.compile detects the device and picks the Neuron backend automatically, with nothing else to configure.
Async weight loading off. The built-in asynchronous weight loading in Transformers is not supported on Neuron, so for now we disable it with HF_DEACTIVATE_ASYNC_LOAD=1.
The command below launches training with torchrun, which starts one process per NeuronCore. TP_SIZE and FSDP_SIZE set the parallelism layout, and their product is the number of processes: here 4 x 8 = 32, matching --nproc_per_node. The 32 processes form a 4 x 8 grid. Tensor parallelism splits each layer across the 4 cores of a TP group, and FSDP shards the parameters, gradients and optimizer state across the 8 TP groups.
TP_SIZE=4 FSDP_SIZE=8 HF_DEACTIVATE_ASYNC_LOAD=1 uv run torchrun --nproc_per_node=32 sft_neuron_example.py \
    --model_name_or_path Qwen/Qwen3-8B \
    --dataset_name HuggingFaceH4/ultrachat_200k \
    --dataset_train_split train_sft \
    --output_dir Qwen3-8B-sft-tp4-fsdp8 \
    --dtype bfloat16 \
    --max_length 2048 \
    --packing true \
    --packing_strategy wrapped \
    --learning_rate 2e-5 \
    --warmup_steps 0.03 \
    --num_train_epochs 1 \
    --logging_steps 2 \
    --per_device_train_batch_size 4 \
    --gradient_accumulation_steps 4 \
    --save_only_model true \
    --torch_compile true

We ran it on 8 Trainium2 chips (32 NeuronCores), which is half a trn2.48xlarge instance.
Training runs to completion, and trainer.save_model writes a standard Transformers checkpoint. Nothing in it is tied to Neuron: you can push it to the Hugging Face Hub as is and load it on any other hardware.




Diffusers








Inference


Many pipelines from the Diffusers library are compatible with TorchNeuron in eager and compiled mode. FLUX.1-dev, FLUX.2, Qwen-Image, Qwen-Image-2.1 and H3 are also compatible with tensor parallelism to make the most of your Neuron devices. The following is an example showing how you can use TP:
import torch, torch.distributed as dist, torch_neuronx # TP
from torch.distributed.device_mesh import DeviceMesh # TP
from diffusers import QwenImage21Pipeline, QwenImage21Transformer2DModel, TensorParallelConfig

# Distributed devices initialization
dist.init_process_group(backend="neuron") # TP
dev = torch.neuron.current_device()
mesh = DeviceMesh("neuron", list(range(8))) # TP=8

# Pipeline initialization
model = "Qwen/Qwen-Image-2.1"
transformer = QwenImage21Transformer2DModel.from_pretrained(
    model,
    subfolder="transformer",
    torch_dtype=torch.bfloat16,
    parallel_config=TensorParallelConfig(mesh=mesh), # TP
)
pipe = QwenImage21Pipeline.from_pretrained(
    model,
    transformer=transformer,
    torch_dtype=torch.bfloat16,
)
pipe.vae.to(dev)
pipe.transformer.compile_repeated_blocks(backend="neuron", fullgraph=True, dynamic=False)

# Image generation
emb, mask, _ = pipe.encode_prompt(prompt="A capybara wearing a wizard hat, oil painting", device="cpu")  # text encoder stays on CPU
image = pipe(
    prompt_embeds=emb.to(dev),
    prompt_embeds_mask=mask.to(dev) if mask is not None else None,
    height=1024,
    width=1024,
    num_inference_steps=40,
    generator=torch.Generator("cpu").manual_seed(0), # same noise on every rank
).images[0]
if dist.get_rank() == 0:
    image.save("out.png")

You can run this piece of code with: NEURON_LOGICAL_NC_CONFIG=2 torchrun --nproc_per_node=8 run.py.
More and more pipleines will be compatible with TP. If a pipeline you like is not, you can also add support for it following this guide.




Kernels


Make sure to check out the kernels from the Neuron team  as more and more Neuron kernels will become available on the Hub to speed up your models.
Neuron kernels can be written using the Neuron Kernel Interface (NKI), which gives lower control to optimize operations. This way, users can run their own custom operations and share them on the hub.
You can use for example this kernel to speed up your vision transformers with up to a x2.4 speedup on Trainium!





Acknowledgments


Special thanks to the AWS team for their work on TorchNeuron and for their reactivity to our feedback to make the HF integration as good as possible.

items.title: Welcome Beam: a 501B open model you can own, customize, and scale
items.content:
Update on GitHub

Beam by Reflection is out on Hugging Face! It is the first model from the new US lab, Reflection, and it’s open! It's a mixture-of-experts (MoEs) model with 501B parameters (23B active per token), supports text as input, has a context window of 1M tokens, and is released under the Apache 2.0 license.

Beam is focused on coding and agentic use cases. It is for teams that want a frontier-scale model on their own hardware, infrastructure, or cloud, and want to customize it to their own use cases. Beam ships with its own dedicated open source Rust based harness that delivers the best performance from the model.

Beam has a native transformers implementation, as well as downstream libraries like vLLM and SGLang. We’ve worked with the Reflection team to bring you inference, SFT (supervised fine tuning), and RL (reinforcement learning) recipes for you to build with this model for your needs. On top of day-0 support in transformers, SGLang and vLLM, this post shows you how to run it, how to post-train it, and what we built with it.

TL;DR

  • 501B-parameter MoEs LLM with 23B active per token. 52 layers, 256 experts per MoE layer, 8 routed per token.
  • Text in, text out with context window of 1M tokens.
  • Checkpoint formats: BF16, FP8, and NVFP4
  • Reasoning that can stay in context across turns (preserve_thinking), tool calling with a dedicated grammar. The model supports five reasoning values: "low", "medium" (default), "high", "xhigh", and "max".
  • Response template in the tokenizer.
  • Speculative decoding drafter model with DFlash2
  • Day-0 libraries: transformers, SGLang, vLLM. Full-parameter RL with Miles.
  • Ships with a Rust-based custom harness.
  • Apache 2.0.

Build with Beam

Reflection is going to give out $10,000 Hub credits to the best projects that use Beam. All you have to do is make a thing, and share it on the Hub:

  • You could make a demo that uses the Beam model on Spaces
  • You could quantize it for your favorite hardware
  • You could generate a synthetic dataset for your favorite problem
  • You could build an RL environment with or for Beam
  • You could benchmark Beam and share the results.
  • You could surprise us!

If you build something with Beam, then share it on the Hub for a chance to win $10,000. All you have to do is build the space, model, or dataset repo and share it on the model’s repo page. We’ll collect all the links, select the best, and send out the credits to your Hub accounts.

What is Beam?

Beam is a text-only model built for long-context (1M context length) reasoning and agentic work. It is a sparse MoE model, where each token is computed by a small fraction of the network, so it runs at the speed of a much smaller model while keeping the capacity of a large one.

Attention

The decoder has 52 layers with a hidden size of 5,120. Most layers use sliding-window attention over the previous 512 tokens; every sixth layer, and the last one, attend to the full context. That gives 43 sliding-window layers and 9 global ones.

Inside the attention block (both layer types)

The two kinds of layers handle position differently. Sliding-window layers use RoPE, since relative position matters most within a short window. Global layers use no positional encoding. Instead, each query is multiplied by a scaler that grows slowly with the number of visible tokens, (1 + (pos + 1) / 2048) ** 0.1. It acts as a temperature: the softmax keeps its precision as the context lengthens instead of flattening out. The implementation calls this scalable-softmax query scaling.

Attention uses grouped-query attention with 48 query heads and 8 key-value heads, with RMSNorm on queries and keys. A learned sigmoid gate, computed from the layer input, scales every channel of every head before the output projection.

Mixture of Experts

The first 3 layers use a dense SwiGLU MLP. The other 49 replace it with a Mixture-of-Experts block of 256 experts, each a SwiGLU MLP with an intermediate size of 2,560, or about 39M parameters. The experts hold 98.4% of the model's parameters.

The router follows DeepSeek-V3's group-limited scheme. It scores all 256 experts with a sigmoid, splits them into 8 groups of 32, keeps the 4 best groups (ranked by the sum of each group's top two scores), then picks the top 8 experts inside them. Beam uses the same group sizes as DeepSeek-V3 but no shared expert. Expert outputs are combined with normalized router weights and scaled by 2.5.

Only 8 experts run per token, so the model computes each token with about 23B parameters. All 256 experts stay in memory, so deployment needs the memory of a 501B model but runs at the speed of a 23B one. The BF16 checkpoint is about 1 TB in safetensors format. The NVFP4 checkpoint stores most parameters in 4-bit precision for NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs, some parameters are kept in BF16 for accuracy. There are also FP8 checkpoints on the hub which are ideal for Hopper and Ampere series chips.

If you want to deploy Beam yourself, check out the vLLM or SGLang recipes below.

Residual Stream

The residual connections are the most distinctive part. A standard transformer adds each sublayer output to the stream with weight 1, so the stream grows with depth.

Beam counts the input embedding as step 1. At step k it adds the sublayer output with weight 1/sqrt(k) and keeps the existing stream with weight sqrt((k-1)/k). The squares of the two weights sum to one, so the stream stays at a constant scale from the first layer to the last. After all 104 additions, every sublayer output and the input embedding carry the same weight in the final hidden state.

Every sublayer is also normalized before and after, and the final logits pass through a tanh softcap at ±30, computed in FP32. The implementation fixes where it computes in FP32: the router, the SwiGLU product, the norms, RoPE, the query scaling and the softcap.

Long Context

Hybrid attention works well for long contexts. Each layer caches 2 x 8 KV heads x 128 dims = 2,048 values per token. If all 52 layers kept every token, the cache would grow by 208 KiB per token. Only the 9 global layers keep the whole sequence. The 43 sliding-window layers hold a fixed 512-token window each and stop growing. So the cache grows by 36 KiB per token, roughly a sixth of the naive rate.

Context If all 52 layers were global Beam
32K tokens 6.5 GiB 1.2 GiB
128K tokens 26 GiB 4.6 GiB
Full context (1M) 208 GiB 36.08 GiB

These numbers are per sequence, in BF16, with the transformers dynamic cache.

Benchmark Results

Here are the benchmark results across different precision levels, as provided by the Reflection team.

Beam (BF16) Beam (FP8) Beam (NVFP4)
Agentic Coding / Terminal
DeepSWE v1.1 43.3% 43.0% 42.7%
SWE Bench Pro v2-Hard 76.5% 78.4% 78.6%
SWE Bench Pro v1 66.1% 65.9% 65.6%
Terminal Bench v2.1 80.1% 78.9% 78.2%
SWE Atlas Codebase QnA 31.8% 32.2% 31.4%
SWEBench Multilingual 78.3% 78.1% 77.5%
SWEBench Verified 81.6% 80.2% 80.7%
Reasoning
AIME 2026 97.7% 98.0% 97.5%
HLE (no tools) 36.0% 36.0% 34.8%
HLE (with tools) 51.1% 51.1% 51.1%
SciCode 49.2% 48.3% 46.9%
CriPT AA 16.3% 17.4% 15.4%
GPQA Diamond 90.6% 90.3% 89.3%
LiveCodeBench 88.3% 88.1% 87.4%
Tool Calling / Search
AutomationBench - public split only 39.3 38.2 39.8%
MCP Atlas 80.8% 81.5% 80.5%
Tau3 Banking 36.1% 36.8% 35.4%
BrowseComp w/ context management 76.8% 76.7% 75.6%
DeepSearchQA w/ context management 80.5% 79.6% 81.1%
General Capabilities
AA-LCR 78.2% 79.4% 78.7%
LongBench v2 67.5% 67.6% 67.2%
IFBench 79.6% 80.7% 79.2%
AA Omniscience (index) - public split only 10.8 8.8 9.8

Hardware Requirements

The most practical way to serve the model is serving the NVFP4 checkpoint, which retains most of the quality of the bf16 checkpoint. NVFP4 stores some weights in 4 bits, and this way, it shrinks the 501B parameters in BF16 from 1 TB to ~280 GB. Blackwell GPUs run NVFP4 natively but GPUs older than Blackwell like the H200 can't. The FP8 checkpoints are suitable for GPUs older than Blackwell.

A B200 has 180 GB of HBM3e, so two of them (360 GB) can hold the Beam weights, with little room left for activations and the KV cache. Plan for four B200s (720 GB), which leaves plenty of room for long contexts and concurrent requests. You can also serve it on a full 8xB200 node, or on two B300s at 288 GB each, or even 8xRTX Pro 6000. If you don't have Blackwell hardware, use Inference Providers (serverless) to test Reflection.

Inference Support

Beam comes with day-0 support in transformers, SGLang and vLLM.

Transformers

Install the latest version of transformers.

pip install -U "transformers>=5.20.1"

The easiest way to run Beam is the text-generation pipeline:

from transformers import pipeline

pipe = pipeline(
    "text-generation", model="reflection/Beam-1.0-501B-A23B", device_map="auto"
)

messages = [
    {"role": "user", "content": "Write a limerick about Python exceptions."}
]
output = pipe(messages, max_new_tokens=2000)
output[0]["generated_text"][-1]

The pipeline returns the whole chat. The last message is Beam's reply, already parsed by the response template.

Going one level lower, use AutoModelForCausalLM and AutoTokenizer.

from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM, AutoTokenizer

model_id = "reflection/Beam-1.0-501B-A23B"
tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(model_id)

model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(
    model_id, dtype="auto", device_map="auto"
)

Chat 

messages = [
    {"role": "system", "content": "You should only answer with a number."},
    {"role": "user", "content": "What is 17 * 23?"},
]

inputs = tokenizer.apply_chat_template(
    messages,
    add_generation_prompt=True,
    tokenize=True,
    return_dict=True,
    return_tensors="pt",
    reasoning_effort="medium" # by default
).to(model.device)

input_len = inputs["input_ids"].shape[-1]

outputs = model.generate(**inputs, max_new_tokens=2000)

tokenizer.parse_response(
    outputs[0][input_len:], prefix=inputs["input_ids"][0]
)

Beam's tokenizer carries a response template. parse_response reads it and turns the raw output into a message dict, with the reasoning, the answer, and any tool calls in separate fields. This avoids the usual regex for splitting reasoning from answers from tool calls. And the rules ship with the tokenizer, so the parsed structure matches what Beam was trained to produce. The chat template can pre-write part of the assistant turn, which the parser needs to see.

Tool calling

Complete tool-calling example 
def get_weather(city: str, unit: str = "celsius"):
    """
    Get the current weather for a city.

    Args:
        city: The city to look up.
        unit: Temperature unit, "celsius" or "fahrenheit".
    """
    ...

tools = [get_weather]
messages = [
    {"role": "user", "content": "I land in Paris tonight. Do I need a coat?"}
]

inputs = tokenizer.apply_chat_template(
    messages,
    tools=tools,
    add_generation_prompt=True,
    tokenize=True,
    return_dict=True,
    return_tensors="pt",
).to(model.device)

input_len = inputs["input_ids"].shape[-1]
outputs = model.generate(**inputs, max_new_tokens=1000)

message = tokenizer.parse_response(
    outputs[0][input_len:], prefix=inputs["input_ids"][0], tools=tools
)
message.get("tool_calls")

Pass tools to parse_response as well. Beam writes tool-call arguments inline, in its own XML-style grammar, so a bare 7 could be a number or a string. With the tool schemas, the parser casts each argument to its declared type.

Multi-GPU and multi-node

Beam's config defines an expert-parallel plan. Expert parallelism puts each expert on one device. Attention, the dense layers, the embeddings and the LM head are replicated on every device. That is 8B parameters, or 16 GB in BF16. Load the model with a DistributedConfig:

import os

from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM
from transformers.distributed import DistributedConfig

model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(
    "reflection/Beam-1.0-501B-A23B",
    distributed_config=DistributedConfig(
        tp_size=int(os.environ["WORLD_SIZE"]), ep_size=int(os.environ["WORLD_SIZE"]), tp_plan={}
    ),
)

Launch the script with torchrun across 16 H200 GPUs. Each one then holds 78 GB of weights. With 8 GPUs each would hold 139 GB, which leaves no room on a 141 GB H200. The number of devices must divide the number of experts, 256.

vLLM

Beam has day-0 support in vLLM. The command below serves the BF16 checkpoint with tensor parallelism across 16 GPUs (two 8x H200 nodes) and exposes an OpenAI-compatible API:

vllm serve reflection/Beam-1.0-501B-A23B --tensor-parallel-size 16 --served-model-name beam

For faster generation, add DFlash2 speculative decoding. A small drafter model proposes up to 15 tokens ahead, and Beam checks them all in one forward pass, so each step can accept several tokens. The cost is a little extra memory for the drafter:

vllm serve reflection/Beam-1.0-501B-A23B \
  --tensor-parallel-size 16 \
  --speculative-config '{ "method": "dflash", "model": "reflection/dflash2-drafter-preview", "num_speculative_tokens": 15 }'

Both commands start an OpenAI-compatible server, so you can point any OpenAI client at http://localhost:8000/v1. For additional serving configurations, see the proposed Beam recipe for vLLM.

SGLang

Beam also has day-0 support in SGLang. We recommend serving it with DFlash2 speculative decoding, which both commands below turn on. On Blackwell, the NVFP4 checkpoint fits on 4 B300s:

python -m sglang.launch_server \
--model-path reflection/Beam-1.0-501B-A23B-NVFP4 \
--served-model-name beam \
--tp 4 \
--attention-backend trtllm_mha \
--page-size 64 \
--context-length 1048576 \
--mem-fraction-static 0.85 \
--enable-unified-memory \
--speculative-algorithm DFLASH \
--speculative-draft-model-path reflection/Beam-1.0-501B-A23B-DFlash2 \
--speculative-dflash-block-size 8 \
--tool-call-parser beam --reasoning-parser beam \
--host 0.0.0.0 --port 30000

On Hopper GPUs, use the FP8 checkpoint on 8 H200s instead. Only three flags change: the checkpoint, the tensor-parallel size (8 instead of 4), and the attention backend (fa3 instead of trtllm_mha, which needs Blackwell):

python -m sglang.launch_server \
--model-path reflection/Beam-1.0-501B-A23B-FP8 \
--served-model-name beam \
--tp 8 \
--attention-backend fa3 \
--page-size 64 \
--context-length 1048576 \
--mem-fraction-static 0.85 \
--enable-unified-memory \
--speculative-algorithm DFLASH \
--speculative-draft-model-path reflection/Beam-1.0-501B-A23B-DFlash2 \
--speculative-dflash-block-size 8 \
--tool-call-parser beam --reasoning-parser beam \
--host 0.0.0.0 --port 30000

Inference Providers

Beam is available on Hugging Face Inference Providers, powered by Baseten, Fireworks, and Together, with more to follow soon.

import os
from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(
    base_url="https://router.huggingface.co/v1",
    api_key=os.environ["HF_TOKEN"],
)

completion = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="reflection/Beam-1.0-501B-A23B:auto",
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "What is the capital of France?"}],
)

print(completion.choices[0].message)

Inference Endpoints

We’ve set up a Beam recipe for you to one click deploy in Inference Endpoints from the catalog in FP8 or NVFP4, or install with the hf cli like so:

hf endpoints catalog deploy --repo reflection/Beam-1.0-501B-A23B --name beam

What we tested

We are sharing some vibe evals of Reflection Beam-501B-A23B on five tasks, once each at low and high reasoning effort through the Reflection platform. These are vibe evals, not benchmarks. If you’re planning on using Beam, this is a great way to kick the tires and see how it behaves on specific use cases, and importantly, where it wins and loses.

Below is an overview of the prompts we ran and the output traces from the hub. The complete inputs, outputs, API usage, task fixtures, graders and conversation traces are in this public Hugging Face bucket.

Category Prompt Description Low reasoning (tokens) High reasoning (tokens)
Multi-step tool calling Fulfill ORD-742: compare stock, reservations, surcharges and arrival dates; reserve the cheapest eligible warehouse. ✅ 544 ✅ 811
Long-context retrieval over a code base Derive Click command configuration and two invocation results from three complete source files; cite six implementation symbols. 🔴 1,613 * ✅ 5,007
Terminal task in a sandbox Inspect and repair a CSV ledger CLI; fix all bugs, preserve tests, run tests and a CLI check. ✅ 582 ✅ 1,548
Math reasoning (AIME-style) How many eight-element subsets of {1, …, 16} have a sum divisible by 17? Give a justification. 🟠 829 † ✅ 2,809
Structured output Convert an out-of-order revision log into strict JSON: merge patches, cancellations, nulls, dates, currencies and totals. ✅ 1,040 ✅ 2,088

* Low's long-context response got all code behavior and all six source citations correct. However, the response did not correspond to the parsers format, so this is partly prompt ambiguity.

† Low returned the correct answer, but omitted the requested justification. High supplied a correct roots-of-unity proof, independently reviewed.

Don’t take our word for it. Dig into the bucket, rewrite for your use case or project and push Beam to the limit.

Post-training Beam

You can fine tune Beam for your own use cases. Here, we share some examples in TRL and Miles to get you started on supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning.

SFT with TRL

The quickest way to adapt Beam to your own data is supervised fine-tuning with TRL's SFTTrainer. To keep memory manageable, we train LoRA adapters with PEFT rather than updating all 501B parameters: We used TRL’s SFTTrainer to adapt Beam to a simple goal: keep its reasoning in the language requested by the user. We fine-tuned on Multilingual-Thinking with LoRA, which trains a small set of adapter weights while keeping the base model frozen.

The setup combines model sharding at load time, expert parallelism, FlashAttention 4 and sequence packing. LoRA SFT fits on a single node with 8 B300 GPUs, reaching around 19,000 tokens per second. The corresponding H100 setup uses four nodes.

After one epoch of Multilingual-Thinking, Beam reasoned in the requested language on 16 out of 16 held-out prompts, compared with 3 out of 16 for the base model. This small evaluation measures language adherence, rather than the correctness of the reasoning itself.

Training loss (left) and mean token accuracy (right) during a separate 500-step run on a reasoning subset of open-r1/Mixture-of-Thought, using one 8-GPU B300 node. These training metrics are from the official TRL example PR.

GRPO with Miles

Reflection and RadixArk built a recipe that trains the model with GRPO in Miles, in BF16. You can update the full model or use LoRA to train adapters while keeping the base weights frozen. Megatron trains, SGLang generates the rollouts, and Miles publishes the new weights to the rollout engines after each update. We reviewed the recipe.

Workload Reference configuration
Inference / eval, BF16 16x H200 per engine
Full-parameter GRPO, BF16 (Miles) 96x H200: 64 train, 32 rollout. Or 64x H200 colocated.
LoRA GRPO, BF16 (Miles) 32x H200: 16 train, 16 rollout.
Full-parameter GRPO, BF16, 128-token context (Miles) 48x H200: 32 train, 16 rollout. The setup Reflection and RadixArk first validated on the real checkpoint.

The recipe runs GRPO on DAPO-Math-17K and evaluates on AIME25. Build the image, download the data, and submit the job to a Ray cluster of twelve 8x H200 nodes:

docker build -f docker/Dockerfile.beam -t miles-beam .

python scripts/run_beam.py prepare \
  --model-id reflection/Beam-1.0-501B-A23B \
  --model-dir /root/models/Beam \
  --data-dir /data/datasets

export MASTER_ADDR=10.0.0.1
export RAY_ADDRESS=http://${MASTER_ADDR}:8265

python scripts/run_beam.py execute \
  --model-dir /root/models/Beam \
  --data-dir /data/datasets \
  --output-dir /root/shared_data/beam-run \
  --num-rollout 100

What happens in a rollout:

Sample: 32 prompts are passed to the model with 8 responses each. Two SGLang engines serve the rollouts on 16 GPUs each.

Score: the boxed answer is checked against the label, with a soft penalty for responses near the length limit.

Update: one optimizer step on all 256 samples. Group-relative advantages with truncated importance sampling, no KL or entropy penalty.

Train in parallel: tensor parallelism 8, expert parallelism 8, data parallelism 8, with sequence parallelism and full recompute.

Optimizer: Adam at a constant 1e-6. Gradients in BF16, master weights in FP32, moments in BF16. The optimizer state streams through node-local NVMe, so each trainer node needs 2 TB of scratch.

Evaluate: AIME25 every five rollouts, eight samples per problem. A checkpoint is saved every twenty.

The next rollout is generated while the current one trains, so responses are one update behind. Add --resume to continue from the last checkpoint. execute-colocate runs the same recipe on eight nodes, with every GPU training and serving in turn.

Train with LoRA

You can also run GRPO with LoRA on four 8× H200 nodes: 16 GPUs for training and 16 for rollouts. The recipe trains rank-16 adapters on Beam’s attention, dense MLP, and expert layers while keeping the base weights frozen. Only adapter weights are synchronized with SGLang, and the optimizer state stays in GPU memory, removing the need for NVMe optimizer offloading.

python scripts/run_beam_lora.py execute \
  --model-dir /root/models/Beam \
  --data-dir /data/datasets \
  --output-dir /root/shared_data/beam-run \
  --num-rollout 100

Build with Beam: Demos

If you build something with Beam, then share it on the Hub for a chance to win $10,000. All you have to do is build a space, model, or dataset repo and share it on the model’s repo page. To inspire you, here are a few things we built.

Hey Beam, build a native local MacOS application!

At Hugging Face we love open and local models that run native to their hardware, but building native apps on Mac can be hard! Let’s see if Beam can help us out.

We asked Beam to build a native MacOS application that turns speech to text, and conveniently drops it at your cursor. We want to use MLX to get the most out of our Mac Metal and the Parakeet Model for great speech-to-text.

Build BeamSpeak, a native macOS menu bar dictation app with a compact recording pill and no main window or account.

Use ⌘⇧Space to start and stop microphone recording, showing elapsed time, microphone level, and transcription status. Run speech recognition entirely locally using a Hugging Face model, preferably Parakeet v3 through MLX, and keep the model loaded between recordings. Paste the transcript into the original app if it remains focused and Accessibility permission is granted; otherwise copy it to the clipboard, preserving newer clipboard changes and never pressing Enter. Handle permissions, cancellation, silence, errors, a two-minute recording limit, and temporary audio cleanup. Deliver source code, a runnable BeamSpeak.app, setup instructions, and verification of offline transcription, the physical shortcut, microphone capture, and text delivery.

We used Beam with the Pi coding harness to build the initial native macOS menu bar app, running Parakeet with MLX. The saved run includes follow-up prompts; the final source also includes later Codex repairs. The prompt above is a condensed version of the build requirements.

You can check out the agent trace of how Beam built this in pi in this trace. If you want to try the demo out, download the source code or read the setup instructions.

Hey Beam, how do you scale on multiple agents?

We wanted to see whether Beam could make faster progress by splitting a programming task across agents. We paired Beam with the open-source Pi coding agent and compared three setups: 1. one agent working alone, 2. five persistent peers collaborating through a shared Git repository, and 3. a lead agent delegating work to asynchronous subagents. The harness ran on Hugging Face jobs with inference through Reflection’s platform API.

For the tasks, we used ProgramBench: agents must recreate a program from its compiled executable and documentation, without seeing its source code or the evaluator’s tests. Each setup had the same 8M API-token ceiling and two-hour solver limit per task, shared across its agents. We saved implementation snapshots and evaluated them against fixed hidden-test suites from the ProgramBench-Tests dataset.

Our score-versus-latency plot shows the average fraction of tests passed. The time axis uses fixed reference rates for model tokens plus measured tool time, rather than elapsed wall time. We initially ran five tasks. The current figure shows a post-hoc subset of jq, xsv, FIGlet, and hexyl; ripgrep was excluded across all three setups because grading its saved artifacts was too slow. The published results retain all 15 original episodes.

You can inspect the runs in the Trackio dashboard, explore the published result data, and reuse the study harness.

Hey Beam, finetune a decision model for my code base!

Decision models are all the rage at the moment because they’re super fast and practical for many use cases. We started with Beam in Pi after Beam’s quota ran out to train and evaluate a custom decision model for developer incident triage.

We wanted to see whether a coding agent could turn an incident-triage policy into a small, fast decision model. The task was to read a developer incident and choose the responsible team, its severity, and whether someone should be pinged immediately. Using Unsloth, we fine-tuned Qwen3.5-0.8B to score these choices directly.

First, the workflow built a synthetic dataset containing 2.3k incidents split by incident cluster for training, calibration, and testing. We trained a LoRA adapter and decision head for three epochs, with a 4-bit backbone, on one H100 80GB on the Science Slurm cluster.

For a baseline, we prompted the unadapted model with the full triage policy and ticket, without examples, and asked it to generate the three decisions as JSON. On the same 320 synthetic test tickets, the fine-tuned decision model got all three answers correct on 76.25%, versus 4.69% for prompted zero-shot. Mean ticket latency fell from 1,218.06 ms to 102.58 ms, an 11.9× speedup.

If you want to try out this experiment for yourself, check out the artifact bucket which contains the data, code, checkpoints and results.

Wrapping Up

Beam is a 501B open model that you can run on your own hardware and change. Start with the BF16 checkpoint, or try one of the quants FP8, NVFP4. If you build something with Beam, share it in the discussions tab.
