Beam by Reflection is out on Hugging Face! It is the first model from the new US lab, Reflection, and it’s open! It's a mixture-of-experts (MoEs) model with 501B parameters (23B active per token), supports text as input, has a context window of 1M tokens, and is released under the Apache 2.0 license.
Beam is focused on coding and agentic use cases. It is for teams that want a frontier-scale model on their own hardware, infrastructure, or cloud, and want to customize it to their own use cases. Beam ships with its own dedicated open source Rust based harness that delivers the best performance from the model.
Beam has a native transformers implementation, as well as downstream libraries like vLLM and SGLang. We’ve worked with the Reflection team to bring you inference, SFT (supervised fine tuning), and RL (reinforcement learning) recipes for you to build with this model for your needs. On top of day-0 support in transformers, SGLang and vLLM, this post shows you how to run it, how to post-train it, and what we built with it.
TL;DR
501B-parameter MoEs LLM with 23B active per token. 52 layers, 256 experts per MoE layer, 8 routed per token.
Text in, text out with context window of 1M tokens.
Checkpoint formats: BF16, FP8, and NVFP4
Reasoning that can stay in context across turns (preserve_thinking), tool calling with a dedicated grammar. The model supports five reasoning values: "low", "medium" (default), "high", "xhigh", and "max".
Response template in the tokenizer.
Speculative decoding drafter model with DFlash2
Day-0 libraries: transformers, SGLang, vLLM. Full-parameter RL with Miles.
Ships with a Rust-based custom harness.
Apache 2.0.




Build with Beam


Reflection is going to give out $10,000 Hub credits to the best projects that use Beam. All you have to do is make a thing, and share it on the Hub:
You could make a demo that uses the Beam model on Spaces
You could quantize it for your favorite hardware
You could generate a synthetic dataset for your favorite problem
You could build an RL environment with or for Beam
You could benchmark Beam and share the results.
You could surprise us!
If you build something with Beam, then share it on the Hub for a chance to win $10,000. All you have to do is build the space, model, or dataset repo and share it on the model’s repo page. We’ll collect all the links, select the best, and send out the credits to your Hub accounts.




What is Beam?


Beam is a text-only model built for long-context (1M context length) reasoning and agentic work. It is a sparse MoE model, where each token is computed by a small fraction of the network, so it runs at the speed of a much smaller model while keeping the capacity of a large one.




Attention


The decoder has 52 layers with a hidden size of 5,120. Most layers use sliding-window attention over the previous 512 tokens; every sixth layer, and the last one, attend to the full context. That gives 43 sliding-window layers and 9 global ones.
Inside the attention block (both layer types)
The two kinds of layers handle position differently. Sliding-window layers use RoPE, since relative position matters most within a short window. Global layers use no positional encoding. Instead, each query is multiplied by a scaler that grows slowly with the number of visible tokens, (1 + (pos + 1) / 2048) ** 0.1. It acts as a temperature: the softmax keeps its precision as the context lengthens instead of flattening out. The implementation calls this scalable-softmax query scaling.
Attention uses grouped-query attention with 48 query heads and 8 key-value heads, with RMSNorm on queries and keys. A learned sigmoid gate, computed from the layer input, scales every channel of every head before the output projection.




Mixture of Experts


The first 3 layers use a dense SwiGLU MLP. The other 49 replace it with a Mixture-of-Experts block of 256 experts, each a SwiGLU MLP with an intermediate size of 2,560, or about 39M parameters. The experts hold 98.4% of the model's parameters.
The router follows DeepSeek-V3's group-limited scheme. It scores all 256 experts with a sigmoid, splits them into 8 groups of 32, keeps the 4 best groups (ranked by the sum of each group's top two scores), then picks the top 8 experts inside them. Beam uses the same group sizes as DeepSeek-V3 but no shared expert. Expert outputs are combined with normalized router weights and scaled by 2.5.
Only 8 experts run per token, so the model computes each token with about 23B parameters. All 256 experts stay in memory, so deployment needs the memory of a 501B model but runs at the speed of a 23B one. The BF16 checkpoint is about 1 TB in safetensors format. The NVFP4 checkpoint stores most parameters in 4-bit precision for NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs, some parameters are kept in BF16 for accuracy. There are also FP8 checkpoints on the hub which are ideal for Hopper and Ampere series chips.
If you want to deploy Beam yourself, check out the vLLM or SGLang recipes below.




Residual Stream


The residual connections are the most distinctive part. A standard transformer adds each sublayer output to the stream with weight 1, so the stream grows with depth.
Beam counts the input embedding as step 1. At step k it adds the sublayer output with weight 1/sqrt(k) and keeps the existing stream with weight sqrt((k-1)/k). The squares of the two weights sum to one, so the stream stays at a constant scale from the first layer to the last. After all 104 additions, every sublayer output and the input embedding carry the same weight in the final hidden state.
Every sublayer is also normalized before and after, and the final logits pass through a tanh softcap at ±30, computed in FP32. The implementation fixes where it computes in FP32: the router, the SwiGLU product, the norms, RoPE, the query scaling and the softcap.




Long Context


Hybrid attention works well for long contexts. Each layer caches 2 x 8 KV heads x 128 dims = 2,048 values per token. If all 52 layers kept every token, the cache would grow by 208 KiB per token. Only the 9 global layers keep the whole sequence. The 43 sliding-window layers hold a fixed 512-token window each and stop growing. So the cache grows by 36 KiB per token, roughly a sixth of the naive rate.

Hardware Requirements


The most practical way to serve the model is serving the NVFP4 checkpoint, which retains most of the quality of the bf16 checkpoint.  NVFP4 stores some weights in 4 bits, and this way, it shrinks the 501B parameters in BF16 from 1 TB to ~280 GB. Blackwell GPUs run NVFP4 natively but GPUs older than Blackwell like the H200 can't. The FP8 checkpoints are suitable for GPUs older than Blackwell.
A B200 has 180 GB of HBM3e, so two of them (360 GB) can hold the Beam weights, with little room left for activations and the KV cache. Plan for four B200s (720 GB), which leaves plenty of room for long contexts and concurrent requests. You can also serve it on a full 8xB200 node, or on two B300s at 288 GB each, or even 8xRTX Pro 6000. If you don't have Blackwell hardware, use Inference Providers (serverless) to test Reflection.




Inference Support


Beam comes with day-0 support in transformers, SGLang and vLLM.




Transformers


Install the latest version of transformers.
pip install -U "transformers>=5.20.1"

The easiest way to run Beam is the text-generation pipeline:
from transformers import pipeline

pipe = pipeline(
    "text-generation", model="reflection/Beam-1.0-501B-A23B", device_map="auto"
)

messages = [
    {"role": "user", "content": "Write a limerick about Python exceptions."}
]
output = pipe(messages, max_new_tokens=2000)
output[0]["generated_text"][-1]

The pipeline returns the whole chat. The last message is Beam's reply, already parsed by the response template.
Going one level lower, use AutoModelForCausalLM and AutoTokenizer.
from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM, AutoTokenizer

model_id = "reflection/Beam-1.0-501B-A23B"
tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(model_id)

model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(
    model_id, dtype="auto", device_map="auto"
)





Chat


messages = [
    {"role": "system", "content": "You should only answer with a number."},
    {"role": "user", "content": "What is 17 * 23?"},
]

inputs = tokenizer.apply_chat_template(
    messages,
    add_generation_prompt=True,
    tokenize=True,
    return_dict=True,
    return_tensors="pt",
    reasoning_effort="medium" # by default
).to(model.device)

input_len = inputs["input_ids"].shape[-1]

outputs = model.generate(**inputs, max_new_tokens=2000)

tokenizer.parse_response(
    outputs[0][input_len:], prefix=inputs["input_ids"][0]
)

Beam's tokenizer carries a response template. parse_response reads it and turns the raw output into a message dict, with the reasoning, the answer, and any tool calls in separate fields. This avoids the usual regex for splitting reasoning from answers from tool calls. And the rules ship with the tokenizer, so the parsed structure matches what Beam was trained to produce. The chat template can pre-write part of the assistant turn, which the parser needs to see.




Tool calling



Complete tool-calling example

def get_weather(city: str, unit: str = "celsius"):
    """
    Get the current weather for a city.

    Args:
        city: The city to look up.
        unit: Temperature unit, "celsius" or "fahrenheit".
    """
    ...

tools = [get_weather]
messages = [
    {"role": "user", "content": "I land in Paris tonight. Do I need a coat?"}
]

inputs = tokenizer.apply_chat_template(
    messages,
    tools=tools,
    add_generation_prompt=True,
    tokenize=True,
    return_dict=True,
    return_tensors="pt",
).to(model.device)

input_len = inputs["input_ids"].shape[-1]
outputs = model.generate(**inputs, max_new_tokens=1000)

message = tokenizer.parse_response(
    outputs[0][input_len:], prefix=inputs["input_ids"][0], tools=tools
)
message.get("tool_calls")

Pass tools to parse_response as well. Beam writes tool-call arguments inline, in its own XML-style grammar, so a bare 7 could be a number or a string. With the tool schemas, the parser casts each argument to its declared type.




Multi-GPU and multi-node


Beam's config defines an expert-parallel plan. Expert parallelism puts each expert on one device. Attention, the dense layers, the embeddings and the LM head are replicated on every device. That is 8B parameters, or 16 GB in BF16. Load the model with a DistributedConfig:
import os

from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM
from transformers.distributed import DistributedConfig

model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(
    "reflection/Beam-1.0-501B-A23B",
    distributed_config=DistributedConfig(
        tp_size=int(os.environ["WORLD_SIZE"]), ep_size=int(os.environ["WORLD_SIZE"]), tp_plan={}
    ),
)

Launch the script with torchrun across 16 H200 GPUs. Each one then holds 78 GB of weights. With 8 GPUs each would hold 139 GB, which leaves no room on a 141 GB H200. The number of devices must divide the number of experts, 256.




vLLM


Beam has day-0 support in vLLM. The command below serves the BF16 checkpoint with tensor parallelism across 16 GPUs (two 8x H200 nodes) and exposes an OpenAI-compatible API:
vllm serve reflection/Beam-1.0-501B-A23B --tensor-parallel-size 16 --served-model-name beam

For faster generation, add DFlash2 speculative decoding. A small drafter model proposes up to 15 tokens ahead, and Beam checks them all in one forward pass, so each step can accept several tokens. The cost is a little extra memory for the drafter:
vllm serve reflection/Beam-1.0-501B-A23B \
  --tensor-parallel-size 16 \
  --speculative-config '{ "method": "dflash", "model": "reflection/dflash2-drafter-preview", "num_speculative_tokens": 15 }'

Both commands start an OpenAI-compatible server, so you can point any OpenAI client at http://localhost:8000/v1. For additional serving configurations, see the proposed Beam recipe for vLLM.




SGLang


Beam also has day-0 support in SGLang. We recommend serving it with DFlash2 speculative decoding, which both commands below turn on. On Blackwell, the NVFP4 checkpoint fits on 4 B300s:
python -m sglang.launch_server \
--model-path reflection/Beam-1.0-501B-A23B-NVFP4 \
--served-model-name beam \
--tp 4 \
--attention-backend trtllm_mha \
--page-size 64 \
--context-length 1048576 \
--mem-fraction-static 0.85 \
--enable-unified-memory \
--speculative-algorithm DFLASH \
--speculative-draft-model-path reflection/Beam-1.0-501B-A23B-DFlash2 \
--speculative-dflash-block-size 8 \
--tool-call-parser beam --reasoning-parser beam \
--host 0.0.0.0 --port 30000

On Hopper GPUs, use the FP8 checkpoint on 8 H200s instead. Only three flags change: the checkpoint, the tensor-parallel size (8 instead of 4), and the attention backend (fa3 instead of trtllm_mha, which needs Blackwell):
python -m sglang.launch_server \
--model-path reflection/Beam-1.0-501B-A23B-FP8 \
--served-model-name beam \
--tp 8 \
--attention-backend fa3 \
--page-size 64 \
--context-length 1048576 \
--mem-fraction-static 0.85 \
--enable-unified-memory \
--speculative-algorithm DFLASH \
--speculative-draft-model-path reflection/Beam-1.0-501B-A23B-DFlash2 \
--speculative-dflash-block-size 8 \
--tool-call-parser beam --reasoning-parser beam \
--host 0.0.0.0 --port 30000





Inference Providers


Beam is available on Hugging Face Inference Providers, powered by Baseten, Fireworks, and Together, with more to follow soon.
import os
from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(
    base_url="https://router.huggingface.co/v1",
    api_key=os.environ["HF_TOKEN"],
)

completion = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="reflection/Beam-1.0-501B-A23B:auto",
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "What is the capital of France?"}],
)

print(completion.choices[0].message)





Inference Endpoints


We’ve set up a Beam recipe for you to one click deploy in Inference Endpoints from the catalog in FP8 or NVFP4, or install with the hf cli like so:
hf endpoints catalog deploy --repo reflection/Beam-1.0-501B-A23B --name beam





What we tested


We are sharing some vibe evals of Reflection Beam-501B-A23B on five tasks, once each at low and high reasoning effort through the Reflection platform. These are vibe evals, not benchmarks. If you’re planning on using Beam, this is a great way to kick the tires and see how it behaves on specific use cases, and importantly, where it wins and loses.
Below is an overview of the prompts we ran and the output traces from the hub. The complete inputs, outputs, API usage, task fixtures, graders and conversation traces are in this public Hugging Face bucket.

Category
Prompt Description
Low reasoning (tokens)
High reasoning (tokens)



Multi-step tool calling
Fulfill ORD-742: compare stock, reservations, surcharges and arrival dates; reserve the cheapest eligible warehouse.
✅ 544
✅ 811


Long-context retrieval over a code base
Derive Click command configuration and two invocation results from three complete source files; cite six implementation symbols.
🔴 1,613 *
✅ 5,007


Terminal task in a sandbox
Inspect and repair a CSV ledger CLI; fix all bugs, preserve tests, run tests and a CLI check.
✅ 582
✅ 1,548


Math reasoning (AIME-style)
How many eight-element subsets of {1, …, 16} have a sum divisible by 17? Give a justification.
🟠 829 †
✅ 2,809


Structured output
Convert an out-of-order revision log into strict JSON: merge patches, cancellations, nulls, dates, currencies and totals.
✅ 1,040
✅ 2,088




* Low's long-context response got all code behavior and all six source citations correct. However, the response did not correspond to the parsers format, so this is partly prompt ambiguity.
† Low returned the correct answer, but omitted the requested justification. High supplied a correct roots-of-unity proof, independently reviewed.
Don’t take our word for it. Dig into the bucket, rewrite for your use case or project and push Beam to the limit.




Post-training Beam


You can fine tune Beam for your own use cases. Here, we share some examples in TRL and Miles to get you started on supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning.




SFT with TRL


The quickest way to adapt Beam to your own data is supervised fine-tuning with TRL's SFTTrainer. To keep memory manageable, we train LoRA adapters with PEFT rather than updating all 501B parameters:
We used TRL’s SFTTrainer to adapt Beam to a simple goal: keep its reasoning in the language requested by the user. We fine-tuned on Multilingual-Thinking with LoRA, which trains a small set of adapter weights while keeping the base model frozen.
The setup combines model sharding at load time, expert parallelism, FlashAttention 4 and sequence packing. LoRA SFT fits on a single node with 8 B300 GPUs, reaching around 19,000 tokens per second. The corresponding H100 setup uses four nodes.
After one epoch of Multilingual-Thinking, Beam reasoned in the requested language on 16 out of 16 held-out prompts, compared with 3 out of 16 for the base model. This small evaluation measures language adherence, rather than the correctness of the reasoning itself.
Training loss (left) and mean token accuracy (right) during a separate 500-step run on a reasoning subset of open-r1/Mixture-of-Thought, using one 8-GPU B300 node. These training metrics are from the official TRL example PR.




GRPO with Miles


Reflection and RadixArk built a recipe that trains the model with GRPO in Miles, in BF16. You can update the full model or use LoRA to train adapters while keeping the base weights frozen. Megatron trains, SGLang generates the rollouts, and Miles publishes the new weights to the rollout engines after each update. We reviewed the recipe.

Workload
Reference configuration



Inference / eval, BF16
16x H200 per engine


Full-parameter GRPO, BF16 (Miles)
96x H200: 64 train, 32 rollout. Or 64x H200 colocated.


LoRA GRPO, BF16 (Miles)
32x H200: 16 train, 16 rollout.


Full-parameter GRPO, BF16, 128-token context (Miles)
48x H200: 32 train, 16 rollout. The setup Reflection and RadixArk first validated on the real checkpoint.




The recipe runs GRPO on DAPO-Math-17K and evaluates on AIME25. Build the image, download the data, and submit the job to a Ray cluster of twelve 8x H200 nodes:
docker build -f docker/Dockerfile.beam -t miles-beam .

python scripts/run_beam.py prepare \
  --model-id reflection/Beam-1.0-501B-A23B \
  --model-dir /root/models/Beam \
  --data-dir /data/datasets

export MASTER_ADDR=10.0.0.1
export RAY_ADDRESS=http://${MASTER_ADDR}:8265

python scripts/run_beam.py execute \
  --model-dir /root/models/Beam \
  --data-dir /data/datasets \
  --output-dir /root/shared_data/beam-run \
  --num-rollout 100

What happens in a rollout:
Sample: 32 prompts are passed to the model with 8 responses each. Two SGLang engines serve the rollouts on 16 GPUs each.
Score: the boxed answer is checked against the label, with a soft penalty for responses near the length limit.
Update: one optimizer step on all 256 samples. Group-relative advantages with truncated importance sampling, no KL or entropy penalty.
Train in parallel: tensor parallelism 8, expert parallelism 8, data parallelism 8, with sequence parallelism and full recompute.
Optimizer: Adam at a constant 1e-6. Gradients in BF16, master weights in FP32, moments in BF16. The optimizer state streams through node-local NVMe, so each trainer node needs 2 TB of scratch.
Evaluate: AIME25 every five rollouts, eight samples per problem. A checkpoint is saved every twenty.
The next rollout is generated while the current one trains, so responses are one update behind. Add --resume to continue from the last checkpoint. execute-colocate runs the same recipe on eight nodes, with every GPU training and serving in turn.




Train with LoRA


You can also run GRPO with LoRA on four 8× H200 nodes: 16 GPUs for training and 16 for rollouts. The recipe trains rank-16 adapters on Beam’s attention, dense MLP, and expert layers while keeping the base weights frozen. Only adapter weights are synchronized with SGLang, and the optimizer state stays in GPU memory, removing the need for NVMe optimizer offloading.
python scripts/run_beam_lora.py execute \
  --model-dir /root/models/Beam \
  --data-dir /data/datasets \
  --output-dir /root/shared_data/beam-run \
  --num-rollout 100





Build with Beam: Demos


If you build something with Beam, then share it on the Hub for a chance to win $10,000. All you have to do is build a space, model, or dataset repo and share it on the model’s repo page. To inspire you, here are a few things we built.




Hey Beam, build a native local MacOS application!


At Hugging Face we love open and local models that run native to their hardware, but building native apps on Mac can be hard! Let’s see if Beam can help us out.
We asked Beam to build a native MacOS application that turns speech to text, and conveniently drops it at your cursor. We want to use MLX to get the most out of our Mac Metal and the Parakeet Model for great speech-to-text.
Build BeamSpeak, a native macOS menu bar dictation app with a compact recording pill and no main window or account.

Use ⌘⇧Space to start and stop microphone recording, showing elapsed time, microphone level, and transcription status. Run speech recognition entirely locally using a Hugging Face model, preferably Parakeet v3 through MLX, and keep the model loaded between recordings. Paste the transcript into the original app if it remains focused and Accessibility permission is granted; otherwise copy it to the clipboard, preserving newer clipboard changes and never pressing Enter. Handle permissions, cancellation, silence, errors, a two-minute recording limit, and temporary audio cleanup. Deliver source code, a runnable BeamSpeak.app, setup instructions, and verification of offline transcription, the physical shortcut, microphone capture, and text delivery.

We used Beam with the Pi coding harness to build the initial native macOS menu bar app, running Parakeet with MLX. The saved run includes follow-up prompts; the final source also includes later Codex repairs. The prompt above is a condensed version of the build requirements.
You can check out the agent trace of how Beam built this in pi in this trace. If you want to try the demo out, download the source code or read the setup instructions.




Hey Beam, how do you scale on multiple agents?


We wanted to see whether Beam could make faster progress by splitting a programming task across agents. We paired Beam with the open-source Pi coding agent and compared three setups: 1. one agent working alone, 2. five persistent peers collaborating through a shared Git repository, and 3. a lead agent delegating work to asynchronous subagents. The harness ran on Hugging Face jobs with inference through Reflection’s platform API.
For the tasks, we used ProgramBench: agents must recreate a program from its compiled executable and documentation, without seeing its source code or the evaluator’s tests. Each setup had the same 8M API-token ceiling and two-hour solver limit per task, shared across its agents. We saved implementation snapshots and evaluated them against fixed hidden-test suites from the ProgramBench-Tests dataset.
Our score-versus-latency plot shows the average fraction of tests passed. The time axis uses fixed reference rates for model tokens plus measured tool time, rather than elapsed wall time. We initially ran five tasks. The current figure shows a post-hoc subset of jq, xsv, FIGlet, and hexyl; ripgrep was excluded across all three setups because grading its saved artifacts was too slow. The published results retain all 15 original episodes.



You can inspect the runs in the Trackio dashboard, explore the published result data, and reuse the study harness.




Hey Beam, finetune a decision model for my code base!


Decision models are all the rage at the moment because they’re super fast and practical for many use cases. We started with Beam in Pi after Beam’s quota ran out to train and evaluate a custom decision model for developer incident triage.
We wanted to see whether a coding agent could turn an incident-triage policy into a small, fast decision model. The task was to read a developer incident and choose the responsible team, its severity, and whether someone should be pinged immediately. Using Unsloth, we fine-tuned Qwen3.5-0.8B to score these choices directly.
First, the workflow built a synthetic dataset containing 2.3k incidents split by incident cluster for training, calibration, and testing. We trained a LoRA adapter and decision head for three epochs, with a 4-bit backbone, on one H100 80GB on the Science Slurm cluster.
For a baseline, we prompted the unadapted model with the full triage policy and ticket, without examples, and asked it to generate the three decisions as JSON. On the same 320 synthetic test tickets, the fine-tuned decision model got all three answers correct on 76.25%, versus 4.69% for prompted zero-shot. Mean ticket latency fell from 1,218.06 ms to 102.58 ms, an 11.9× speedup.
If you want to try out this experiment for yourself, check out the artifact bucket which contains the data, code, checkpoints and results.




Wrapping Up


Beam is a 501B open model that you can run on your own hardware and change. Start with the BF16 checkpoint, or try one of the quants FP8, NVFP4. If you build something with Beam, share it in the discussions tab.

summaries.en: Beam is a 501B-parameter open-source MoEs model (23B active per token) released by Reflection under Apache 2.0, supporting text input with a 1M token context window. Designed for coding and agentic use cases, it allows teams to own, customize, and scale the model on their infrastructure. Beam includes a Rust-based harness, supports BF16, FP8, and NVFP4 formats, and features reasoning across turns and tool calling. It integrates with transformers, SGLang, and vLLM, offering inference, SFT, and RL capabilities. Reflection is offering $10,000 Hub credits for projects using Beam.

items.title: Apertus 1.5 Release Notes
items.content:
Our latest release, Apertus 1.5, extends the 8B and 70B Apertus 1.0 models with image/audio understanding, an optional thinking mode, a four times longer context window, improved instruction-following, and better tool use. The updated 8B and 70B model weights were released to Hugging Face on July 24, 2026 under an Apache 2.0 license. Further details are now available from the project Technical Report, and summarized here.

Apertus 1.5 is a continued pretraining of the first generation model: adding 4 trillion tokens of text and multimodal training data to the 8B model and 2 trillion tokens to the 70B model, for a total of 19T and 17T, respectively. As with every Apertus release, the models are fully open: open weights, open data, open values, and full training details.

Key Enhancements

  • Native Multimodal Understanding: Apertus 1.5 accepts images and audio alongside text, bringing documents, diagrams, and photos into the conversation. The models can also process spoken language, though this remains experimental.
  • Thinking Mode: The models can be switched into a thinking mode to reason about the input before answering, which improves performance on reasoning problems.
  • Long Context: The context window grows to 262,144 tokens, a 4x increase over Apertus 1.0.
  • Improved Instruction-Following: Better instruction adherence than Apertus 1.0 gives more predictable and accurate responses.
  • Improved Tool Use: The models are trained for better tool integration, allowing more effective use of external tools and APIs.
  • Open Values: Stronger adherence to the Apertus Charter, which brings transparency to the model’s values and principles.

Training Process

The full Apertus 1.5 training pipeline

Multimodality Through the Tokenizer

We introduce multimodality in v1.5 models in an early-fusion manner, where images and audio enter Apertus as discrete tokens in the same sequence with text tokens, instead of using a separate vision encoder. Images are tokenized with the Emu3.5 tokenizer (a 512×512 image becomes 1,024 tokens) and audio with WavTokenizer (40 tokens per second). We only extend the vocabulary, so the architecture stays unchanged and training runs at text-only speed. The models understand images and audio but generate only text.

Pre-Training

Starting from Apertus 1.0, we continue pretraining in four stages:

  1. Unpaired: text plus standalone images and audio, so the model learns the new modalities.
  2. Paired: image–caption and audio–transcript pairs, so it aligns them with language.
  3. Cooldown: higher-quality data with more math and code.
  4. Long context: the window grows step by step from 8k to 262k tokens.

Overall, more than half of the training tokens are text-only, which preserves the language abilities of Apertus 1.0. The text data is refreshed with sources such as FineWeb2-HQ+, FinePDFs, and Nemotron-CC. All new data, multimodal included, meets the same bar as before: publicly available, permissively licensed, and with robots.txt opt-outs respected retroactively. Every source is listed in apertus-data-transparency.

Post-Training

Post-training runs in five stages: SFT → long-context SFT → RL → DPO → charter alignment (SDPO).

  1. SFT on 3.7M text samples plus image and speech data. Reasoning traces are added only to prompts the model can't already solve without them. Tool-use data is restricted to execution-verified trajectories. We release the text SFT mix we used on Hugging Face.
  2. Long-context SFT at the full 262k window restores the long-context ability that short-context SFT erodes.
  3. RL with verifiable rewards (RLVR) on about 350k math, code, instruction-following, multilingual, and vision prompts, mixing thinking on and off.
  4. DPO with judge-scored preference pairs improves chat quality, tool use, and safety. We release the preference pool and training pairs.
  5. SDPO aligns the model with the Apertus Charter through judge feedback and self-distillation.

Evaluation Results

Alongside the extended model capabilities, we also significantly expanded the scope of evaluations. Beyond the existing text-based evaluations used for Apertus 1.0, we added multimodal evaluations (image & audio), and thinking-mode evaluations.

The multimodal evaluations are done through MLLM-eval-suite pipeline, merging two major multimodal evaluation frameworks lmms-eval and VLMEvalKit. We also added a series of text-based benchmarks, as well as extended benchmarking for translation and multilingual capabilities, safety, and tool use. These can be found in our post-training evaluation repository, based on lm-evaluation-harness fork.

While still trailing frontier open-weight models, the new release has also significantly improved performance in coding and instruction following capabilities with Apertus 1.5 8B outperforming similarly sized open-weight models on IF and multilingual tasks. Thinking further improves performance on challenging reasoning-heavy benchmarks like AIME. The multimodal performance of the model is closer to Gemma 4 12B and other current open-weight models. Apertus 1.5 multimodal performance is competitive in spatial understanding among open-weight models and document/chart understanding among open-source models.

We also thank our collaborators and external evaluators for their help with efficient benchmarking of Apertus capabilities. In particular, Apertus 1.5 shows strong performance on Swiss Legal tasks, being on par with leading open-weight models (blog, code). Additionally, on Last Translation Benchmark, Apertus 1.5 8B presents machine translation capabilities which match GPT-OSS-20B and outperform models like Claude Haiku 4.5 or Google Translate (leaderboard, paper).

Evaluation Cards: Apertus ❤️ EvalEval

Apertus collaborates with the EvalEval Coalition to ensure fully transparent and reproducible benchmarking. We publish the Apertus 1.5 results in the Every Eval Ever (EEE) schema, a shared format that records not only scores, but also who ran the evaluation, how the model was accessed, the generation settings, and how each metric should be interpreted: details that are routinely missing from leaderboards and that often explain why similar-looking scores differ.

The results are shown in the Eval Card below, which combines the run data with benchmark and model metadata into one interpretable record, and are also available through Hugging Face Community Evals. This is the same infrastructure the UK AI Security Institute uses to publish its evaluations openly. Since our text evaluations run on our public fork of lm-evaluation-harness, which EEE supports with a dedicated converter, anyone can rerun them and compare their numbers against ours under identical settings.

Structured evaluation reporting also matters beyond research. EvalEval has mapped Evaluation Cards to AI governance requirements, including Article 55 of the EU AI Act and the GPAI Code of Practice, and found that the EEE schema can represent 56 of the 60 evaluation-reporting elements these frameworks call for. This fits how we already release Apertus: alongside the models, we publish a Public Summary of Training Content and, voluntarily, a Code of Practice document. Machine-readable evaluation records are a natural next step: making it easier for regulators, deployers, and researchers to find, interpret, and compare the evidence behind a model.

We are committed to promoting reproducible and transparent evaluation through Eval Cards and the EEE schema, and encourage other model developers to report their results in the same way, so that scores can be compared across models and organizations.

Apertus 1.5 Reproducibility

All recipes, ablations, and data mixtures are documented in the Technical Report. We aim to popularize open model development by making the v1.5 training process public and accessible. Intermediate checkpoints are hosted in our Apertus 1.5 Hugging Face collection, including the base weights, SFT, RLVR and DPO, as well as our curated training data mixes/custom datasets in Apertus 1.5 datasets collection. Sharing them allows researchers to investigate how each stage changes the model behavior.

The report covers numerous ablations on the effect of post-training data in different stages, where we observed that the multimodal data mixed in together with text data during SFT helps improve across all modalities. We also find that the benefits of multimodal reasoning traces survive the subsequent text-only reinforcement learning: starting from an SFT checkpoint trained with multimodal traces, RL improves mathematics more than when starting from a text-only checkpoint, and the advantage on reasoning tasks persists throughout training.

Models 8B 70B
Pre-training (long-context base) Apertus-v1.5-8B-base Apertus-v1.5-70B-base
Supervised finetuning (SFT) Apertus-v1.5-8B-SFT Apertus-v1.5-70B-SFT
Reinforcement learning (RLVR) Apertus-v1.5-8B-RL Apertus-v1.5-70B-RL
Preference alignment (DPO) Apertus-v1.5-8B-DPO Apertus-v1.5-70B (final)
Charter alignment (SDPO) Apertus-v1.5-8B (final) –
Stage Data Code / recipe
Pre-training: Stages 1–2 (unpaired, paired) All sources with versions and licenses in apertus-data-transparency; vision and audio processing recipes in multimodal-data Megatron-LM, launch scripts in pretrain-code, apertus-omni-tokenizer, benchmark-image-tokenizer, benchmark-audio-tokenizer (incl. interleaved speech–text builder)
Pre-training: Stage 3 (cooldown) apertus-data-transparency; curated image datasets NASA, Our World in Data, Smithsonian, swisstopo Megatron-LM, launch scripts in pretrain-code
Long-context extension apertus-data-transparency; synthetic long-context tasks in LongContextQA Megatron-LM, launch scripts in pretrain-code
SFT Apertus-v1.5-SFT-mix (multimodal SFT mix listed in the report) posttraining-data, Megatron-LM (SFT launch scripts)
Long-context SFT Subsets of the SFT mix (listed in the report), plus LongContextQA tasks Megatron-LM
RL (RLVR) Mixture listed in the report verl, verl-recipe
DPO Apertus-v1.5-Preference-Pool (annotated completions), Apertus-v1.5-Preference-Data (pairs) posttraining, verl
SDPO (charter alignment, 8B only) gretelai/gretel-safety-alignment-en-v1 self-distillation

Model Availability

Proton Lumo and Infomaniak Euria are two widely used apps that have recently integrated Apertus 1.5. These deployments are linked in the Community Showcase among others - see this discussion thread for a preview.

Access to Apertus 1.5 in the form of an API for developers has been announced by a range of providers, including Swisscom, Infomaniak, Phoeniqs, and other companies listed in our General Availability guide. The report also provides details on how we work with external evaluators to test and prepare the models.

Technical instructions for running the models are in the model cards of the Apertus releases on Hugging Face and in our Quickstart guide.

How to Get Involved

Thank you for reading this blog post and being part of our community! We just celebrated five million downloads in our Hugging Face analytics 🤗 and are not slowing down. At the recent AI+X Summit in Zurich, our team announced the roadmap for Apertus 2.0: sparse/MoE architecture, ~600B total parameters, extended training schedule, with agents, mathematics and coding as priorities.

In summary: we invite you to read our report, download the models, explore the intermediate checkpoints, finetune the weights, and reproduce our evaluations. Questions that are not already covered in our publications or website FAQ are always welcome, and we would also love to hear which topics would be most useful to the community for future deep dives.

If you build with or use Apertus, please fill out the Showcase form, and reach out through the options on our Contact page. We are looking forward to highlighting more work, learning what you are building, and hearing how Apertus can be improved!

Citation

Project Apertus, et al. “Apertus 1.5: From Open Text Models to Open Multimodal Reasoners.” arXiv:2610.15542. Preprint, arXiv, October 11, 2026. https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2610.15542.

Our latest release, Apertus 1.5, extends the 8B and 70B Apertus 1.0 models with image/audio understanding, an optional thinking mode, a four times longer context window, improved instruction-following, and better tool use. The updated 8B and 70B model weights were released to Hugging Face on July 24, 2026 under an Apache 2.0 license. Further details are now available from the project Technical Report, and summarized here. 
Apertus 1.5 is a continued pretraining of the first generation model: adding 4 trillion tokens of text and multimodal training data to the 8B model and 2 trillion tokens to the 70B model, for a total of 19T and 17T, respectively.  As with every Apertus release, the models are fully open: open weights, open data, open values, and full training details.




Key Enhancements



Native Multimodal Understanding: Apertus 1.5 accepts images and audio alongside text, bringing documents, diagrams, and photos into the conversation. The models can also process spoken language, though this remains experimental.
Thinking Mode: The models can be switched into a thinking mode to reason about the input before answering, which improves performance on reasoning problems.
Long Context: The context window grows to 262,144 tokens, a 4x increase over Apertus 1.0.
Improved Instruction-Following: Better instruction adherence than Apertus 1.0 gives more predictable and accurate responses.
Improved Tool Use: The models are trained for better tool integration, allowing more effective use of external tools and APIs.
Open Values: Stronger adherence to the Apertus Charter, which brings transparency to the model’s values and principles.




Training Process



The full Apertus 1.5 training pipeline




Multimodality Through the Tokenizer


We introduce multimodality in v1.5 models in an early-fusion manner, where images and audio enter Apertus as discrete tokens in the same sequence with text tokens, instead of using a separate vision encoder. Images are tokenized with the Emu3.5 tokenizer (a 512×512 image becomes 1,024 tokens) and audio with WavTokenizer (40 tokens per second). We only extend the vocabulary, so the architecture stays unchanged and training runs at text-only speed. The models understand images and audio but generate only text.





Pre-Training


Starting from Apertus 1.0, we continue pretraining in four stages:
Unpaired: text plus standalone images and audio, so the model learns the new modalities.
Paired: image–caption and audio–transcript pairs, so it aligns them with language.
Cooldown: higher-quality data with more math and code.
Long context: the window grows step by step from 8k to 262k tokens.
Overall, more than half of the training tokens are text-only, which preserves the language abilities of Apertus 1.0. The text data is refreshed with sources such as FineWeb2-HQ+, FinePDFs, and Nemotron-CC. All new data, multimodal included, meets the same bar as before: publicly available, permissively licensed, and with robots.txt opt-outs respected retroactively. Every source is listed in apertus-data-transparency.




Post-Training


Post-training runs in five stages: SFT → long-context SFT → RL → DPO → charter alignment (SDPO).
SFT on 3.7M text samples plus image and speech data. Reasoning traces are added only to prompts the model can't already solve without them. Tool-use data is restricted to execution-verified trajectories. We release the text SFT mix we used on Hugging Face.
Long-context SFT at the full 262k window restores the long-context ability that short-context SFT erodes.
RL with verifiable rewards (RLVR) on about 350k math, code, instruction-following, multilingual, and vision prompts, mixing thinking on and off. 
DPO with judge-scored preference pairs improves chat quality, tool use, and safety. We release the preference pool and training pairs.
SDPO aligns the model with the Apertus Charter through judge feedback and self-distillation.




Evaluation Results


Alongside the extended model capabilities, we also significantly expanded the scope of evaluations. Beyond the existing text-based evaluations used for Apertus 1.0, we added multimodal evaluations (image & audio), and thinking-mode evaluations. 

The multimodal evaluations are done through MLLM-eval-suite pipeline, merging two major multimodal evaluation frameworks lmms-eval and VLMEvalKit. We also added a series of text-based benchmarks, as well as extended benchmarking for translation and multilingual capabilities, safety, and tool use. These can be found in our post-training evaluation repository, based on lm-evaluation-harness fork. 

While still trailing frontier open-weight models, the new release has also significantly improved performance in coding and instruction following capabilities with Apertus 1.5 8B outperforming similarly sized open-weight models on IF and multilingual tasks. Thinking further improves performance on challenging reasoning-heavy benchmarks like AIME. The multimodal performance of the model is closer to Gemma 4 12B and other current open-weight models. Apertus 1.5 multimodal performance is competitive in spatial understanding among open-weight models and document/chart understanding among open-source models. 
 We also thank our collaborators and external evaluators for their help with efficient benchmarking of Apertus capabilities. In particular, Apertus 1.5 shows strong performance on Swiss Legal tasks, being on par with leading open-weight models (blog, code). Additionally, on Last Translation Benchmark, Apertus 1.5 8B presents machine translation capabilities which match GPT-OSS-20B and outperform models like Claude Haiku 4.5 or Google Translate (leaderboard, paper).




Evaluation Cards: Apertus ❤️ EvalEval


Apertus collaborates with the EvalEval Coalition to ensure fully transparent and reproducible benchmarking. We publish the Apertus 1.5 results in the Every Eval Ever (EEE) schema, a shared format that records not only scores, but also who ran the evaluation, how the model was accessed, the generation settings, and how each metric should be interpreted: details that are routinely missing from leaderboards and that often explain why similar-looking scores differ. 
The results are shown in the Eval Card below, which combines the run data with benchmark and model metadata into one interpretable record, and are also available through Hugging Face Community Evals. This is the same infrastructure the UK AI Security Institute uses to publish its evaluations openly. Since our text evaluations run on our public fork of lm-evaluation-harness, which EEE supports with a dedicated converter, anyone can rerun them and compare their numbers against ours under identical settings. 
Structured evaluation reporting also matters beyond research. EvalEval has mapped Evaluation Cards to AI governance requirements, including Article 55 of the EU AI Act and the GPAI Code of Practice, and found that the EEE schema can represent 56 of the 60 evaluation-reporting elements these frameworks call for. This fits how we already release Apertus: alongside the models, we publish a Public Summary of Training Content and, voluntarily, a Code of Practice document. Machine-readable evaluation records are a natural next step: making it easier for regulators, deployers, and researchers to find, interpret, and compare the evidence behind a model. 


We are committed to promoting reproducible and transparent evaluation through Eval Cards and the EEE schema, and encourage other model developers to report their results in the same way, so that scores can be compared across models and organizations.




Apertus 1.5 Reproducibility


All recipes, ablations, and data mixtures are documented in the Technical Report. We aim to popularize open model development by making the v1.5 training process public and accessible. Intermediate checkpoints are hosted in our Apertus 1.5 Hugging Face collection, including the base weights, SFT, RLVR and DPO, as well as our curated training data mixes/custom datasets in Apertus 1.5 datasets collection. Sharing them allows researchers to investigate how each stage changes the model behavior.
The report covers numerous ablations on the effect of post-training data in different stages, where we observed that the multimodal data mixed in together with text data during SFT helps improve across all modalities. We also find that the benefits of multimodal reasoning traces survive the subsequent text-only reinforcement learning: starting from an SFT checkpoint trained with multimodal traces, RL improves mathematics more than when starting from a text-only checkpoint, and the advantage on reasoning tasks persists throughout training.

Model Availability


Proton Lumo and Infomaniak Euria are two widely used apps that have recently integrated Apertus 1.5. These deployments are linked in the Community Showcase among others - see this discussion thread for a preview. 
Access to Apertus 1.5 in the form of an API for developers has been announced by a range of providers, including Swisscom, Infomaniak, Phoeniqs, and other companies listed in our General Availability guide. The report also provides details on how we work with external evaluators to test and prepare the models.
Technical instructions for running the models are in the model cards of the Apertus releases on Hugging Face and in our Quickstart guide.




How to Get Involved


Thank you for reading this blog post and being part of our community! We just celebrated five million downloads in our Hugging Face analytics 🤗 and are not slowing down. At the recent AI+X Summit in Zurich, our team announced the roadmap for Apertus 2.0: sparse/MoE architecture, ~600B total parameters, extended training schedule, with agents, mathematics and coding as priorities.
In summary: we invite you to read our report, download the models, explore the intermediate checkpoints, finetune the weights, and reproduce our evaluations. Questions that are not already covered in our publications or website FAQ are always welcome, and we would also love to hear which topics would be most useful to the community for future deep dives.
If you build with or use Apertus, please fill out the Showcase form, and reach out through the options on our Contact page. We are looking forward to highlighting more work, learning what you are building, and hearing how Apertus can be improved!

summaries.zh: Apertus 1.5版本扩展了8B和70B模型的图像/音频理解能力，新增可选思考模式，将上下文窗口延长四倍，并提升了指令遵循和工具使用效果。模型在Hugging Face上发布，采用Apache 2.0许可。通过添加4万亿和2万亿token的文本及多模态数据，模型总规模达19万亿和17万亿。版本保持完全开放，包括权重、数据和训练细节。主要改进包括：原生多模态理解、思考模式、长上下文、改进指令遵循和工具使用。训练过程分为四个阶段，后训练包含五阶段优化。评估范围扩展至多模态和思考模式，Apertus 1.5在编码和指令遵循任务上表现显著提升。
summaries.en: Apertus 1.5 extends the 8B and 70B models with image/audio understanding, a thinking mode, a four times longer context window (262,144 tokens), improved instruction-following, and better tool use. The models were pretrained with 4 trillion tokens (8B) and 2 trillion tokens (70B) of text and multimodal data, trained under an Apache 2.0 license and released on Hugging Face. Key features include multimodal input, reasoning mode, enhanced context handling, and improved tool integration. The training process includes unpaired, paired, cooldown, and long-context stages, followed by SFT, RL, DPO, and SDPO phases. Evaluations expanded to include multimodal and reasoning tasks, showing improved performance in coding and instruction following. Models remain fully open-source.
